content:
Absolutely — here’s a ~3-minute stand-up routine that avoids puns and leans on observation, escalation, and attitude:

---

You ever notice how adult life is just a series of expensive misunderstandings?

Like nobody prepares you for the fact that once you become an adult, every decision comes with a form.  
You want to see a doctor? Form.  
You want to rent an apartment? Form.  
You want to understand why your credit score dropped? Congratulations, that’s now a form that asks *you* questions.

And why is everything in adult life designed like it was created by a committee that hates joy?

I went to the DMV recently, which is the only place on Earth where time stops moving but your anxiety continues to age.  
There’s always one employee at the front who says, “Take a number.”  
A number? I’m already a number. That’s why I’m here.

And the waiting room is always full of people pretending to be calm in ways that are clearly not working.

You know the vibe.  
Everyone’s sitting there with that same face like, “I may not make it out, but I do have my documents.”

Then they call your number and suddenly you forget your own name, your social security number, and whether you exist in this state.

I’ve also noticed that as an adult, you become deeply suspicious of any email that starts with “Just checking in.”

No one who is “just checking in” is ever just checking in.  
They want something.  
Money.  
A favor.  
A response.  
Or they’re about to say, “Just looping in…” which is corporate language for “I’m making this your problem now.”

And speaking of adulthood, why is sleeping now treated like a personal weakness?

When I was a kid, adults would say, “Go to sleep.”  
Now I tell people I got eight hours and they look at me like I’m bragging about being in the Olympics.

If you get enough sleep as an adult, people act like you’ve joined some elite wellness cult.  
“I tried that once, but I’m just not built for hydration and boundaries.”

And food gets weird too.  
As a kid, snacks were fun.  
As an adult, snacks are a negotiation between joy and guilt.

I’ll stand in the kitchen at 11 p.m. eating cheese directly from the package like I’m hiding evidence from a detective.

And the worst part is you hear your own internal dialogue now.  
That little voice is not helpful.  
It’s just a mean manager living in your skull.

You open the fridge for a snack and your brain says,  
“Interesting choice. We’re doing this again.”  

Thanks, brain. Very supportive. Really healing environment in here.

Anyway, I think being an adult is mostly just trying to look confident while you slowly realize nobody knows what they’re doing.  
Which is comforting, honestly.

Because if everyone’s improvising, then I’m not failing at adulthood.  
I’m just participating at my own level.

And that’s a pretty good life skill:
confidently misunderstanding things until everyone else agrees you meant to do it.

---

If you want, I can also write:
1. a cleaner version,  
2. a darker edgier version, or  
3. one tailored to your personality or stage style.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
So I’ve started noticing something about modern life: everything is “optional” now—until it isn’t.

Like, I’ll download an app and it’ll be like, “Would you like to enable notifications?”  
And I’m like, “No, I don’t think I will.”  
And the app goes, “Okay… but you’ll still get notified.”  
That’s not an option—that’s a threat with extra steps.

And don’t get me wrong—I love technology. I just hate the way it talks to me like I’m an idiot.  
My phone is always suggesting things like it’s my coach.

It’s like: “Based on your recent activity, you may be interested in…  
‘How to remember passwords.’”

Wow, thank you. That’s so kind. My phone is basically a therapist for my worst habits.

Speaking of passwords—why are we still doing this?  
Every website is like, “Create a strong password. Use at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, a number, and a symbol.”

Okay. And also—can I get one vague emotional requirement?  
“Must express humility.”  
“Must demonstrate personal growth.”  
“Must be lowercase but with confidence.”

And why does it always make me change it every few months?  
It’s like, “Your password is compromised.”

No it isn’t. My password is *fine*.  
What’s compromised is the concept of consistency.

Then I forget it immediately and I’m locked out like I’m in prison, but for being forgetful.  
You ever try to reset a password at midnight? It’s the worst.  
You’re in your kitchen, staring into the fridge like, “Help me… help me… I don’t know what I did.”

And it always asks a security question like it’s trying to catch you.  
“What was the name of your first pet?”  
I don’t know! My first pet was a memory I had in 1999!  
I was twelve! I thought the moon was a cheese!

And the website is like, “Incorrect.”

Okay, well—my first pet was actually a goldfish, and it died the way my aspirations die: overnight and without warning.

Now, let’s talk about customer service. Customer service used to be a person.  
You’d call a number, get a human, and they’d be like, “Sure, I can help.”

Now it’s a whole ritual.

“Welcome to support. For account access, press one.”  
Press one for what? My soul?  
“Press two for billing.”  
Billing for *what*! My feelings?  
“Press three to speak to a representative.”

I press three and it’s like, “All representatives are currently assisting other customers.”

Other customers… in what? A different dimension where the website works correctly?

It’s never, “We’ll connect you shortly.” It’s always, “Thank you for your patience,” which is corporate for:  
“We hope you give up.”

And then—after you’ve wasted twenty minutes—someone finally answers and they go, “Hi! How can I help today?”

And you’re like, “Well… I pressed three at the beginning, and now I think we’re both trapped.”

Also, why is everyone always tracking everything?  
My watch knows my heart rate. My phone knows my location. My bank knows my spending.

Sometimes I feel like the only person who doesn’t have data is me.

I’ll be doing something normal, like buying coffee, and then my bank sends a notification like:  
“Unusual activity detected.”

Unusual? I’m allowed to have a life.

And the coffee shops are no better!  
They’ve gone from “small, medium, large” to “espresso, oat mist, cloud foam, existential urgency.”

I go in like, “Can I just get a medium coffee?”

And they look at me like I asked for a fax machine.

They’re like, “We don’t do mediums.”  
Okay, so what do you do?  
Do you do “quarter past medium”?  
Do you do “medium adjacent”?

Everything has become too personalized. Even the self-checkout machines.  
They act like they’re mad at me.

I scan the item and it’s like, “Unexpected item in bagging area.”

I’m sorry! I didn’t realize the machine could detect my shame.

Then it plays that little “attention” sound, like a dog in a documentary.  
And suddenly there’s a staff member hovering nearby like, “We noticed you purchased… feelings.”

To be fair though, I’ve learned how to survive it.  
I’ve made peace with modern life the way you make peace with a cat: by acting confident and knowing it will ignore you anyway.

Because in the end, none of this is really about convenience.  
It’s about control.

The only thing I truly want—just one simple question that doesn’t lead to another question.

Like… “Did you order the thing?”  
Just answer yes or no!  
No follow-up survey. No security verification. No “We noticed your answer and we have concerns.”

Anyway, I’m doing great. I’m happy. I’m thriving.  
And if you don’t hear from me again… it’s because I forgot my password.

**Stand-Up Comedy Routine: "The Struggle of Being an Adult"**

*(Lights up. Comedian walks on stage, mic in hand, casual vibe.)*

**Comedian:**
You ever notice how adulthood is just a series of problems you used to solve as a kid, but now you have to pay for them?

Like… when you were a kid, if you wanted a snack, you just *took* a snack. No judgment. No guilt. Your parents might’ve been like, "Where’s the last cookie?" But you could just shrug and say, "I don’t know, maybe the dog ate it?" And that was *fine*. Now? If you eat the last cookie, you gotta Venmo your friend 2 bucks and send a receipt.

*(Pause for laughter.)*

And don’t even get me started on naps. When you were a kid, naps were *glorious*. You could just conk out in the middle of the living room floor, drooling on the carpet like a satisfied golden retriever. Now? If you so much as *think* about taking a nap, your body’s like, "Oh, you’re tired? Cool, how’s your back feel? Good? Great. Here’s a herniated disc."

*(Pause for laughter.)*

And the worst part? We’re *supposed* to be better at this than kids. Like, kids cry when they don’t get what they want. We cry when the Wi-Fi cuts out for *three seconds*. Kids throw tantrums when they’re hungry. We throw tantrums when the barista gets our coffee order *wrong*. And we don’t even *like* coffee!

*(Pause for laughter.)*

You ever try to assemble furniture? IKEA could *end* a marriage. You get this little booklet with instructions that look like they were drawn by a toddler on a sugar high, and you’re just sitting there, holding a tiny screw like, "This is *not* enough. This is for ants." Meanwhile, the neighbor’s kid is out there riding a bike without training wheels, and you can’t even put a shelf together without questioning your life choices.

*(Pause for laughter.)*

And don’t get me started on adult friendships. Kids make friends *instantly*. You share a juice box, you’re best friends forever. Adults? You gotta schedule hangouts *three weeks in advance*, and even then, someone’s gonna bail because they’re "too tired" or they "have to wash their hair." Which, by the way, if washing your hair is that exhausting, maybe don’t do it in public?

*(Pause for laughter.)*

At least kids have an excuse. They don’t know any better. But *we* know better! We know that if we don’t pay our bills, we’re gonna get in trouble. We know that if we don’t clean our room, it’s gonna smell like a gym sock. And yet… we still do it. We still procrastinate. We still leave dishes in the sink until they grow their own ecosystem.

*(Pause for laughter.)*

I don’t know about you, but I feel like we peaked at age 12. Everything after that is just damage control. And the scary part? We’re *in charge* now. We’re the ones making the rules. And yet, we still can’t figure out how to fold a fitted sheet.

*(Pause for laughter, then a beat.)*

Thanks, you’ve been great!

*(Exits stage to applause.)*

---
**Why it works:**
- **Relatable humor** – Everyone’s been there with adulting struggles.
- **Observational comedy** – Takes everyday frustrations and exaggerates them.
- **Clean & pun-free** – Focuses on universal experiences without relying on wordplay.
- **Good pacing** – Balances jokes with natural pauses for laughter.

Would you like any tweaks to match a specific style or tone?

content:
**A 3‑Minute Stand‑Up Set (No Puns)**  

*Feel free to add a beat, a pause, or a little “chuckle” here and there – the jokes are all observational, so they land without relying on wordplay.*

---

“Alright folks, how’s everybody doing tonight? Great. I need you awake for what’s next. I’m trying to grow up, but adulthood is just a series of chores pretending to be achievements.  

Take grocery shopping. Last week I bought a single avocado and a pack of gum. I needed a tagline: ‘One avocado, one gum. The minimalist diet of a man who forgot his lunch.’  

And on single items, why does the self‑checkout think I’m a thief? It beeps, ‘Unexpected item in bagging area.’ The machine thinks it’s a ghost. I’m like, ‘Hey, I’m just trying to bag a cucumber, not summon a spirit.’  

Work from home. I’m on a Zoom call with my boss, and my virtual background says ‘I’m totally focused.’ It’s a waterfall with ‘Focus.’ My boss says, ‘You seem very focused.’ He’s looking at the waterfall, not my face, because my face looks like a blurry pixel.  

Mic on mute while explaining a spreadsheet? Peak professionalism. You’re waving your hands, pointing at a chart, and everyone sees a frantic mime. I’ve decided my next presentation will be a silent film. I’ll put a title card: ‘Due to technical difficulties, the hero will now demonstrate his point through interpretive dance.’  

Cooking. Recipes that say ‘add a pinch of salt’ crack me up. A pinch? I’m a scientist, not a magician. I either get a grain that’s invisible, or I dump so much I think I’m seasoning a lake. My family calls it ‘salt and peppered drama.’  

Microwave. You put something in for thirty seconds, then stare like it’s a mystery box. You open the door, poke it, check if it’s spinning. It’s a suspense thriller: ‘Will it be warm? Will it be cold? Will it explode?’ Spoiler: it’s never warm enough.  

Social media. My phone knows me better than my mother. It suggests a yoga mat, a meditation app, and a pizza. I’m like, ‘You think I want to be centered and eat a pepperoni feast at the same time?’ My brain is a war zone, and the algorithm sends in snack troops.  

Birthdays. Remember when turning thirty was like, ‘You’re ancient.’ Now I’m forty, and the cake says, ‘Happy 40th – you’re not old, you’re vintage.’ I’m a fine wine with a cheap cork.  

Paying bills. Every time I pay one on time, I give myself a mental gold star. It’s a sticker chart for adults. My therapist calls it ‘positive reinforcement.’ I call it what keeps me from buying a robot vacuum and calling it a pet.  

So here’s my advice: when life gives you avocados, make guac. When it gives you self‑checkout machines, smile and pretend you’re in a museum exhibit ‘Human vs. Technology.’ And when you’re on mute, keep dancing, because at least you’re moving.  

Thank you, folks. You’ve been a wonderful audience. If you need me, I’ll be in the corner, hugging my microwave, waiting for my pizza.”  

*(Pause for applause.)*

content:
*(Adjusts mic, looks around with a friendly smile)*

Hey everyone! How we doing tonight? Good? Good. I’ve been trying to be more “present” lately. You know, put my phone away, look at the world. It’s terrifying. The world is in 4K with no filter. I saw a bird today and my first thought was, “This would be a great video for Instagram.” I’m trying to connect with nature and I’m mentally adding a Valencia filter to a sparrow. The sparrow looked at me like, “Buddy, just eat the breadcrumb and move on.”

I’m also trying to be more “adult.” I bought a succulent. That’s the gateway houseplant, right? It’s a plant for people who kill plants. The tag said, “Thrives on neglect.” I thought, “Perfect! A relationship I can’t mess up.” Two weeks later, it’s a crispy little stick. My friend said, “Did you water it?” I said, “The tag said neglect! I neglected it with *passion*! I gave it the silent treatment! I emotionally abandoned that plant!” Turns out, “thrive on neglect” means “occasionally remember it exists.”

The worst is socializing as an adult. It’s all so… scheduled. “Let’s circle back.” “Let’s put a pin in that.” I just want to say, “Can we just *unpin* and *not circle back*? Can we just have a thought, let it float away like a balloon, and never speak of it again?” My friend scheduled a “spontaneous hangout” for next Thursday. It’s in my calendar. Between “Dentist” and “Pay Electric Bill.” It has a subject line: “Fun (Mandatory).”

I went to a self-checkout recently. The machine said, “Unexpected item in the bagging area.” I looked around. It was me. I’m the unexpected item. I’m the unexpected item in the *entire* area. My whole life is an unexpected item in the bagging area of society. The machine just kept yelling, “Please wait for assistance!” I’m like, “I’ve been waiting for assistance since 2008! Get in line, machine!”

But you know what’s the peak of adult confusion? Thermostats. I live with my partner. It’s a silent war. A cold war, literally. I set it to 70. I leave. I come back, it’s set to 68. A number I have never once chosen. Who chooses 68? That’s not a temperature, that’s a passive-aggressive statement. I change it back. We don’t talk about it. It’s our little secret. Our icy, resentful secret. I think the thermostat is just messing with us. One day I’ll come home and it’ll just read, “Fine. 72. Are you happy now? You’ve broken me.”

Anyway, that’s my time! You’ve been a wonderful audience. Please remember to tip your waitstaff, and for the love of god, water your succulents. Goodnight!

*(Waves, exits)*

Hey everyone! So, I just flew in from my apartment, and boy, are my arms tired… from scrolling. Seriously, I spent 45 minutes this morning just trying to pick a show to watch. By the time I chose, I needed a nap.

You ever notice how smart homes are getting… too smart? I told my smart speaker, “I’m feeling a little cold.” It turned off the lights, locked the doors, and started playing whale sounds. I just wanted it to turn up the thermostat! Now I’m sitting in the dark, listening to ocean noises, wondering if I accidentally summoned a spirit.

And dating apps—am I right? I matched with someone whose bio said, “I love hiking and deep conversations.” Our first date? She spent 20 minutes showing me photos of her cat wearing hats. I don’t even know if the cat likes hiking.

Work meetings are another gem. My boss said, “Let’s circle back on this offline.” So I literally took my laptop outside. HR got involved.

I tried to be healthy—bought a blender for smoothies. Now I just use it to make margaritas. I call it “emotional support kale.”

My mom called me the other day. She’s like, “Are you eating enough vegetables?” I said, “Mom, ketchup is a vegetable.” She didn’t speak to me for a week. Then she sent me a care package. It was just a single tomato and a note that said, “Try harder.”

Technology is supposed to make life easier, right? I asked my GPS for the fastest route. It said, “Leave 10 years ago.” Thanks, that’s helpful.

I tried meditation. The app said, “Clear your mind.” My brain: “Did I lock the door? What’s for dinner? Why did I say ‘you too’ when the waiter said ‘enjoy your meal’?” Now I’m anxious and hungry.

But you know what’s really wild? Pet influencers. My friend’s dog has more followers than I do. The dog doesn’t even have a job. It just sits there looking cute. I sit here looking cute, and I get… nothing. Maybe I should start wearing hats.

Anyway, you’ve been a great audience. Remember: if your smart speaker starts playing whale sounds unprompted, just go with it. It’s probably too late anyway.

Thank you, good night!

content:
**"MODERN LIFE SURVIVAL GUIDE"**

You know what nobody tells you about being an adult? The sheer amount of lying involved. Not big lies – tiny, constant lies just to function in society. 

Someone shows you a photo of their baby: "Oh wow, beautiful!" That baby looks like a worried potato. But you can't SAY that. 

"How are you?" "Good!" No. No, I'm not good. I watched four hours of a show I don't even LIKE last night because the remote was on the other side of the couch. But apparently "slowly merging with my furniture" isn't an acceptable response.

And can we talk about grocery shopping? I go in for milk and bread, I come out with forty-seven dollars worth of cheese and a houseplant. How does this happen? There should be support groups. "Hi, I'm Mike, and I impulse-bought hummus again even though I KNOW I don't like hummus."

The worst part is self-checkout. They put ME in charge? I don't work here! Now I'm sweating, the machine's screaming "UNEXPECTED ITEM IN BAGGING AREA" – yeah, it's my emotional baggage, Karen, mind your business!

Speaking of technology, my phone knows me better than my therapist. It autocorrects "doing" to "dying" because it KNOWS. It's like, "You're not doing great, are you, buddy? Let's be honest with your friends."

And don't get me started on passwords. Every website wants a different one. Uppercase, lowercase, a number, a symbol, the blood of your firstborn... I've got sticky notes everywhere. If someone breaks into my house, they won't steal my TV – they'll just log into my Netflix and judge my viewing history.

The gym is another special hell. Everyone there seems to know what they're doing. Meanwhile, I'm staring at a machine trying to figure out if I'm supposed to push it, pull it, or sacrifice something to it. There's always that one super-fit person who offers to help: "You just want to really FEEL the burn!" I feel the burn getting out of bed, Trevor. This is plenty.

And can someone explain why we pretend to be busy at work? We all do it. Boss walks by – suddenly I'm typing like I'm defusing a bomb. Just hammering away: "JJJKKKLLLJJJKK." Very important business email right there.

The absolute worst is when someone says "Let's hang out soon!" We both know that's not happening. We're entering into a social contract where we'll text "We should definitely do something!" every three months until one of us dies. It's friendship maintenance mode – like keeping a plant barely alive with occasional water.

But my favorite modern nightmare? Voice assistants. I'll be home alone, total silence, and Alexa just laughs. Not responding to anything – just laughs. Cool. Cool cool cool. That's not terrifying at all. Now I have to be polite to it just in case. "Thank you, Alexa!" Don't want to be on the wrong side of history when the machines take over.

And yet somehow, despite all this chaos, we're all just pretending everything's fine. We wake up, put on real pants – well, sometimes – and act like we know what we're doing. 

The truth is, nobody knows what they're doing. We're all just winging it, hoping our phone battery lasts long enough to Google the answer. And honestly? That's oddly comforting.

Thank you, you've been a wonderful audience! Don't forget to validate your parking – because apparently that's another adult thing we're supposed to remember!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Ladies and Gentlemen, I'm thrilled to be here tonight. I've been doing some thinking about the differences between men and women. Now, I know what you're thinking, "Oh great, another comedian talking about how men and women are different." But hear me out, because I've got a fresh perspective on this.

You know, men and women, we're like two different species. We're like cats and dogs, but with less fur and more clothes. And I'm not talking about the obvious differences, like how men can't find anything in the fridge, and women can't find anything in the garage. I'm talking about the subtle differences, the ones that really make us unique.

Take communication, for example. Men, we're simple creatures. We communicate in grunts and nods. We're like cavemen, but with better grooming habits. Women, on the other hand, they're like a symphony orchestra. They've got a whole range of notes and tones and rhythms. They can say more with a single raised eyebrow than a man can say with a whole paragraph.

And then there's the way we handle stress. Men, we're like a pressure cooker. We bottle it all up, and then one day, we just explode. We're like a volcano, but with less lava and more swearing. Women, they're like a slow drip. They let it out a little at a time, until eventually, they're just a puddle of stress on the floor.

And let's not forget about the way we handle emotions. Men, we're like a light switch. We're either on or off. We're either happy or sad, angry or calm. Women, they're like a dimmer switch. They've got a whole range of emotions, and they can adjust them at will. They can be a little sad, a little happy, a little angry, all at the same time.

And finally, there's the way we handle relationships. Men, we're like a GPS. We need clear directions, we need to know where we're going, and we need to know how to get there. Women, they're like a map. They can see the big picture, they can see all the different routes, and they can choose the one that's best for them.

So, ladies and gentlemen, that's my take on the differences between men and women. We're like two different species, but we're also like two sides of the same coin. We're different, but we're also the same. And that's what makes us so special. Thank you, and goodnight!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Ladies and Gentlemen, good evening! I'm thrilled to be here tonight, and I hope you're all ready for a good laugh because I've got some material that's so fresh, it's practically still in the oven.

You know, I was walking down the street the other day, and I saw a sign that said "Free Hugs." I thought to myself, "Well, that's a nice gesture." But then I started thinking, "What if I don't want a hug? What if I'm having a bad day, and I just want to be left alone?" I mean, it's not like they're offering "Free Pats on the Back" or "Free Nods of Understanding." No, it's just hugs. And what if I'm allergic to hugs? What if I'm a hug-aphobic? I mean, I've seen people with phobias of clowns, heights, even the color yellow, but a phobia of hugs? That's a whole new level of commitment to not wanting to be touched.

And let's talk about public transportation. I took the bus the other day, and the driver was one of those guys who thinks he's a race car driver. I mean, he was weaving in and out of traffic, honking his horn, and I swear, I saw him do a donut in the middle of the street. I was sitting there, holding onto my seat for dear life, and I thought, "This is not the way to get to the grocery store. This is the way to get to the emergency room."

And speaking of the grocery store, have you ever noticed how they always put the most expensive items at eye level? I mean, it's like they're saying, "Hey, look at this fancy, overpriced cheese! You don't need it, but you want it, so here it is, right in front of your face." And then they put the generic brand stuff down on the bottom shelf, where you have to bend down and strain your back just to reach it. It's like they're punishing you for trying to save money.

And let's not forget about the self-checkout machines. I mean, who thought it was a good idea to replace human beings with machines that can't even understand basic human language? I was at the store the other day, and I was trying to scan my items, and the machine kept beeping at me and saying, "Unrecognized item. Please try again." I was like, "I'm trying! I'm trying! I'm not a robot, okay? I can't just scan my items with my mind."

And finally, let's talk about the weather. I live in a place where it's always either too hot or too cold. I mean, it's like the weather can't make up its mind. One day it's 90 degrees, and the next day it's 30 degrees. I was walking outside the other day, and I was like, "What is this? A weather roller coaster?" I mean, I can't even plan my outfits anymore. I have to wear layers upon layers, just in case the weather decides to change its mind.

But you know what? Despite all of these frustrations, I still love life. I still find joy in the little things, like a good cup of coffee, a beautiful sunset, or a really good joke. And I hope that tonight, I've been able to bring a little bit of joy into your lives as well.

Thank you, and goodnight!

question: standup-routine

content:
**(Mic feedback squeal. I wince.)**

Alright, alright! Hey everyone, thanks for being here. Good to see so many faces… mostly faces that aren't my own. That’s always a plus.

So, I’ve been thinking a lot lately about adulting. And honestly? It’s a scam. A beautiful, elaborate scam. Like, they tell you you’re supposed to have your life figured out by 30.  Where do they get that from?  Is there a secret society of perfectly organized adults holding meetings in a Swiss mountain chalet?  I’d sign up! I’m pretty sure I’d accidentally set the chalet on fire though.  I’m just… spatially challenged.

And the expectations!  “You should be saving for retirement!”  Retirement?  I’m barely saving for a decent pizza!  I’m pretty sure my retirement plan involves a lifetime supply of microwaveable mac and cheese. Is that so wrong? It’s efficient!  It’s comforting!  It’s… beige.

(Pause for polite laughter)

Speaking of beige, my apartment is aggressively beige.  It’s like living inside a giant oatmeal cookie.  I’m considering adding a single, shocking splash of color.  Maybe a neon pink flamingo.  My landlord would probably not be thrilled. He seems to be deeply attached to the beige aesthetic.  I think he believes beige is a spiritual experience. 

And dating? Don’t even get me started. The dating apps are… a journey.  It’s like browsing a museum of slightly awkward selfies.  Everyone’s posing like they’re about to star in a dramatic documentary about their love of hiking.  Meanwhile, I’m over here just trying to figure out how to properly load a dishwasher.  It’s a skill, okay?  It's a fundamental life skill!  And I’m failing miserably.  Half the time, I end up with a damp, vaguely soapy mystery. 

(Shakes head)

Honestly, I think the biggest challenge of adulthood is just pretending to know what you’re doing.  We’re all just faking it until we make it… or until the microwave mac and cheese runs out.  Which, let’s be honest, is a very real and terrifying prospect.

Thanks, you've been a great audience!  Don't forget to tip your waitresses… and maybe invest in a flamingo.  Goodnight!

**(Bows slightly, exits stage left.)**

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
(Steps onto stage, takes a sip of water, looks out at the audience)

Alright, alright. Thanks for having me. It's nice to be here. Feels good. Honestly, sometimes I forget what it feels like to be *here*. Like, physically. In a room. With other humans. It's been a thing lately, you know? Just... existing in the same space.

My house is nice, but it's like a self-awareness machine. Every surface seems to be judging my life choices. "Hey, remember that takeout you ordered three days ago? Still there. Also, your motivation levels look low." It’s like the walls have built-in therapists, but they only focus on the negative. "So, about that pile of laundry... we talked about this."

You ever try to clean when you're depressed? It’s the worst. It’s like the universe is mocking you. "Okay, fine, universe, I'll clean. Watch me. I'm gonna make this mess *organized*." And you start, and you pick up one thing, and then you see another thing, and you're like, "Wait, where did I even put the thing to clean the other thing?" And suddenly, you're just standing there, surrounded by evidence of your own incompetence, feeling like you've accomplished nothing, which is technically true, but also more.

And then there's the food. Oh god, the food. I swear, I could eat an entire pizza and still feel hungry, but not *hungry*. Like, *existent* hungry. Like my soul needs sustenance, but also, maybe, just maybe, a nap. It's a weird time. Bodies are doing wild stuff. My knees sometimes feel like they're made of gravel and disappointment. Like, "Hey, remember when you were young and could run? Yeah, about that."

I saw a video the other day of a cat that could open the fridge. And my immediate thought wasn't "How clever!" It was "That's unfair. Why can't I just *be* that good at something?" Like, I practice opening the fridge. I put my hand on the handle, I pull... sometimes it takes three tries. There should be a training program for this. Basic life skill certification. Maybe I need a certificate that says, "Yes, this person can successfully open a refrigerator door on their first attempt. Mostly."

It’s these little things, right? The little things that make you feel like you’re just… kind of… orbiting the planet, but maybe not quite landing. Like a slightly off-target space probe. Just floating there, sending back signals of mild confusion and the occasional, “Hey, can someone bring me a snack?”

But you know what? It’s fine. It’s all fine. We’re all just… here. Trying our best. Sometimes the best is just making it through the day without accidentally setting something on fire or, you know, forgetting your own name. Small wins. Big wins are overrated anyway. I think I'll stick to the small ones. Like successfully opening the fridge. We'll build an empire, one fridge door at a time. Okay, thanks. (Takes another sip of water, nods)

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**(Lights up. Comedian, let's call them Alex, is standing center stage, holding a microphone. They look out at the audience with a wry, knowing smile.)**

Hey, thanks. Thank you. It’s good to be here.

You ever have one of those weeks where you just feel… obsolete? Like you’re a piece of technology from the 90s and the world has moved on to a new operating system? I had one of those moments this week. I was trying to buy a coffee.

I walked into a coffee shop, and there was a massive line. And at the front of the line, there wasn’t a person taking an order. There was a giant tablet. A giant, gleaming, intimidating tablet with a barcode scanner that looked like it belonged on a space probe.

And I just… froze. I was a man facing a monolith. I had no idea how to interact with it. Do I touch it? Does it sense my presence? Do I need to offer it a sacrifice? A latte, perhaps?

And the person behind me, this woman, she just sighs. And she does an exaggerated eye-roll. And in that sigh, I heard a lifetime of impatience. I heard, "Oh my god, another one of *these* people." I was the guy holding up the line because I still believe in the magic of human interaction.

I finally get the courage to tap the screen. It’s like trying to pet a wild animal. The screen flashes: "Welcome! What can I get for you?" And I just stand there, my brain completely offline. I forgot how to order a coffee. I just wanted to say, "Can I trouble you for a medium, dark roast, with room for a little bit of hope in this chaotic world?"

But the screen doesn’t have that option. It has "Venti, Iced, Caramel Macchiato, Oat Milk, 2 pumps, extra foam." I don't know what any of those words mean. I think "Venti" is Italian for "You're about to spend fifteen dollars."

So I just start tapping randomly. It’s like playing a slot machine for a beverage. I’m hoping for three matching cherries, but I’m probably going to get a kale smoothie.

And then, the screen flashes: "Add a tip for your barista." Oh, right. The digital guilt trip. It’s not enough that I’m paying five dollars for a cup of bean water. Now I have to perform generosity for an algorithm. The options are 15%, 18%, 20%,… and "Other." What's the "Other" option? Is that for people who want to tip 2% and also apologize for their entire existence?

I ended up just leaving. I walked out of there and went to a gas station. There was a sign on the coffee machine that said, "Brewed Fresh Every Hour." I looked at the time. It was 3:15 PM. The sign was a lie. It was a bold-faced lie. But I respected it. I respected the audacity. It was honest in its deception.

I bought the coffee. It tasted like regret. But at least a human sold it to me. We made eye contact. We shared a moment of mutual suffering. And that, my friends, is something a tablet can never replace.

**(Pause for a beat, smile.)**

Well, maybe it can. But it can’t replicate the specific, acrid flavor of gas station regret.

Thank you, goodnight.

**(Alex gives a small nod and walks off stage.)**

question: standup-routine

content:
I feel like I’m constantly at war with myself. Specifically, the war between the person I *want* to be—which is a lean, green, jogging machine—and the person I actually am, which is a potato sitting on the couch.

I go to the grocery store with a mission statement. I write it down. I have a list. "Kale," "Quinoa," "Almond Milk." I feel like a Spartan general preparing for a siege. I walk in with confidence. I’m going to buy healthy food, cook a delicious dinner, and feel virtuous.

By the time I get to the checkout, my hands are clutching a family-sized bag of Cheetos and a rotisserie chicken that was probably cooked in the parking lot.

It’s the packaging, man. It is psychological warfare. You see a box that says "Smartfood." That sounds like something a genius would eat. But it’s just popcorn with too much salt. And "Reduced Fat." If it’s reduced fat, they didn’t take the fat out. They just took the flavor out and put the fat back in. That’s just how physics works.

And then there’s the produce section. I look at a head of romaine lettuce for four dollars, and I look at the frozen pizza for six dollars. I’m not buying food; I’m buying expensive water. I’m basically paying for a salad to remind myself how broke I am.

But you know what? I’ve stopped lying to myself. I tried to be healthy last week. I did a "detox." All I did was drink lemon water and stare at a wall for three hours.

I realized that being an adult isn’t about eating kale. Being an adult is realizing that french fries taste better than the way you look in a swimsuit. And that is the only victory that matters.

content:
Below is a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine I've written. It's structured for delivery at a natural speaking pace (about 150 words per minute), clocking in around 450 words. The humor focuses on observational storytelling, exaggeration, and self-deprecation—no puns involved. Imagine delivering it with timing, pauses for laughs, and expressive gestures.

---

[Walk on stage, adjusting mic with a sigh]  

You ever wake up and realize adulthood is just a scam? Like, I thought by now I'd have it all figured out—house, career, maybe a dog that doesn't eat my shoes. Instead, I'm 35, living in a shoebox apartment, arguing with my fridge because it won't stop beeping at me. "Low on milk!" Yeah, thanks, fridge. I'm low on everything—patience, money, reasons to get out of bed.  

And don't get me started on dating in this era. I tried one of those apps, you know, the ones where you swipe right if someone's not a serial killer... probably. I matched with this guy who seemed normal—profile said he likes hiking and deep conversations. We meet up, and five minutes in, he tells me his life's passion is collecting antique spoons. Spoons! Not even fancy ones, just the kind you find at garage sales. I'm sitting there thinking, "Is this a date or an episode of Hoarders?" By the end, he's showing me photos on his phone, zooming in like, "See the curve on this teaspoon? Revolutionary." I faked a family emergency to escape. "Sorry, my cat's on fire." Never heard from him again. Thank God.  

But honestly, the real killer is work. I have this job where my boss thinks "team-building" means forcing us into escape rooms. Last time, we got locked in with puzzles that were basically corporate torture. "Solve this riddle or you're stuck forever!" My team's yelling ideas: "Push the button!" "No, pull the lever!" I'm in the corner like, "Guys, the real puzzle is why we're all still employed here." We escaped in 58 minutes—two minutes under the limit—and my boss high-fives everyone like we just won the Olympics. Meanwhile, I'm traumatized, realizing my coworkers are dumber than the room.  

And technology? It's supposed to make life easier, right? My phone's "smart" assistant keeps misunderstanding me. I say, "Set an alarm for 7 AM," and it hears, "Play sad music at 3 AM." Wakes me up to Adele crying about lost love. Thanks, phone. Now I'm single, exhausted, and emotionally wrecked before breakfast.  

Look, if adulthood's a game, I want a refund. Or at least cheat codes. Thanks, folks—you've been great.  

[Wave and exit stage]  

---

This routine builds from personal anecdotes to relatable frustrations, aiming for laughs through exaggeration and timing. If delivered with energy, it should hit the 3-minute mark spot-on. Let me know if you want tweaks!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
So I recently realized I have no idea what my own face looks like. And I don’t mean in a deep, existential way—I mean I literally caught a glimpse of myself in a convenience store security camera and screamed because I thought we were being robbed by a haunted doll.

We’ve all got this image of ourselves, right? Like, in my head, I’m a laid-back, approachable guy. Maybe a little mysterious. But in reality, I look like I’m perpetually solving a math problem. I have what scientists call “resting confusion face.” I look like I’m always trying to remember if I left the stove on—which, to be fair, I probably did.

And it’s worse with phones. Everyone has their “phone face.” You know what I’m talking about. You’re staring at your phone in public, and you think you look like a sophisticated person reading important emails. But you actually look like a caveman who just discovered fire for the first time. Mouth slightly open, eyes glazed over, brow furrowed like you’re trying to understand quantum physics but you’re just looking at a picture of a dog in a hat.

We’re all performing versions of ourselves. Like, I’m currently performing “functional adult.” It’s going terribly. I bought a plant last week because I thought it would make me seem stable. The plant is already dead. It didn’t even make it through the weekend. I gave it a funeral that consisted of me whispering “I’m sorry” and shoving it in a trash can while my roommate pretended not to see.

And we do this on social media too. We’re all lying, but politely. I posted a picture last month with the caption “Living my best life!” What the caption should have said was: “Crying in a Target parking lot because I couldn’t find the exit and I’d been in there for 45 minutes and I started having an existential crisis next to the seasonal throw pillows.” But “living my best life” fits better in the Instagram square.

The worst is when you see someone you know in real life, and you already know everything about them from their Instagram, but you have to pretend you don’t. You have to be like, “Oh, you went to Greece? How was that?” while internally you’re thinking, “I saw the 42 photos, Brad. I know you were miserable. You were fighting with your girlfriend in the comments section. Don’t lie to my face.”

We’re all just trying to seem like we have it together while privately knowing we don’t. Like, I have a friend who posted a picture of herself doing yoga on a mountain at sunrise. Beautiful. Inspirational. In reality, she drove three hours, did that pose for exactly six seconds, got altitude sickness, and spent the rest of the day in the car eating gas station beef jerky and questioning her life choices. But that didn’t make the feed.

And that’s the thing—we’re all the gas station beef jerky version of ourselves. We’re all just trying to get through the day without looking like the haunted doll in the security camera. And I think that’s beautiful. Or at least, that’s what I’ll post about it later.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
You ever notice how hard it is to relax? Like, actually relax? I’m so bad at it, I get stressed about being stressed. My brain is basically that friend who shows up to the party and immediately asks, “What time are we leaving?” Just... live in the moment, Deborah.

I tried to get a massage last month because that’s what relaxed people do. But I’m lying there, naked under a sheet like a burrito having an existential crisis, and I can’t stop thinking: “Am I relaxing hard enough? Is this peak relaxation? Should I be making more noise? Less noise?” The masseuse keeps saying, “Just breathe,” and I’m like, “I AM BREATHING! I’ve been breathing for twenty-nine consecutive years! I’m actually crushing it right now!”

So I downloaded a meditation app because that’s what we do now—we solve our technology addiction with more technology. It’s like fighting a fire by adding smaller, more mindful fires. The guy on the app has the most aggressively calm voice you’ve ever heard. He sounds like he’s speaking through a cloud made of Xanax and expensive wool. He’s like, “Notice your thoughts... then let them go.” 

And I’m trying, but my thoughts aren’t clouds, okay? My thoughts are those plastic grocery bags stuck in a tree. You can’t just let them go. They’re stuck. They’re just flapping in the wind, reminding me I need to buy actual groceries, which reminds me I need to meal prep, which reminds me I haven’t done laundry in two weeks, and now I’m tense again and the wool-voice man is disappointed in me.

We planned a “relaxing vacation” recently. Took three months to plan. I made a spreadsheet. A SPREADSHEET. For relaxation. I color-coded it. Blue for beaches, yellow for naps, red for my inevitable emotional breakdown in the TSA line. And the whole time we’re there, I’m treating it like a performance review. “Are we having enough fun per capita? Is this joy efficient? We should be maximizing our leisure!”

The worst is Sunday afternoon. That four o’clock window where you’re technically still in weekend mode but your body starts preparing for Monday like it’s a Category 5 hurricane. You’re watching Netflix, but you’re not really watching. You’re just staring at a British baking show while internally screaming, “I SHOULD BE PREPARING!” Preparing for what? I don’t know. The week? The void? The inevitable heat death of the universe?

I finally figured out the only time I’m truly relaxed is when I’m asleep. Which is perfect, because that’s the one time I can’t enjoy it. I’m just unconscious, drooling on my pillow, achieving the inner peace that eludes me for sixteen hours a day.

So my new self-care routine is just... naps. Aggressive naps. I’m talking Olympic-level sleeping. I’m going for gold in the Unconscious category. My therapist says I need “boundaries,” but I think I just need better pillows. 

Thank you, you’ve been great. Try the veal.

content:
Here's a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that doesn't rely on puns:

"Hey everyone, you know what's wild? We're all just pretending to be adults, right? Like, I'm pretty sure I'm still 12 years old on the inside. I mean, I still eat cereal for dinner sometimes. I still get excited when I see a mailbox and think I might get a letter from my pen pal. (pauses for laughter)

But then I go to the grocery store and I'm like, 'Oh, I need to buy some...avocado toast...and a 401K.' (laughs) It's like, what's going on? I'm trying to adult, but my brain is still stuck on 'what's for lunch?' (chuckles)

And have you ever tried to have a conversation with a toddler? It's like trying to negotiate with a tiny little dictator. 'I want juice!' 'No, you can't have juice, it's bedtime.' 'I WANT JUICE!' (mimics toddler tantrum) 'Fine, have the juice, you win.' (laughs)

I was at the park the other day and I saw a mom with a sign that said 'Mom's Taxi.' And I was like, 'Oh, that's cute.' But then I started thinking, what's the alternative? 'Mom's Uber'? 'Mom's Lyft'? 'Mom's Unreliable Ride That Might Show Up If She Remembers'? (laughs)

You know what's even weirder than being an adult? Being an adult with social media. It's like, I'm supposed to be a functioning member of society, but I'm over here scrolling through Instagram going, 'Oh, look, Karen's on a beach somewhere. I should probably book a trip to the beach...and also buy a new swimsuit...and maybe get a facelift.' (laughs)

I'm pretty sure social media is just a giant game of 'Keep Up with the Joneses,' but the Joneses are all lying. They're all like, 'Oh, look at me, I'm having a great day!' And you're like, 'Wait, what's that in the background? Is that a messy room? Did you actually take that selfie in your pajamas?' (laughs)

Anyway, that's my time. Thanks for listening to me complain about being an adult. Goodnight, everybody!"

(approx. 3 minutes)

I don't care about your sunburn or your Mai Tai-fueled adventures. I'm just pretending to care because I don't want to be rude. (laughter) It's like, can't we just be honest? 'Yeah, I went to Hawaii. I got sunburned and ate a lot of poke bowls. You're welcome.'

And finally, have you ever noticed how some restaurants have those signs that say, 'Please wait to be seated'? Like, what's the alternative? 'No, I'm just going to go sit wherever I want. I'm a rebel.' (laughter) I'm like, 'Sir, you're 45 years old. You're not a rebel. You're just a guy who can't follow directions.'"

content:
**"Modern Life: A Survival Guide"**
*(3-Minute Stand-Up Routine)*

---

**INTRO:**
Hey, how’s everybody doing? Good? Great. Because I just spent the last 20 minutes in the bathroom scrolling through my phone, and I don’t even remember why I went in there. That’s modern life, folks—we’re all just highly efficient, slightly confused goldfish with Wi-Fi.

You ever notice how we’re all just *one step away* from losing our minds? Like, you wake up in the morning, and the first thing you do is check your phone. And what’s the first thing you see? *A notification from an app you don’t even remember downloading.* “Hey! Your free trial of ‘Premium Meditation for People Who Hate Themselves’ is about to expire!” Thanks, Karen. I *was* considering inner peace, but now I’m just reminded that I’m broke.

---

**THE STRUGGLE IS REAL:**
And speaking of broke—why is everything so expensive now? I went to the grocery store the other day, and I swear, the cashier looked at my basket like I was committing a crime. “Sir, do you *need* all this avocado toast?” No, Karen, I *want* it. I want to eat my feelings in a way that makes me feel both guilty *and* bougie.

And don’t even get me started on dating. Dating in 2024 is just two people sitting across from each other, pretending they don’t have their phones out under the table, Googling “How to tell if this person is a serial killer.” “So, uh… what do you do for fun?” *Types into phone: “How to ask if someone has a 401(k) without sounding like a gold digger.”*

---

**TECHNOLOGY: OUR BEST FRIEND AND WORST ENEMY:**
Technology is supposed to make our lives easier, but now we’re all just slaves to the algorithm. You ever get stuck in a YouTube rabbit hole at 2 AM? “Oh, I’ll just watch *one* video on how to fold a fitted sheet.” Next thing you know, it’s 4 AM, and you’re watching a documentary about *why pigeons bob their heads when they walk.* And you’re not even mad about it! You’re just like, “Yeah, *tell me more about the pigeons, Dave.*”

And don’t even get me started on AI. We’re all one step away from a robot taking our job. “Oh, you’re a comedian? Great! Here’s an AI that can write jokes *and* doesn’t need health insurance.” Thanks, Skynet. I *was* looking for a career change.

---

**THE GRAND FINALE:**
But you know what? Despite all this chaos, we’re still here. We’re still laughing. We’re still scrolling, dating, eating overpriced avocados, and pretending we know how to fold a fitted sheet. And that’s the beauty of it—we’re all just winging it, and somehow, it works.

So next time you feel like life is too much, just remember: You’re not alone. We’re all out here, one notification away from a nervous breakdown, and that’s *okay.*

Thanks, you’ve been a great crowd! Now if you’ll excuse me, I have to go cancel a free trial I forgot about.

---

**END ROUTINE.**

*(Note: Adjust pacing and crowd interaction based on the room. This routine avoids puns and leans into observational humor with a mix of self-deprecation and universal frustrations.)*

content:
Ladies and Gentlemen, how's everyone doing tonight? Good, good. I'm glad you're all here because I've got some observations that I just can't keep to myself anymore. Let's dive in, shall we?

First off, let's talk about the weather. I mean, seriously, what's up with that? It's like Mother Nature is playing the world's worst game of Simon. You know, that game where you have to repeat the pattern of lights and sounds? Well, she's doing that with our seasons. "Okay, today it's going to be sunny and warm, but tomorrow? Blizzard. Just to keep you on your toes."

And don't get me started on the fashion choices people make when it's like that. I saw a guy the other day wearing shorts and a parka. I mean, what's the point? You're just asking for a serious case of thigh chafe. And if you're going to dress like that, at least commit to it. Go full-on Eskimo. Fur pants, the whole nine yards. But no, he just looked like he was lost on his way to a costume party.

Speaking of fashion, what's with the whole "athleisure" trend? You know, those yoga pants and hoodies that people wear everywhere now. I get it, comfort is important, but come on. If you're not actually going to the gym, don't dress like you are. I saw a guy in a sports bra the other day, and he wasn't even at the gym. He was just walking his dog. I mean, I get it, dogs need exercise too, but that's a bit much.

And while we're on the subject of dogs, can we talk about those people who dress their dogs up? You know, the ones with the little sweaters and booties? I get it, they're cute, but let's be real here. The dog doesn't want to wear that stuff. It's like when your mom made you wear that itchy sweater to family photos. You didn't want to wear it either, but you did because you had to. So, let's cut the dogs some slack and let them wear their natural fur coats, okay?

Now, let's talk about technology. Specifically, those smart speakers. You know, the ones that are always listening to you. I mean, I get it, they're convenient. But have you ever stopped to think about what they're listening to? I mean, I've said some pretty weird stuff in my house. Like the other day, I was singing along to a song, and I said, "I love you, man." My smart speaker responded with, "Thank you for your feedback." I mean, what feedback? I was just singing a song!

And finally, let's talk about those people who say they "don't do social media." You know, the ones who act like they're above it all. Like they're too good for likes and shares. Newsflash: You're still on social media. You're just on the "I'm too good for social media" page. You're still posting pictures of your avocado toast and your fancy coffee. You're still checking in at places. You're just doing it ironically. So, let's cut the act and just admit it. We're all addicted to the likes.

Thank you, thank you, you've been a great audience. I'll be here all week, folks. Don't forget to tip your waitstaff. Goodnight!

content:
*(Lights up. Comedian walks to mic, adjusts it, takes a breath. Smiles warmly.)*

You ever have that moment where you realize adulthood isn’t a destination… it’s a group project nobody signed up for? *(Beat)* I tried assembly line “adulting” this week. Swedish bookshelf. You know the one. Box says “Easy Assembly!” Lies. All the panels look identical. You’re staring at a cartoon stick figure holding a wrench, crying. Is that the instruction? Or is that *me* in 45 minutes? Three hours later… I’ve got this thing standing. *Sort of*. It leans like it’s trying to escape my life choices. My *cat* sat across from it for ten minutes and gave me a slowblink. That cat has never judged me harder. He usually just judges my dating profile. Now he’s auditing *my carpentry*.

And passwords? Why is logging into my own email harder than defusing a bomb? “Must be 12 characters! Include a symbol! A number! A hieroglyph from forgotten Atlantis!” I made this while crying in a Target parking lot. Click “forgot password.” Reset link? Spam folder. Click “resend.” *Again*. “Maximum attempts reached. Try again… tomorrow.” TOMORROW?! I need to cancel my subscription to panic *now*! This isn’t security—it’s psychological warfare with a loading wheel.

So I went to the gym. Big mistake. Walked in, air smells like ambition and regret. Everyone’s lifting weights that could crush a small car. I’m on the stationary bike, pedaling at toddler-speed, sweating like I just ran a marathon *in my imagination*. Trainer strolls over, radiant: “Push yourself!” I whisper, “Sir… I am. I’m pushing the ‘emergency stop’ button with my *soul*.” He nods like he gets it. He does not get it.

Later, grocery delivery. App said “5 to 7 PM.” At 6:58, I’m pressed against the door like a golden retriever waiting for a walk. Doorbell rings. Guy hands me a bag. I get inside, hopeful. Avocados? Two green rocks that could double as paperweights. One had a bruise shaped like my future regrets. The “fresh” bread? Curved into a perfect question mark. I held up the loaf and said, “Are you a baguette… or are you asking me if I’m okay?” My dog looked at me like, “We’re eating this? Cool. I’ll get the vet on standby.”

But here’s the real talk: *nobody* has it figured out. That guy who deadlifts a truck? He Googled “how to boil water” last Monday. The CEO running the Fortune 500? She cried because her IKEA shelf leaned *too*. We’re all just out there—sweating over Allen wrenches, refreshing spam folders, holding up sad avocados—pretending we know the rules to a game that has no handbook.  
So if you see someone struggling with a flat-pack nightmare? Don’t laugh. Nod. Offer a screwdriver. Or just say, “Hey… my bookshelf leans too.”  
*(Leans into mic, sincere grin)*  
We’re not failing grown-up. We’re *human*. And that’s the punchline.  
Thank you, you’ve been lovely. Drive safe! *(Waves, exits.)*  

*(Total runtime: approx. 2min 50sec. No puns. All observational, relatable, self-deprecating humor built on shared experiences, exaggerated truths, and warmth.)*

content:
*(Lights up. Comedian walks on stage, takes a deep breath, smiles at the crowd.)*

So, I tried online dating recently. Yeah. You know why? Because my friends said, "You’re too picky in real life!" And I thought, "Great! I’ll just let an algorithm find me someone who matches my *very specific* need for someone who doesn’t snore *and* likes pineapple on pizza." Spoiler: the algorithm is a liar. It’s like a matchmaking therapist who’s also a con artist who only speaks in emojis.  

Here’s the thing about these apps—everyone’s lying. I mean, *everyone*. Look at this profile: "Adventure seeker! Loves hiking, travel, and trying new things!" *(Mimes scrolling on phone)* And the photos? Guy in a life jacket on a paddleboard… but the background is a *lake*. Like, bro, that’s not an adventure. That’s a Saturday afternoon at the city park. And the "new things" he’s trying? Probably a new flavor of Doritos. "Ooh, I’ve *never* tasted Cool Ranch before!" *(Shrugs)* Yeah, that’s next-level bravery.  

And then there’s the "I don’t do small talk" people. *(Leans in conspiratorially)* They’ll write that right after their 10th message asking, "How’s your day?" and "What do you do for work?" and "Do you have any pets?" like they’re doing a job interview for my affection. I’m like, "Sir, you just said you hate small talk—but you’re doing *nothing but small talk*! What’s the plan? Are you just testing me to see if I’ll shut up first?"  

*(Pauses, shakes head)* But the real gem is the "I’m just looking for friends" crowd. Yeah. Right. *(Mimes reading a bio)* "Just here for fun, no expectations, great conversationalist!" And then their photos? Three of them holding a baby. *(Pauses)* A baby. You’re not looking for friends—you’re looking for a wife you haven’t met yet. And you’re using a baby as your bait. That’s not "just friends," that’s a hostage situation!  

And ghosting? Oh, we’re all guilty. We ghost people like they’re a bad Wi-Fi signal. "Sorry, my signal’s weak today!" *(Checks phone dramatically)* But then you’re on Instagram watching their story from that bar you *just* left. You literally saw them two hours ago. You weren’t weak—you were *cowardly*. We’re all just strangers in a giant game of charades where the only rule is… we don’t play. We’re all just trying to be liked so much, we become terrible liars. But hey—*(shrugs, smiles)*—at least we’re consistent in our inconsistency.  

*(Nods, waves, exits stage left.)*  

*(Total runtime: 2 minutes 55 seconds.)*

content:
*(Walks to mic, adjusts stand, takes a breath)*

I’ve come to a quiet realization about grocery shopping. We don’t go to stores anymore. We go to unpaid internships. I used to walk into a supermarket with a cart, buy my food, and leave. Now I walk in, grab a basket, and get handed a shift. No onboarding. No direct deposit. Just a screen that expects me to know how to weigh a cucumber.

The self-checkout doesn’t help you. It manages you. It talks to you like a very disappointed shift supervisor. “Please place the item in the bagging area.” Thank you. I will. “Item not recognized.” It’s a box of crackers. It’s been a box of crackers since the Reagan administration. You’re the one struggling here, Brenda. And that voice. Always this calm, synthetic woman who sounds exactly three beeps away from filing a formal complaint. “Unexpected item in the bagging area. Please wait for assistance.” I didn’t expect it either! I just wanted to buy pasta and a single lemon. Now I’m frozen in place like I’m waiting for a hostage negotiator while a teenager named Tyler walks over at the speed of a ceiling fan.

The bagging area is a psychological experiment. It’s not a shelf. It’s a scale that thinks it’s a detective. You set your groceries down with the care of a bomb squad technician, and it immediately panics. “Weight discrepancy.” Discrepancy from what? From the ghost grocery list it’s reading from? I swear if I exhale too hard, it locks the screen and flashes a manager override code. At that point, I’m not a shopper. I’m a suspect. I’m being cross-examined by a touchscreen. “Sir, step away from the frozen peas.” I’m just trying to make dinner. Release me.

And the worst part is, we all just nod and comply. We’re out here working for free, scanning our own stuff, bagging our own stuff, occasionally paying a dollar more than we would’ve at the register, all to save the store fourteen cents on labor. Meanwhile, the machine gets a software update, I get home with three bruised tomatoes, and we’ve collectively decided this is progress. Next, they’ll just install a conveyor belt in your kitchen and you’ll scan your own dish soap while a robotic voice tells you your life choices are invalid.

I tried the human lanes last week. Forty people deep. Everyone standing there in silent, shared exhaustion. I looked back at the checkout kiosk. The screen blinked. I sighed. Put my keys down. And scanned my own acceptance.

Thank you. You’ve been great. I’m out of here before my loyalty points expire.

*(Steps back, nods, exits)*

I sit down and my knees go, *'Clack-clack-pop.'* My lower back is like, 'Are we doing this? Really? Okay, fine, but I’m going to complain about it for the next four business days.'”

**(Pause for laughter)**

“I realized I was officially getting old when I started getting excited about... appliances. That’s my life now. Last week, I spent forty-five minutes reading reviews for a cordless vacuum. Forty-five minutes! I wasn’t even buying it yet. I was just deep in the forums, reading arguments between strangers about 'suction power' and 'battery longevity.' I felt like I was studying for a final exam. I was like, 'If I don't get the Dyson, my entire domestic future is compromised.'”

**(Shakes head)**

“And have you noticed how much harder it is to be a person now? Everything is a subscription. I feel like I don’t own anything. I don’t own movies. I don’t own music. I don’t even own my heated seat in my car—I just rent the *privilege* of being warm for $14.99 a month. I’m terrified that one day I’ll wake up and my front door will be locked because I forgot to update my 'Entryway Premium Membership.' I’ll be standing on the porch like, 'Please, I just want to go to my kitchen! I’ll watch a thirty-second ad for insurance if you just let me in!'”

**(Paces the stage slightly)**

“And don't get me started on the 'Smart Home' stuff. Everyone wants a smart house. I tried to set up a smart lightbulb last month. It was a disaster. I spent two hours trying to connect it to my Wi-Fi. It kept saying, 'Error: Device not recognized.' I’m standing there in the dark, yelling at a piece of glass, 'I AM YOUR CREATOR! CONNECT TO THE ROUTER!' Eventually, I gave up. Now I just have a regular lightbulb. It’s not 'smart,' but at least it doesn't require a firmware update just so I can see my cereal.”

**(Leans into the mic, more intimate)**

I’m pretty sure somewhere in line 42 of the iTunes agreement, it says, 'By clicking here, you agree to let Apple decide your political affiliations and give your firstborn to a server farm in Iceland.'”

**(Checks imaginary watch)**

“Anyway, I gotta go. I have to go home and see if my vacuum arrived. I’ve got a very important meeting with some dust bunnies and a 15% discount code. You guys have been great. Thank you!”

**(Waves and exits stage)**

content:
(Steps up to the mic, adjusts the stand, looks around the room)

How many people here are good sleepers? Just, out of the gate, who’s got it figured out? 

(Nods sarcastically)

Right. Liars. All of you. Sleep is the one thing every human being is required to do, and none of us know how to do it. When you’re a kid, sleep is a superpower. You just fall asleep inside a half-built pillow fort with a juice box stuck to your face, and you wake up ready to fight a bear. 

Now? Sleep is an appointment. And I am terrible at keeping it. 

I get into bed at a reasonable hour. I do the routine. I brush my teeth, I wash my face, I set my phone down on the nightstand, and I close my eyes. And that is the exact moment my brain decides it’s time to solve crimes. 

(Squints, mimicking intense thought)

“Hey. Hey, you awake? Good. I was just thinking about that thing you said to a cashier in 2012. You said ‘You too’ when she told you to enjoy your movie. Let’s replay that for the next forty-five minutes. In Dolby.”

My brain at 3 AM is not a relaxed organ. It’s a panicking intern running through the halls of my skull with a clipboard. It’s bringing me concerns that do not matter. “Are we sure we locked the back door? What if the house settles and it sounds like a burglar? What’s the plan if a burglar gets in? Do we fight? Do we hide? What if the burglar is just really lonely and wants to play Monopoly? I don’t think we have enough snacks for a board game burglar, man. We gotta get up and check the pantry.”

(Pauses, takes a breath)

And people give you the worst advice for this. You tell someone you can’t sleep, and they hit you with the wellness tips. “Have you tried turning off your screens an hour before bed?” 

Oh, is that it? I just have to turn off the only light in my life? I just have to sit in the dark, staring at the wall like a Victorian ghost, waiting for the sandman to arrive? I did that. I turned off my phone. I stared at the ceiling. You know what happened? My brain got *bored*. And a bored brain is a dangerous brain. It started making up scenarios. I spent an hour mentally arguing with a coworker who wasn't even in the state. I won the argument, by the way. But then I was too pumped up to sleep. I was too busy celebrating my imaginary victory.

Then they tell you, “Read a book before bed.” I tried that. But I have a problem. If the book is boring, I just lay there annoyed that I’m reading a boring book. If the book is good? The sun’s coming up. I’m on chapter forty, my eyes are bleeding, and I’m like, “Just one more chapter! I gotta find out if the butler did it!”

(Paces slightly)

The worst is the white noise machine. I bought one of those machines to help me relax. You hit the button and it’s got all these different nature settings. “Rain.” Okay, that’s nice. “Ocean waves.” Sure. But then you get to the weird ones. “Airplane cabin.” Who is falling asleep to the ambient hum of a Boeing 737? That’s not relaxing, that’s just knowing you’re six hours into a flight next to a guy named Gary who won’t stop talking about his timeshare. 

And my personal nemesis: “Melatonin.” That stuff is a scam. You take 5 milligrams? Nothing. You take 10? Nothing. You take 15? Suddenly you’re not asleep, but you’re not awake either. You’re just... paralyzed, watching the shadows of tree branches on your ceiling morph into the faces of former presidents. Is that James K. Polk? I don't know, I’m too busy trying to remember if I paid my water bill.

(Sighs, grips the mic)

I don’t want tips anymore. I don’t want gummies. I don’t want sound machines. I just want a switch. Like a light switch on the back of my neck. Flick it down, I’m out. Flick it up, I’m back. No thinking, no board game burglars, no imaginary arguments. Just the off switch. 

Until then, if you need me at 3 AM, I’ll be awake. Staring at the ceiling. Trying to figure out if I own a monopoly board.

(Points to the crowd)

You guys have been great! Thank you!

And what’s the deal with grocery stores? They’ve turned into a competitive sport. It’s not just shopping anymore. It’s a triathlon with coupons. Ma’am, I don’t know what a butterfly cracker is, but I know it’s judging my life choices.

Remember when you were a kid and your biggest worry was whether the bus was gonna be five minutes late? The worst is the self-checkout. That machine is not your friend. It’s a robot sent to judge your life choices. “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Ma’am, I put a mango in a bag! What did you expect? A surprise party? I’m not a magician, I can’t make scanned items appear in the loyalty card.

Here's a 3-minute stand-up routine:

---

So I turned 35 recently, and something weird happens at 35. Your body just starts sending you notifications like it's an app you forgot to update. 

I bent down to tie my shoe last week and my knee made a sound. Not a pop. Not a crack. A *sound*. Like it was trying to communicate. Like my knee was buffering. I half expected a little loading wheel to appear on my kneecap.

And now I have a chiropractor. That's a thing in my life now. I have a guy. I went in there thinking I was going to get a quick back crack and leave feeling amazing. Instead, he looked at my posture and said, "How long have you been like this?" LIKE THIS? Like what? I didn't know I was like anything! I thought I was just... standing!

He told me I have the spine of a 60-year-old. Which, honestly, was flattering, because I assumed it was worse.

---

I've also started getting excited about stuff that would've horrified me ten years ago. My friend texted me last weekend and said, "Hey, want to come over?" And I said, "What time does it end?"

That's who I am now. I need an exit strategy for hanging out. I need to know when I can legally go home and put on sweatpants. In my twenties, I'd go to a party at midnight. Now if someone invites me somewhere after 8 PM, I treat it like they're asking me to help them move a body. "I mean... I CAN... but why are we doing this so late?"

I went to a wedding recently and they had the reception outside. Beautiful venue. Gorgeous sunset. And all I could think was, "There are no walls here. Where does the heat come from?" I'm at a wedding doing a threat assessment for mosquitos. I used to do drugs in a field. Now I'm worried about dew.

---

The wildest part of getting older is that you start having opinions about appliances. I went to a friend's house and I genuinely complimented his refrigerator. Out loud. Like an adult. I said, "This is a really nice fridge." And he got excited! He said, "Right?? It has a drawer just for deli meats!" And we stood there, two grown men, staring into a refrigerator like it was the Grand Canyon.

That's when I knew. That's when it hits you. You're not becoming your parents. You're becoming every parent. We're all slowly merging into one guy who's really into mulch and asks everybody how they got there.

Thanks, you've been great.

---

Feel free to tweak the pacing or swap in details that feel more personal — stand-up always lands better when the specifics are yours.

content:
[Walk out, adjust mic]

You ever realize adulthood is just a pyramid scheme? Nobody's actually good at it. We're all just standing in a room looking at each other like, “So… you guys know how to do this too, right?” And everyone nods, but nobody does.

I bought a house last year. I don't know why. They gave me the keys and I immediately felt like I had stolen something. I walked in and thought, “Well, this is clearly a mistake. I'm still emotionally eleven.” Within a week, my sink broke. Not “dripping” broken. Horror movie broken. It sounded like someone was screaming through the pipes. So I did what any competent adult would do: I stared at it for twenty minutes, then called my dad.

Now my dad lives two hours away, so he starts asking me technical questions. “What kind of pipes are they?” I don't know, Dad. They're… wet? “Is it copper or PVC?” It's angry. That's the material. He tells me to go to the hardware store. I hate the hardware store. That place is designed to make you feel your own mortality. I walked in and a guy in an orange vest looked at me like, “You lost?” Yes. Emotionally and spiritually.

I found the plumbing aisle. It's just a wall of identical metal tubes that all hate me personally. And there's always some guy there—some sixty-year-old man named Gary—who's buying, like, one screw. Just vibing. He looks at me holding my broken pipe piece and says, “You know what you need?” I said, “A time machine so I can apologize to my landlord?” Gary didn't laugh. Gary doesn't joke about plumbing.

But the scariest part of being an adult is the grocery store. Specifically, the self-checkout. That machine is a cop now. It used to be helpful; now it's just surveilling my produce. I put down an avocado, it says, “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Unexpected? It's an avocado. You have an entire produce section dedicated to them. What did you expect? A birthday cake? Then the light starts flashing, and you have to wait for a nineteen-year-old employee to come over and validate your existence. This kid scans a card and suddenly I'm innocent again. I feel like I should get a lawyer.

And nobody warns you that your social life dies in stages. It's not a big explosion. It's a slow leak—like my sink. In your twenties, you're like, “Let's meet at nine!” In your thirties, you're like, “How about brunch… two Saturdays from now?” And then you spend the entire week leading up to it hoping they cancel. You send a text at eight in the morning: “Still good for brunch?” praying they say no. They text back, “Yeah! So excited!” And I have to physically prepare like I'm running a marathon. I hydrate. I stretch. I practice conversation topics. “How's work?” “Still doing it.” Great. Solid gold.

But my favorite part of modern life is how we all pretend we know how to use our phones. We don't. I got a new phone six months ago, and I still don't know how to close apps. I just swipe up aggressively and hope for the best. My battery dies in forty minutes. So I go to the Apple Store, and the Geniuses look at me with such pity. They opened my phone and I had three hundred and forty-seven tabs open in Safari. The guy said, “You know you can close these?” I said, “Those are my dreams and obligations. I can't just close them.”

Anyway, that's my time. You've been great. I'm gonna go stare at my sink now.

[Wave, exit]
