content:
*(Takes a bow, adjusts the mic)*

Alright, settle down, settle down. Or don’t. I’m not the boss of you, I’m just the guy standing on a box yelling about his feelings. For $20.

You ever notice how every generation thinks the one before them is *so* old? My dad looks at my phone and goes, “How do you fit your entire social life into a device that can’t find a Wi-Fi signal in a room full of routers?” And I look at my dad and go, “How do you function without a button that tells you the exact percentage of your life that has been a lie?”

We’re living in a world where we trust a blinking light on a box more than our own instincts. “The thermostat says 72 degrees, so it *must* be 72 degrees.” My thermostat is a liar. It’s like a tiny, digital politician promising comfort it has no intention of delivering.

And have you tried calling customer service lately? It’s a trap. You press 1 for English, then 3 for “I am not calling to complain, I am calling to validate my existence,” and suddenly you’re in a queue for 45 minutes listening to muzak that is *definitely* judging you. “Yes, Karen, transferring you to a department that doesn’t exist is the correct choice.”

We’ve turned simple tasks into quests. “I need to buy groceries.” It’s not shopping, it’s a boss battle with a coupon you can’t read. “Do I have the loyalty card? What’s the promo code? Why is the reusable bag folded in a way that suggests it holds a grudge?” By the time I get home, I’m exhausted. I’ve defeated the coupon dragon, and all I have to show for it is a receipt longer than my patience.

And let’s talk about walking. Why do we walk like we’re being chased? We’re not. We’re just trying to get to a chair. It’s the human hustle. We see a seat three feet away and our heart rate spikes. It’s not exercise, it’s a competitive sport where the prize is a slightly less sore back.

But you know what? For all our complaining, for all our “adulting is hard” memes, we’re actually doing okay. We’re navigating a weird, chaotic world with phones and snacks and the occasional good podcast. We’re making it up as we go, and that’s kind of hilarious.

So next time you’re stuck in a hold, or wrestling with a flatulent vending machine, just remember: we’re all just monkeys with Wi-Fi, trying not to drop the banana.

Thanks, you’ve been a great, mostly silent audience. Go home, touch grass. Or at least your therapist. Goodnight!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
*(Takes the mic, adjusts it, looks around with a friendly, slightly tired smile)*

Hey everyone! Thanks for coming out. I just got back from visiting my parents. It’s always... an experience. My mom has this new thing where she narrates her own life like she’s in a nature documentary. I’ll be sitting there, and she’ll go, *[in a whisper]* "And here we see the adult son, foraging for leftover pizza in the refrigerator. He is unaware that his mother has already claimed the last slice. A tense standoff is imminent." 

I’m like, Mom, I can hear you. She goes, *[normal voice]* "Shhh! The wildlife is getting agitated."

The best part is my dad. He’s entered his "tech support" phase. Not giving it—*needing* it. He called me last week, panicked. "The internet is broken!" I say, "Dad, did you try turning the router off and on again?" There’s a long silence. Then... *[mimics sound of violent unplugging and plugging back in]* "...Okay, it’s fixed." 

He didn’t even wait to see if it worked! He just performed the ritual and hung up. I think he thinks the router is like a scared animal. You have to show it who’s boss.

Dating in your 30s is weird, too. I went on a date recently, and the woman asked me, "What’s your biggest flaw?" I panicked and said, "I’m too honest." She said, "I don’t think that’s a flaw." I said, "I don’t care what you think." 

*(Pause, lets it land)*

...We did not have a second date.

But you know what’s worse than dating? Group projects. Even as an adult. I’m in this volunteer committee. We had to plan a bake sale. One guy, Dave, suggested we theme it around "the lifecycle of a raisin." I said, "Dave, who is this for? Depressed farmers?" He got so defensive. He presented a PowerPoint. *A PowerPoint.* Slide one: "The Grape: A Life Unfulfilled." I left. I just walked out. I donated fifty dollars to the cause just to never have to see that presentation again.

The worst is when you’re trying to be healthy. I bought a salad the other day. The guy at the counter asked if I wanted a cookie with it. I said, "No, I’m being good." He said, "Are you sure? It’s a double chocolate chip." 

And that’s when you realize the whole system is a lie. They’re not selling you a salad. They’re selling you the *right* to have a cookie. The salad is just the receipt. I bought the cookie. And then I felt guilty. So I went to the gym. And at the gym, I saw a guy eating a protein bar that tasted like chocolate cake. I thought, "You bastard. You found the loophole."

Anyway, that’s my time. You’ve been a great audience. Try the veal. And remember, if you ever feel useless, just remember that somewhere, right now, Dave is updating his raisin PowerPoint.

*(Mic drop. Walks off.)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
# "Adulting Is a Scam"
### A 3-Minute Stand-Up Set

---

*(walks up to mic, adjusts it)*

Hey, everybody! Great to be here. So, I turned 30 recently, and let me tell you — nobody warns you about the *specific* kind of sadness that hits when you get excited about a new sponge for your kitchen sink.

*(pause)*

I was at the store, and I saw this sponge — it had two sides, one for scrubbing, one for wiping — and I literally whispered, "Oh, that's *nice*." Out loud. In public. A teenager heard me. He looked at me with the same pity I used to give my dad when he'd get excited about a new leaf blower.

I've become my father. The transformation is *complete*.

*(shifts weight)*

And you know what nobody tells you about being an adult? You have to make dinner. *Every. Single. Night.* What kind of scam is this? You finish dinner, you feel accomplished, and then your body's like, "Cool, but we're gonna need that again tomorrow." It never ends! I didn't sign a contract for this!

I remember when I was a kid, dinner just *appeared*. Like magic. I thought my mom was a wizard. Turns out she was just *exhausted and resentful*.

*(beat)*

I tried meal prepping. You know, that thing influencers do where they put identical containers of chicken and rice in their fridge and film it like they just performed a miracle? I tried it. Sunday night, I felt like a *king*. By Tuesday, every container tasted like sadness and regret. By Wednesday, I was eating cereal over the sink at 11 PM like the animal I truly am.

*(leans into mic)*

And can we talk about group chats? I'm in, like, nine group chats, and I have not voluntarily contributed to *any* of them. I'm just an archaeological observer at this point. I scroll through 200 messages to find the one piece of information that actually affects me. "Oh, brunch is at 11? Cool. See you in three weeks when I have the emotional energy to respond."

*(beat)*

My friend added me to a group chat last month called "Guys' Trip Planning." It's been six weeks. They've planned *nothing*. But they've sent 4,000 messages, seventeen memes, and one guy keeps sharing articles about crypto. We're not going on a trip. That chat is a *support group* now.

*(pauses, then smiles)*

But honestly? The worst part of being an adult is that you *can* eat ice cream for breakfast. Nobody stops you. That sounds great until you realize the only thing protecting you from yourself was *other people*. Left to my own devices, I will eat frosting out of the jar with a spoon and call it "meal prep."

*(grins)*

Thanks, you've been great! Good night!

---

**Runtime:** ~3 minutes at natural speaking pace (~420 words).

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’m going to keep this to three minutes, which means I have to talk fast, and I have to be honest. I don’t do puns. Puns are for people who want to be clever without having feelings. I have feelings, and they are mostly annoyed.

Let’s start with doors. Have you noticed how doors now have personality? Not the door itself—the thing attached to the wall. The automatic door. You walk up, and it’s like, “I don’t know you. Prove you deserve me.” You stand there. You do the little shuffle. Nothing. You raise a hand like you’re about to pledge allegiance to a vending machine. Still nothing. Finally it sighs and slides open like it’s doing you a favor. And then when you leave, it closes so gently you think it’s whispering, “Don’t come back.”

And doors are better than elevators. Elevators have no personality and too much power. You get in with six strangers and suddenly you’re in a social experiment designed by a monk. Nobody looks up. Nobody breathes loud. If your phone rings, you decline it like you’re defusing a bomb. And then someone says, “It’s a beautiful day,” and everyone else stares at that person like, “Pick a lane, Karen. We’re in a metal box falling through a shaft. Pick a lane.”

Which brings me to food. I went to a coffee shop and ordered a coffee. Just coffee. Black. The barista asked if I wanted to “explore my palate.” I told her my palate is fine. It’s not lost. It doesn’t need a wellness retreat. I just want caffeine so I can pretend to listen to my coworkers. She gave me something that tasted like dirt water and hope. I drank it and my anxiety got artisanal.

And the cups. They write your name on the cup. They never spell it right. I’m not “Shawn.” I’m not “Shon.” I’m not “Shaun with a U, like a you.” I’m the guy who’s about to be late for a meeting because you’re drawing a smiley face on my cup like we’re going on a date. We’re not going on a date. This is caffeine and regret.

Speaking of meetings. Work. Why do we all pretend we know what “bandwidth” means? Someone says, “I don’t have the bandwidth,” and everyone nods like it’s a real limitation. I don’t have the bandwidth. I don’t have the Wi-Fi. I don’t have the emotional support router. I have a desk and a will to live that gets weaker every time someone says, “Let’s circle back.” Circle back to what? To the thing we didn’t want to do in the first place? If I wanted to go in circles, I’d marry a revolving door.

And dating. Don’t get me started. I went on a date and the guy asked, “What are your dealbreakers?” I said, “People who ask what my dealbreakers are on a first date.” He said, “That’s a dealbreaker.” I said, “Congratulations. You just broke the deal.” Now I’m single, and my only match is with a toaster that keeps burning my bread but at least it’s consistent.

I’m not asking for much. I just want a door that opens when I get there. Coffee that tastes like coffee. A meeting that ends on time. And a dating app that just says, “You’re fine. They’re fine. Go eat something.” But instead, I get artisanal anxiety, sliding doors that judge me, and a name spelled “X Æ A-12” on a cup I paid six dollars for.

And you know what? I’ll take it. Because tomorrow I’ll do it again. I’ll shuffle at the door. I’ll ride the elevator with strangers who are pretending not to hear my stomach growl. I’ll drink the dirt water. And I’ll be here, telling you about it, because at least for three minutes, we’re all in the same box, sliding open, pretending we’re not terrified, and trying not to spill the coffee.

Thank you. You’ve been great.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
*(Strolls to center stage, adjusts mic, gives a weary smile to the audience)*

Thank you. Thank you so much. That’s very kind. I’m glad you’re all here. Because I have some news. I have finally figured out adulthood.

It happened about six months ago. I bought a house. And the second you buy a house, you are inducted into a secret society. And the only rule of this society is: you will now spend every weekend at a hardware store, buying a tool you already own, to fix a problem you don’t understand, in a room you forgot existed.

And the funny thing is, I used to think “homeowner” was a romantic term. Like, “Behold, a sovereign of his own domain.” Now I know it means “janitor with a mortgage.” I spend my Saturdays looking at PVC pipe joints. I have a favorite brand of caulk. I get excited about a wet-dry vacuum. I’m one more trip to Home Depot away from asking my plumber for his autograph.

But it’s not just the house. The real trap is the “life maintenance” you have to do. Every day, I’m hit with a bizarre, impossible task. Yesterday, I had to find the exact tiny, proprietary battery for my bathroom scale. It’s not an AA. It’s not a AAA. It’s called a CR-2032. It looks like a silver aspirin. I spent an hour online searching for it. I didn’t lose weight that day. I just lost an hour of my life to a battery the size of a booger.

*(Pause, more conversational)*

And let’s talk about work. I do a corporate job. And I’ve noticed an interesting phenomenon. The more important my job title sounds, the more time I spend on tasks that are absolutely meaningless. My day is now 80% “moving a file from one folder to another folder three clicks away.” And then I get an email: “Great job on the file migration, team!” I am a digital janitor.

The other 20% is a meeting to schedule another meeting to prepare for the first meeting. And we spend the first 10 minutes of every meeting talking about the *weather*. We all just watched the weather. We all just saw the same weather. We’re all trapped indoors, together! The weather is the one thing we have in common, the one universal human experience we all just had, and we’re using it to avoid talking about the Q3 projections.

*(Takes a breath, switches tone to slightly conspiratorial)*

But you know what the ultimate trap is? The thing I’m most tired of? Silence in a house with another person.

I’m in a long-term relationship. And we recently moved in together. And you realize that when you live alone, you lie to yourself. You think, “I’m a tidy person.” Then someone moves in. And suddenly, you realize you’re not tidy. You’re just… less messy than your parents.

But the worst part is the negotiation. For example: the dishwasher. You ever notice that loading a dishwasher is not a chore. It’s a political stance. A religious affiliation. How you load a dishwasher is who you are as a person. I’m a “stack-er.” Everything goes on the top rack. Glasses, mugs, the stray measuring cup. My partner is a “Tetris-master” who believes every single item has one, specific, sacred place.

So now, every night, we have a silent, passive-aggressive chess match. I load the dishwasher my way. She comes in ten minutes later, sighs like I just kicked a puppy, and re-loads it her way. And I have to pretend I didn’t see her do it. This is our relationship. We communicate entirely through the rearrangement of dirty plates.

*(Leans into mic, more direct)*

So that’s where I’m at. I’m a guy who owns a favorite brand of caulk, moves digital files for a living, and has a silent, ongoing war over cutlery orientation. And the crazy part? I’m happier than ever. Because I’ve finally learned the most important lesson of being an adult:

It’s not about solving the problems. It’s about getting really good at negotiating the terms of the surrender.

Thank you, you’ve been a great room. *(Exits, with a wave)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
(Strolls to center stage, grabs the mic, grins)

You ever notice how companies are like, “Your call is very important to us,” and then immediately prove they’re lying by making you navigate a phone menu designed by a sadist? I called my bank last week because I had a simple question. Just one question. And the robot voice goes, “Please say your sixteen-digit account number.” I don’t know it by heart! I’m not a spy memorizing launch codes. So I mumble something, and it says, “I didn’t get that. Let’s try a different approach. Please say your full name.” I say my name. “I think you said, ‘Elephant Gerald.’ Is that correct?” No! How did you get Elephant Gerald from a name that has zero elephants in it? Now I’m yelling “REPRESENTATIVE” like it’s a safe word.

And finally, a human picks up. But she says, “Can you verify your sixteen-digit account number?” You called me, essentially! You dragged me through a voice maze, subjected me to hold music that sounds like a saxophone falling down stairs, and now you want me to prove I’m me? This is the only relationship where I have to prove my identity after you’ve already interrupted my breakfast.

Speaking of hold music—what is that? They pick the most distorted, crackly, sad jazz you’ve ever heard, as if to say, “We’re sorry you’re waiting. Here’s a musical representation of your soul decaying.” And every two minutes, a recorded voice breaks in: “Did you know you can do this online?” YES, I KNOW, but your website asked for my password, which I forgot, and the password reset sent a code to an email I haven’t used since I was nineteen and had a vampire-themed username. So now I’m locked out of my own money because teenage me thought “Nosferatina4ever” was a good idea.

And why is it that when you finally explain your simple question—like, “Hey, was that a fee or a mistake?”—they transfer you? “Let me get you to our Specialist department.” Then you hear *click*… and hold music starts again, but this time it’s a pan flute version of a song you hate. I’m convinced Specialist department is just a guy named Steve who has a slightly better chair. He gets on, you repeat the whole story, and he says, “Hmm, that is strange. Hold on.” And back to the saxophone. The cycle of life.

At this point, I’ve aged. I started the call as a hopeful young person and now I’m a weathered ghost. By the time they solve it, I’m just grateful. They could tell me my account is now in Ecuador as long as they stop the pan flute. “Thank you for calling, is there anything else?” Yeah, can you erase my memory of the last forty-five minutes? Great. Bye. *click* And then I realize—they never fixed the fee, did they? And I have to call back tomorrow. (Mimes screaming into the void) Goodnight!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
So I’ve been trying to be healthier lately, which is just a polite way of saying I bought vegetables and watched them die slowly in my refrigerator.

Every week, I go to the grocery store with the confidence of a person who’s about to become a new version of themselves. I’m like, “This week? Spinach. Salmon. Blueberries. Greek yogurt.” I get home, put it all away, and then immediately order pizza because “I don’t want to mess up the kitchen.”

That’s adulthood: spending $84 on ingredients so you can feel guilty while eating takeout over the sink.

And groceries have gotten so expensive. The other day I picked up a carton of eggs and checked the price like I was buying jewelry. I was holding them with two hands, like, “Do you have financing options?” The cashier scanned them and I whispered, “Be careful, those are my retirement plan.”

I’m also trying to exercise, but gyms are weird. Everyone at the gym looks like they know what machine does what. I walk in and every piece of equipment looks like it was designed to interrogate me.

There’s always one machine where you sit down, grab two handles, push with your legs, pull with your arms, and somehow your neck hurts. And there’s no instructions, just a little diagram of a faceless human doing it perfectly. That diagram is so judgmental. It’s like, “Simply become this triangle man.”

And personal trainers are intense. They’ll say things like, “We’re going to activate your core.” I don’t even know if my core is still on the payroll. My body has departments I haven’t contacted in years.

I tried a fitness class once. The instructor was like, “Listen to your body.” My body was saying, “Leave.” But apparently you’re not supposed to listen to that part.

Everyone else was moving in sync, and I was always half a beat behind, like a haunted office chair. At one point the instructor said, “Great energy!” and looked directly past me, which felt fair.

The worst part about trying to improve yourself is your phone gets involved. My phone is constantly giving me little reports on my behavior like it’s my parole officer.

“Your screen time was up 18% this week.” Okay, phone, you were there too. Don’t act innocent. You’re not reporting a crime you didn’t participate in.

And it always says it so calmly. “You averaged 7 hours and 42 minutes a day.” That’s not a statistic, that’s a cry for help with a battery icon.

Then it breaks it down by app, which is cruel. It’ll be like, “You spent 3 hours on maps.” Maps? Where was I trying to go? Emotionally?

And the apps all want notifications. Every app thinks it’s urgent. My flashlight app is like, “Allow notifications?” For what? “It’s dark now.” I know. That’s why I opened you.

Even my bank app sends notifications like it’s trying to scare me straight. “You spent $6.75 at a coffee shop.” Yeah, I was there. I made that mistake with my whole body.

I don’t need a notification every time I buy something. Imagine if a tiny accountant followed you around all day. You tap your card for a muffin and he just appears: “Interesting choice for someone with goals.”

Honestly, I think that’s why people say they want to live “off the grid.” They don’t want to chop wood or raise chickens. They just want one full day where no device tells them they’re failing.

That’s my real wellness plan: fewer notifications, more naps, and a fridge full of vegetables that at least died believing in me.

question: standup-routine

content:
**Title: The Unexpected Item**
**Time: Approx. 3 Minutes**
**Style: Observational / Storytelling**
**Constraint Check: Zero puns used.**

**(Comedian walks to the mic, adjusts the stand, looks at the audience.)**

How's everyone doing? You look good. You look like you've successfully navigated the self-checkout today. That's a win. That deserves applause.

I'm convinced we're all just faking it with technology. We're all bluffing. I have a smart speaker in my kitchen. I call it "The Cylinder of Judgment." I asked it to play "relaxing jazz" yesterday, and it played a recording of a garbage disposal fighting a cello. I didn't even correct it. I just stood there in the kitchen, listening to the screaming metal, and whispered, "You know what? Yeah. That's exactly how I feel."

I tried to set up a routine to make my life easier. I said, "Alexa, when I say 'I'm home,' turn on the lights, adjust the thermostat, and order a pepperoni pizza." So I walk in after a long day, drop my keys, and yell, "I'm home!" Nothing. Silence. I yell it again. Finally, the blue light spins up and it says, "I found a bakery named 'I'm Home' in Ohio. Want me to call them?"

I don't want a bakery! I want pizza! But I can't argue with a plastic tube. I'm a grown adult taking advice from a device that doesn't know the difference between a light switch and a pizzeria. I feel like a toddler in a smart house.

And don't get me started on grocery stores. Self-checkout is a psychological thriller. You're in there, trying to scan your bananas, and suddenly the machine screams, "UNEXPECTED ITEM IN THE BAGGING AREA!"

There is no item! I'm looking at the bagging area. It's empty! But the machine has accused me of a crime. The red light starts flashing. The shame light. You're standing there waving your hands like you're trying to restart a router from 2004. Then the teenager at the desk looks over. He's chewing gum so hard his jaw is a separate entity. He doesn't even walk over. He just points at you. "You gotta rescan your existence, buddy."

And passwords. Why do passwords have to be a capital letter, a number, a symbol, and the blood of a virgin? I tried to change my password and it said, "Too similar to previous password." How is it too similar? It's the exact same words! It's not similar, it's identical! The computer is lying to me. It's gaslighting me. I'm being gaslit by an app that sells me shoes.

I went on a date last week, and it felt just like the self-checkout. Met on an app. Profile said he liked "long walks" and "trying new restaurants." I showed up, and he's already holding the menu, critiquing the font size. He looks up and goes, "If they can't space these letters correctly, what's the steak quality?"

We get the check, and he pulls out a calculator. He's splitting the bill down to the penny. "You had tap water. I had tap water with a lemon wedge. I put the lemon in. You didn't. So I owe you four cents." I sat there thinking, "The algorithm matched us because we both have anxiety about money, didn't it?"

But look, we keep doing it. We keep yelling at the robot. We keep scanning our own groceries. We keep swiping. Why? Because deep down, we're all just hoping for the best-case scenario at the checkout. We're all just waiting for that moment where the machine stops, the light turns green, and someone says, "Unexpected item in the bagging area."

And you look over, and it's just the person you've been looking for. You're the unexpected item! You're the surprise! You're the good kind of error!

Thank you, you've been amazing! Drive safe!

**(Comedian waves, exits.)**

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**(Stage direction: Walk out, adjust the mic stand, take a breath. Smile like you're about to confess something.)**

**[0:00 – 0:30] Intro: The Illusion of Choice**

Hey everyone. How's it going? Good? Good.

You know, people talk about "Adulting" like it's a skill you learn. Like there's a class you pass. I took that class. I failed. Being an adult isn't a skill; it's just a series of small, meaningless choices that we pretend matter.

Remember when you were a kid? The hardest decision was: Do I eat the cookie now, or save it for later? That was it. That was the burden. Now? I have to choose between the "Eco-friendly Bamboo Toothbrush" and the "Charcoal-infused Bamboo Toothbrush with a hint of mindfulness."

What does mindfulness taste like? Is it minty? Or is it just expensive anxiety?

**[0:30 – 1:15] Bit 1: The Grocery Store & Brenda**

I went to the grocery store yesterday. I just wanted milk. Just milk. But I'm in the dairy aisle, staring at a label that says, "Grass-fed, regenerative agriculture, happy-cow approved."

I'm holding a carton that costs twelve dollars, reading the backstory of the cow. Her name is Brenda. Brenda has a therapist. Brenda meditates. And I'm thinking, "Brenda, I just need some calcium. I don't need your trauma healing in my cereal."

Then I get to the self-checkout. The machine immediately hates me. I scan the milk, and it yells, "Unexpected item in bagging area!"

I put the milk in the bag! That's the plan! I'm shouting at a kiosk, "I am bagging the milk, Brenda! I am the bagger now! That's my job!" A teenager in a vest has to come over and tap a screen to let me live. I'm begging a seventeen-year-old for permission to buy dairy. I'm an adult; my back hurts and I have a mortgage. Let me bag the milk.

**[1:15 – 2:00] Bit 2: The Sleep Tracker**

It's not just shopping. It's how we're supposed to live. I bought a sleep tracker watch. Great idea, right? I want to sleep better. So I wear this device to monitor my sleep.

And the first thing it tells me is that I'm a terrible sleeper. "Good morning," it says. "You only achieved 40% deep sleep. Your heart rate variability suggests you are stressed about your sleep heart rate variability."

Now I'm stressed! I woke up, looked at the watch, saw a red frowny face, and immediately my blood pressure spiked. So now I have to go to sleep *trying* to sleep so the watch doesn't judge me tomorrow.

It's like having a teacher sit in on your dream to give you a grade. "B-minus for REM cycle. You were tossing and turning during the commercial break. See me after class."

I'm lying in bed, whispering, "Please, watch, I'm trying. I'm closing my eyes. Don't dock my points!" I'm negotiating with my wrist like it's a hostage situation.

**[2:00 – 2:30] Bit 3: The Quick Sync**

And don't get me started on the "Quick Sync." You know this email? "Hey, do you have five minutes for a quick sync?"

I don't. I literally do not have five minutes. My life is a series of five-minute segments where I answer to other people. If I had five minutes, I'd use it to stare at a wall and remember what my own face feels like.

But no, I click the link. I join the call. And I have to turn on my camera. I look like a goblin. I haven't shaved since the Obama administration. I just want to whisper into a microphone from under a blanket, but no, I have to perform wellness.

And they say, "Thanks for the quick sync!" It took twelve minutes. We spent twelve minutes discussing the five minutes we just wasted. I left that call realizing I've been an adult for twenty years and I still don't know how to say "No" without writing a three-paragraph apology email that includes a GIF of a handshake.

**[2:30 – 3:00] Outro: Survival Mode**

So, I made a resolution. I'm simplifying. I'm going back to basics.

No more Brenda the cow. No more sleep grading. No more syncing.

Tonight, I'm eating a sandwich. I'm going to bed when I'm tired. And if my watch beeps, I'm throwing it out the window. Because adulting isn't about optimization. It's about survival.

And right now, I'm surviving on caffeine, denial, and the hope that one day, the milk will just be milk.

Thank you, you've been great!

**(Stage direction: Drop the mic, wave, walk off.)**

question: standup-routine

content:
**Title: High-Maintenance Electronics**
**Time:** Approx. 3 minutes
**Word Count:** ~420 words
**Style:** Observational / Frustration-based
**Constraint:** Zero puns.

**(Walk to mic, adjust stand. Take a deep breath. Look tired.)**

I've reached that age where I'm just trying to negotiate with my own life. I'm not fighting for my dreams anymore; I'm fighting for the ability to get a glass of water without my knees making a sound like a bag of chips falling down a staircase.

So, naturally, I let technology take the wheel. I bought a "Smart Home" system. And I want to address the naming convention here. It's a misnomer. It's not smart. It's just high-maintenance. It's like a cat, but electronic. It doesn't do anything for me; it just judges me and occasionally locks me out of my own kitchen.

I started with a smart speaker. Classic. I just wanted convenience. I didn't want a roommate who mishears me.

Last night, I was trying to relax. I'm lying in bed, and I say, "Alexa, play some relaxing music."

And it plays "The Sound of Silence" by Disturbed. At maximum volume.

I live alone! I wasn't trying to summon a demon! I just wanted to hear a harp! And right in the middle of the scream-guitar solo, it pauses and says, "I'm sorry, I didn't catch that. Would you like to add 'Exorcism' to your shopping list?"

No! I want to add "Sleep" to my shopping list! But you can't buy sleep!

And it's not just the speaker. My fridge is smart now. It has a touchscreen. Great. So now, to find the ketchup, I have to unlock a tablet inside a cold box. It's 2:00 AM. I'm wearing sweatpants that haven't seen sunlight since 2019. I just want a slice of cold pizza.

But the fridge goes, *"Please enter your passcode."*

I don't have a passcode for my lunch! I'm a prisoner in my own house! And they put a camera in there! So now, if I'm eating cheese at 3 AM, my data is on the cloud. I'm sure Amazon has a profile on me. *"User consumed four pounds of cheddar. Recommended action: Shame yourself."*

It's embarrassing. I tried to turn on my smart TV last night, and the screen went black. I thought the power died. I was panicking. Then a little progress bar appeared. *"Updating: 45%."*

I screamed at the TV, "I don't care about the new features! I just want to see if my team is winning! You have ruined my life for a patch note on the remote control!"

We aren't the masters of our devices; we're the customer service reps for our own electronics. I'm down there with a screwdriver, whispering, "Hey, bulb, if you don't turn on, I'm going to leave you in the box forever." And it works. It flickers on. I win.

I've lowered myself to bickering with appliances. And the worst part? My smart watch just buzzed. It's telling me I should meditate to reduce stress.

I hit "Snooze" on my wrist.

I'm losing the battle. Thank you, you've been great!

**(Wave and exit.)**

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**Title: The Passive-Aggressive Universe**
**Time:** Approx. 3 Minutes
**Word Count:** ~380 words (allows for pauses, laughter, and delivery speed)

**(Walk to mic, adjust stand, take a breath. Look at the audience with a tired smile.)**

You know how we're supposed to be living in a utopia? Technology is supposed to make life easier. But lately, I feel like the universe is just pranking us with passive-aggressive inanimate objects.

Take the microwave. I put my leftovers in. Thirty seconds. I walk away to check my phone, just a quick glance. I come back, and the microwave has screamed at me so loud I'm pretty sure the neighbors called the police. It's not just a beep; it's an accusation. *Beep-beep-beep.* It's like, "You forgot me. I am cold. You are a bad person. I hope you choke on your own sadness."

I've actually developed a relationship with my microwave. I have to say, "Hey buddy, you're doing great," before it accepts the time. If I don't compliment it, it runs for forty-five seconds and turns my lasagna into a carbon brick.

And self-checkout. Don't get me started. I love self-checkout because I love being yelled at by a robot. You're scanning your stuff, feeling independent, and then—BAM. "Unexpected item in bagging area."

What is unexpected? Me! I'm the unexpected item! I'm holding the banana! The machine doesn't trust me. It's like a paranoid jailer. It sees me move my hand near the produce and it thinks, "Oh, look at that. The human is thinking about swiping a grape. Lock down! I'm calling security!"

Then it asks for a signature. On a banana. Who needs a signature for a banana? Do I need my mom's permission? "Sorry, machine, I can't sign for this produce, my mom says I'm not ready for fresh fruit."

It's not just machines, though. It's signs. You know the sign that says, "Please Close the Door After You." Why is that a sign? Why is that a rule? If people were actually closing the door, there would be no sign. The sign is the evidence of failure. It's a confession. It's the building admitting, "We have tried everything. We have locked the handle. We have bribed the janitor. But you guys are still letting the heat out. Please help."

Even the thermostat is judging me. The thermostat is the most passive-aggressive object in the house. You change it by one degree, and the whole house knows. The AC kicks on like you just declared war. "Oh, you want 72? Well, I'm going to 68 and fighting for it! You think you're the boss? I control the air quality!"

And don't get me started on passwords. You try to create a password, and it says, "Must contain a capital letter, a number, a symbol, and the blood of a virgin." I'm like, "I just want to reset my email!"

And then you reset it, and it says, "New password cannot be the same as the old password." Well, the old password was "Password123" because I'm an idiot, but now you're gaslighting me. You're telling me I'm not the same person I was five minutes ago.

We're not masters of the universe. We're just tenants in a smart home that thinks we're idiots. And the worst part? The Wi-Fi always goes out right when you're trying to prove them wrong.

**(Nod to audience, step back.)**

Thank you, you've been great!

content:
Here is a 3-minute stand-up routine focused on observational humor, relatability, and escalation. It contains **zero puns**. The humor relies on the shared frustration of modern digital security.

**Title: The Human Verification Test**
**Estimated Time:** 3 Minutes (approx. 430 words with pauses and act-outs)
**Style:** Observational / Frustration / Act-out

***

**(Walk on stage, adjust mic, look exhausted.)**

**COMEDIAN:**
How's everyone doing? Good? I'm tired. I spent forty-five minutes this morning trying to prove I'm a human being to a website that sells discount socks.

You know this struggle. It starts with the password. I type in "Fluffy123." The computer laughs at me. A red box pops up: *"Password must contain a capital letter, a number, a symbol, and the blood of a virgin."*

So now my password is `X9#mK!2$zL`. I have no idea what that is. I have to write it down. Where? On a yellow sticky note attached to the bottom of my keyboard. That's security! I'm protecting my bank account with paper and glue. If a hacker breaks into my house, they just have to lift the keyboard. "Aha! The treasure!"

And then the site says, *"Password cannot be the same as your last ten passwords."*

Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't realize I was creating a lineage. Do I need a family tree for my login? "This is Password the Third. He died in the data breach of 2022. Rest in peace, buddy."

**(Pause for laugh.)**

Finally, you get the password in. You think you're safe? No. Now comes the boss battle. Two-Factor Authentication.

*"We have sent a code to your device."*

Which device? I have a phone, a tablet, a laptop, and a refrigerator that judges my milk consumption. The code is on the fridge. I'm in the bedroom. The code expires in thirty seconds.

Suddenly, I'm an Olympic sprinter. I'm diving into the kitchen. I rip open the fridge door. The light comes on. The code is there. `4-8-2-9`. I run back. I'm panting. I type `4-8-2...`

The screen turns red. *"Code Expired."*

I'm standing there, sweating, holding a half-eaten yogurt, defeated by a timer. The website is basically saying, "Nice try, robot. Humans run faster."

**(Act out the panic of the phone delay.)**

And sometimes the text doesn't even come. You hit "Send Code." Nothing. You wait. You hit it again. Nothing. You go take a shower. You're shampooing your hair, eyes closed, and *buzz*. The text arrives.

You fumble for the phone with wet hands. You're naked, sliding across the bathroom floor, screaming "WHAT'S THE CODE?" You look at the screen. *"Your code is 5555."* Sent twenty minutes ago. I'm just washing my hair in defeat now.

**(Pause.)**

If you fail that, you get the ultimate insult. The Captcha.

*"Select all squares containing a traffic light."*

I have a college degree. I pay a mortgage. But I'm sweating over a grid of blurry pixels. I click the lights. But then I panic. Does the pole count?

This is the moral dilemma of our generation. If I click the pole, am I safe? Or if I click the pole, does the nuclear launch sequence start?

I leave the pole. I hit "Verify." The box shakes. *"Please try again."*

Try again?! I missed a sliver of a crosswalk? That's it? I'm questioning my reality. Maybe I *am* a bot. Maybe my whole life is a simulation and I just failed the update.

**(Wind down, calmer tone.)**

By the time I get through, I've aged four years. My hands are shaking. I finally log in. I'm verified. I'm human. I'm inside the account.

And I stare at the screen. I forgot what I wanted. Socks? I don't need socks. I need therapy.

I close the laptop. The screen goes black. My reflection stares back. And I whisper, "Face ID recognized."

Because at this point, even I don't trust me.

Thank you, you've been great!

***

### Performance Notes:
*   **Timing:** The word count is optimized for a 3-minute set assuming a standard stand-up cadence with pauses for laughter. If the audience laughs hard, pause and let it ride; the routine is modular enough to trim the "Shower" or "Lineage" tags if you're running long.
*   **Delivery:** The humor comes from the escalation of frustration. Start conversational, build the physical energy during the "Sprinter/Fridge" and "Shower" bits, and drop to a deadpan exhaustion for the Captcha and Outro.
*   **No Puns:** This routine avoids wordplay entirely. The jokes are based on hyperbole, relatable scenarios, physical act-outs, and the absurdity of technology treating users like enemies.

content:
Alright, hello everyone! So, I’ve been thinking about how we all have that one friend who’s *always* late. Not just late—like, fashionably late. Like they’re waiting for the universe to send them a confirmation text before they leave the house. “Is it okay to arrive yet? Has the planet aligned? Did Mercury retrograde clear?” Meanwhile, I’m standing outside in the rain, checking my watch like it’s a lifeline.

And don’t even get me started on group chats. You send a message, and someone replies three days later with, “Sorry, I was busy.” Busy doing what? Reorganizing their sock drawer? Watching paint dry? I once saw someone type “BRB” and come back 47 hours later like nothing happened. That’s not “be right back”—that’s “biological reboot.”

Also, why do we still say “I’ll call you” when nobody calls anymore? It’s like saying “I’ll send you a carrier pigeon.” We just text “k” and pretend that counts as communication. My mom still leaves voicemails—actual voicemails—with full sentences, punctuation, and emotional depth. Meanwhile, I’m over here sending voice notes that are just me whispering “uhhh… never mind…” into my phone at 2 a.m.

Anyway, thanks for listening! Remember: if you’re late tonight, don’t apologize—just blame Mercury. Works every time. Good night!

content:
Alright, so I decided this year I was finally going to become one of those organized people. You know, the ones who meal prep on Sundays and have matching Tupperware. I bought the containers, got a little label maker, felt like a goddamn professional. Cooked enough chicken and rice to feed a small army. By Wednesday the rice had turned into a science experiment and I was eating cereal over the sink at 11 p.m. like a raccoon who pays rent.

The worst part is how quickly your own body betrays you once you try to be responsible. I joined a gym. Not one of those fancy ones with the juice bar—just a regular place where the equipment makes concerning noises. Signed up for a class because I figured someone yelling at me would be motivating. The instructor looked like she could deadlift a Buick. She says, “We’re starting with burpees.” I had never done one. I thought maybe it was a baby noise. Ten minutes in I’m on the floor, not resting, just fully accepting that this is how I die. Meanwhile the woman next to me, who’s probably 65, is still going like she’s late for something. I asked her what her secret was. She said she has three grandkids under five. That’s the real workout—trying to stop a toddler from eating a houseplant while simultaneously negotiating with another one about pants. Compared to that, burpees are apparently a vacation.

I realized then that discipline isn’t about motivation or apps or color-coded calendars. It’s about consequences that actually scare you. Like if I don’t do laundry, I have to wear the weird shirt from 2019 that says something I no longer agree with. If I don’t pay my credit card, some guy named Chad from the bank is going to call me “buddy” in that tone that makes you want to move to another country. The only thing that actually gets me out of bed early is the knowledge that if I don’t respond to my boss’s email by 9 a.m., I have to spend the rest of the day pretending I was “in meetings” when really I was just emotionally unavailable.

So now I’ve stopped pretending I’m going to become that organized person. I just try to be the kind of adult who remembers to buy toilet paper before the current roll becomes a historical artifact. Low bar, but at least I’m clearing it.

content:
(Walks onto the stage, adjusts the mic stand, looks around the room.)

So, I recently turned thirty. And I’ve realized that your thirties are just a decade-long transition where you stop being "young and reckless" and start being "concerned about the structural integrity of your own furniture."

I spent my entire twenties sleeping on a mattress that was essentially a pile of gym socks held together by hope. I didn't care. Now? I went to a friend’s house, sat on a beanbag chair, and I had to call a Uber to get out of it. I just sat there. I had to look at my friend and say, "This is my life now. Leave me here. Tell my family I died doing what I loved—experiencing lumbar support failure."

And you know you’re getting older when your body starts making noises that sound like a dial-up modem connecting to the internet. I stood up yesterday, and my knee made a sound like a wet sponge being wrung out. Just *squeak-crunch*. I’m not even doing anything! I’m just existing! Gravity is just bullying me at this point. 

I’ve also started noticing that I have "old person" opinions now. I went to a restaurant last week, and the music was so loud I had to ask the waiter to speak into my good ear. I’m twenty-something, but I’m yelling, "WHAT? IS THIS THE NEW TAYLOR SWIFT? IT SOUNDS LIKE A VACUUM CLEANER FALLING DOWN A FLIGHT OF STAIRS!"

And the waiter is just looking at me like I’m a Victorian ghost who just wandered into a Chili’s. 

But the worst part of adulthood is the "Email Anxiety." You know what I’m talking about. You get an email from your boss, or your landlord, or—God forbid—your dentist. And you see the notification on your phone, and your heart rate goes from 60 to 180 in half a second. 

I stare at the phone like it’s a bomb. I’m like, "I can’t open this. If I don't open it, it doesn't exist. It’s Schrödinger’s Email. Until I click it, I am both employed and unemployed." I’ll spend three hours pacing my apartment, mentally drafting a response to an email I haven’t even read yet. I’m preparing a defense for a crime I haven’t committed. 

Then I finally open it, and it’s just, "Hey, can you send me that spreadsheet?" 

And I’m like, "Oh. Okay. I’ve already lived through the stages of grief, but sure, I’ll send the spreadsheet."

(Pause)

I think that’s why we’re all so obsessed with true crime podcasts. It’s the only way we can feel something. My life is just "did I leave the stove on?" and "is this light headache actually a brain tumor?" So I listen to a podcast about a guy who built a bunker in the woods, and I’m like, "Honestly? I get it. He just wanted to be away from his notifications. He’s the most relatable person I’ve ever heard of."

My therapist told me I need to "practice mindfulness." I tried it. I sat in a chair, closed my eyes, and tried to focus on my breath. Within thirty seconds, my brain went, "Hey, remember that embarrassing thing you said to a coworker in 2014? Let’s analyze that for the next four hours." 

I don't need mindfulness. I need a lobotomy or a nap. Preferably both.

Anyway, I’m gonna go home, sit on my couch, and pray my back doesn't give out before I reach the remote. Thank you, you’ve been great!

content:
**Title: "Modern Survival Guide"**  

[*Stage lights up. Comedian leans on stool, grinning.*]  

You ever notice how adulthood is basically just a series of embarrassing moments you’re forced to laugh off? Like, the other day I tried to make a smoothie… *[pauses, mock serious]* …which is already a red flag, because I’m 32 and still call it a “smoothie.” I’m not five. I should be calling it a “nutritional slurry” or “adult chalk.”  

Anyway, I’m blending kale—*kale*, the leafy green that’s basically nature’s way of saying, “Hey, eat this and feel guilty about everything”—and I’m adding almond milk, which is just milk’s vegan cousin who’s always judging you. Then, *[snaps fingers]* disaster strikes! The blender starts making this noise like a lawnmower stuck in a tar pit. I’m standing there, holding the lid like, “If I let go, will this liquid murder me?”  

[*Mimes frantic blending, spilling green goo on shirt.*]  

Now I’m wearing a shirt that says, “I tried.” And let’s be honest, that’s the theme of my life. I “tried” to go to the gym yesterday. Walked in, saw a guy doing deadlifts while wearing a fanny pack and a visor. I was like, “Ah, yes, the three stages of man: baby, adult, and ‘I’ve peaked at 47.’”  

[*Pauses, nods.*]  

Speaking of peak adulthood, have you ever tried to assemble furniture? I bought a bookshelf last week. The instructions were in *Swedish*. Not kidding. I Googled “how to translate IKEA manuals,” and it just said, “Cry louder.” So I’m there, 45 minutes in, holding a wooden dowel like a sword, yelling, “WHERE DO YOU GO?!” My cat just stared at me like, “You’re the reason we can’t have nice things.”  

[*Mimes hammering finger, wincing.*]  

And don’t get me started on dating apps. It’s like shopping for a personality on clearance. You swipe left on “I enjoy long walks on the beach,” right on “I own a snake,” and then wonder why your love life feels like a National Geographic special. I matched with a guy whose bio said, “Here for a good time, not a long time.” I was like, “Sir, we’re 30. A ‘good time’ is finding socks that match.”  

[*Leans in, conspiratorial.*]  

But here’s the real kicker: technology. My phone knows more about me than I do. It suggests restaurants I’ve never heard of, tracks my sleep like a concerned parent, and once auto-corrected “I’m fine” to “I’m drowning in existential dread.” Thanks, Siri. You’re a real pal.  

[*Steps back, arms out.*]  

So yeah, adulthood’s great. It’s just a never-ending loop of trying not to embarrass yourself, failing, and then laughing so you don’t cry. But hey, at least we’re all in this together… unless you’re that IKEA manual. Then you’re just laughing *at* us.  

[*Exit stage left, tripping over imaginary stool.*]  

[End.]  

**Timing Notes**:  
- Opener/smoothie bit: ~45 sec  
- Gym/furniture assembly: ~1 min  
- Dating apps/tech: ~1 min  
- Closing/exit: ~30 sec  
*Total: ~3 minutes*  

**Key Elements**:  
- Relatable absurdity (smoothies, IKEA, dating apps)  
- Physical comedy (miming blending, hammering)  
- Self-deprecating humor with a wink  
- No puns—just observations with a twist

content:
**[The comedian walks onto the stage, adjusts the mic stand, and smiles at the crowd.]**

How’s everyone doing tonight? 

*(Wait for response)*

Good, good. I’m doing okay, but I recently crossed a major threshold in my life. I hit the age where my body has started making its own decisions without consulting me first. 

When you’re in your twenties, you injure yourself doing cool things. Skateboarding, snowboarding, jumping off a roof into a pool. 

Now? I get injured by sleeping. 

I woke up yesterday with a sprained neck. *Sleeping.* How do you even explain that to a doctor? 

"Well, Doc, I was completely unconscious for eight hours, and apparently, my pillow won the fight. I think it used a chokehold around 3:00 AM." 

My doctor didn't even look up. He just said, "Yeah, you’re thirty-five. That’s not an injury, that’s just how your neck looks now."

**[Pause for laughs. Shift weight.]**

So, because of this, I decided I needed to start stretching. Because that’s what we do when we get older, right? We don't exercise to get ripped anymore; we exercise so we can look at our shoes without groaning. 

I went to a yoga class. It’s wild in there. The instructor is at the front of the room, folded in half like a piece of origami, whispering, "Find your inner peace." 

Lady, my inner peace is currently trapped under my left hamstring, and it is screaming for help. I’m not stretching; I’m just making noises usually reserved for a haunted house. I looked around the room, and everyone else looked so serene. Meanwhile, I’m sweating through my shirt just trying to touch my shins. My shins! I didn’t even make it to the ankles. My body was like, "Whoa, buddy, who do you think we are? Cirque du Soleil? Go back to the couch."

**[Step forward, look down at wrist]**

And then there’s the technology. I bought a smartwatch to "track my health." Big mistake. I didn't buy a fitness tracker; I bought a tiny, passive-aggressive wrist-boss. 

It vibrates at 2:00 PM. I look down, and it says: *"It's time to stand up."* 

Excuse me? I am in the middle of a job interview. But the watch is like, *"I don't care about your career, Dave, stand up and wiggle."* 

And if I don't stand up, it judges me. It sends me a notification at the end of the day: *"You did not meet your movement goal today."* 

I know! I was sitting on the couch eating block cheese! Mind your own business, Apple! You don't know my life!

But the absolute worst part is the sleep tracker. It tells me how bad my sleep was *after* I wake up. Yesterday, I woke up feeling great. I had energy. I was ready to take on the world. 

Then I looked at my watch: *"Your sleep quality was 34%. You are technically dead."* 

And instantly, I was exhausted. "Oh, wow, the watch is right. My bones *do* hurt. I need to cancel my plans." 

We’ve let machines take over our self-esteem. I miss the old days when you knew you were healthy just because you weren't currently on fire. 

Anyway, I’m going to go sit down before my watch vibrates and calls the cops on me. You guys have been great, thank you!

**[Wave, walk off stage]**

content:
I’ve reached the age where my body just randomly decides to be in pain. Not from an injury. Not from sports. Just from… existing. I woke up yesterday and my neck hurt. Why? Because I slept. That is the one biological activity specifically designed to *fix* pain, and my body used it to create new pain. You know you’re getting older when sleep stops being a basic human function and becomes a high-stakes negotiation.

So, I went to a mattress store to see if a new bed would help. Have you noticed how many mattress stores there are now? There are more mattress stores than people who need mattresses. It’s the only retail industry where the entire business model is based on you lying down in public while a guy named Greg watches you. 

Greg’s just standing there in a tight polo shirt, watching me try to get comfortable. I’m in my jeans, fully clothed, under harsh fluorescent lights, and Greg goes, “How does that feel?” It feels like I’m having a panic attack in a public square, Greg. And they make you take your shoes off. Why? It’s a mattress, not a mosque. I’m not praying to the polyurethane.

Eventually, Greg tried to upsell me on a "smart mattress." I don’t want my bed to be smart. I want it to be unconscious. That’s the whole point. I don’t need my mattress to have an app. I don’t need a push notification at 8:00 AM telling me my REM sleep was suboptimal. I already know my sleep was suboptimal, I was awake at 3:00 AM worrying about a weird look my boss gave me in 2018. I don’t need a pie chart confirming it. 

And what is the bed going to do with that data? It’s just going to judge me. It’s going to sync with my smart fridge and lock me out of the cheese drawer because I didn't get my eight hours.

So I gave up on the smart bed and bought a weighted blanket. Everyone told me, “It feels like a warm hug.” It doesn’t. It feels like a golden retriever is sitting on your chest while you try to breathe. The first night, I woke up trapped. I had to physically roll off the bed just to escape the blanket. I ended up on the floor, tangled in twenty pounds of glass beads, thinking, “This is how they catch ghosts.” I couldn't even reach my phone to call for help. Who would I call? The fire department? “Yes, hello, my bedding is being too aggressive.”

So now I just sleep on a regular, dumb mattress. No apps, no weights. Just me, a standard pillow, and the crushing realization that I have to wake up in six hours and do it all again. 

Thank you guys, you’ve been great. I’m going to go take an ibuprofen.

content:
**Stand-Up Routine: "Adulting Is a Scam"**

So I turned 30 recently, and everyone keeps asking me, "Do you feel like an adult yet?" And I have to be honest—no. No, I do not.

I still get nervous ordering at a restaurant. The waiter comes over and suddenly I forget how to talk like a person. "Yes, hello, I will have the... food. The food, please. With drink." Meanwhile my brain is screaming, *Don't mess this up, the waiter is judging you, the whole table is judging you, your dead grandmother is judging you.*

You know you're an adult when buying a houseplant feels like adopting a child. I bought one succulent—a succulent, the cactus's lazy cousin, the plant designed for people who kill plants—and I killed it. In a week. The internet said, "These are impossible to kill." I took that as a personal challenge and I won.

And nobody warns you about the laundry situation. As a kid, you just take off your clothes and they reappear, clean, folded, smelling like a meadow. It's like magic. Then you move out and discover laundry is a *system*. There are temperatures. There are settings. There's a thing called "delicates," which I assume is French for "I'm going to ruin this anyway."

I have a chair in my bedroom. You know the chair. It's not for sitting. It's the throne of clothes. It's a wardrobe purgatory where pants go to think about what they've done. Those clothes aren't clean, but they're not dirty enough for the wash. They exist in a third category—"feral."

And let's talk about texting, because I'm at the age now where I overthink every message. Somebody texts me "ok." Just "ok." Lowercase. No punctuation. And I spiral. "Are they mad at me? Is this passive aggressive? What did I do?" Meanwhile when *I* respond, I'm out here writing essays. "Hahaha yes totally, sounds great, let me know! 😊" Exclamation point, emoji, the works. I'm not a person, I'm a golden retriever with a phone.

The worst part of being an adult is that you have to *decide what to eat* every single day. Three times a day. Forever. Until you die. No one prepared me for this. I stand in my kitchen at 7 p.m. staring into the fridge like it's going to confess something. It does not. The fridge has nothing for me. The fridge contains ketchup, a wilted celery, and the broken dreams of someone who once said, "This week, I'm gonna meal prep."

I did meal prep once. I made five identical containers of chicken and rice on a Sunday. By Tuesday I hated my Sunday self so much. "Who DID this to me? Who thought I wanted the same sad lunch five days in a row?" That guy. That guy with the dream. He's gone now.

So no, I don't feel like an adult. But I have a houseplant graveyard and a chair full of feral pants, so I'm clearly thriving.

Thank you, you've been great!

content:
# "The Future Is Now and I Want a Refund"

*[Walks on stage, adjusts mic]*

So I was at the grocery store yesterday. Self-checkout. I love self-checkout. You know why I love self-checkout? Because nothing builds character like being publicly shamed by a machine.

*[Pause]*

I scanned a banana. Just a banana. And the screen said — I'm not making this up — "Unexpected item in bagging area." And I'm standing there, in line, holding the banana like it's a weapon, and I'm whispering to it, "It's a banana! It's a BANANA! What did you THINK it was?!"

*[Pause]*

And then some 19-year-old comes over with their little vest, and they look at the screen, and they look at me, and I'm just standing there like a criminal. A banana criminal. They'll never find out what I did with that produce.

You know what else I love? Food delivery apps. I have a complicated relationship with delivery apps. On one hand, I'm lazy. On the other hand, I have standards. So my algorithm is just a war zone.

I get suggestions like "Try this place! 30 minutes!" And I think, no. I want it in 15. Then it says "Try this other place! 45 minutes!" And I think, no, I'll be dead by then. So I end up eating crackers standing over the sink at 10:47 PM like a raccoon in a trench coat.

*[Pause]*

And don't get me started on the tipping. I ordered a sandwich. Through an app. That I found through a website. On a phone that cost me a thousand dollars. And at the end, it's like, "Tip your driver?" TIP MY DRIVER? Sir, I would like to tip the algorithms that conspired to make me pay $18 for a turkey sandwich in the first place. Where's THAT screen?

*[Pause]*

I joined a gym last month. Big mistake. The last time I was in shape, "in shape" meant I could eat a whole pizza without regret. Now I'm 38 and they're sending me emails like "It's been 14 days since your last visit." FOURTEEN DAYS. I've had leftovers in my fridge longer than that and I'm not judging THEM.

I went in last week. I used the treadmill. I put it on the "fat burn" setting because I thought that was a setting. It's not. It's just a setting that makes you hate yourself slower. I'm walking, and the screen is showing me a TV show, and I'm watching TV while exercising, which means I've essentially come full circle. I'm on a couch. Just a moving couch. In a room with strangers. Who are also on moving couches. And we all paid $60 a month for this.

*[Pause, leans into mic]*

But the worst part? The worst part of the gym is the mirror. They have mirrors everywhere. At the gym! It's like they WANT you to see yourself. Like, "Here. Here's a 360-degree view of your situation. Would you like to reconsider the taco truck you followed on Instagram?"

*[Longer pause for laugh]*

I'll tell you what, I saw my reflection doing a squat last week and made a sound I didn't know a human could make. It wasn't a grunt. It was a question. My body was ASKING me why.

*[Big pause]*

Anyway, technology is great. The future is now. And if anyone needs me, I'll be at the self-checkout, arguing with a scale about a banana. Thank you, you've been wonderful!

*[Bows, walks off]*

---

**Time estimate:** ~3 minutes at a natural stand-up pace
**Comedic techniques used:** observational humor, self-deprecation, callbacks (the banana/closing), rule of three (delivery app scenarios), hyperbole, relatable specifics
**No puns used** — all humor comes from observation, exaggeration, and absurd real-life comparisons

content:
*(Walks up to the mic, adjusts the stand, takes a deep breath)*

I am officially at the age where my body has a "check engine" light, but instead of a dashboard, it’s just a vague, lingering sense of dread in my lower back. 

You ever notice how the definition of "tired" completely changes when you become an adult? When you’re a kid, tired means you ran outside for three hours and ate a popsicle too fast. As an adult, tired means you blinked twice while sitting in a chair, and now you need a three-to-five business day recovery period. 

So, naturally, we try to fix it. We turn to "self-care." I recently fell for the self-care industrial complex. I spent forty dollars on a weighted blanket. The marketing says it’s supposed to "simulate the feeling of a comforting hug."Listen, I don’t need a blanket to simulate a hug. I need a responsible roommate who doesn’t eat the good yogurt. But I bought it anyway. 

Now, I go to bed, and I’m just trapped under thirty pounds of tiny glass beads. I’m sweating. I can’t roll over. I am basically mummifying myself in my own anxiety. I wake up in the middle of the night, and the only thing I can move is my left pinky toe. 

And then morning comes. The morning routine is no longer a routine; it’s a series of intense negotiations with gravity. You wake up, and your first thought isn't, "What are my goals for today?" It’s, "Can I make it to the coffee maker without my joints making a sound that alerts the neighbors?"

We treat coffee like it’s some kind of magical, ancient elixir. It’s not. It’s just hot bean water that makes your heart beat fast enough to remind you that you’re alive, but also late for a meeting you didn't want to attend anyway. 

We spend Monday through Friday dreaming about the weekend. We build it up in our heads like it’s a tropical vacation. We say, "Oh, Saturday is going to be amazing. I’m going to be so productive." 

Then Saturday arrives. And what do you actually do? You spend four hours staring at the ceiling, waiting for a sudden, magical surge of motivation to fold *one* single shirt. You finally build up the courage to stand up and do it, and your knee makes a sound like a glow stick cracking in the dark. 

So you just sit back down. 

And just like that, the weekend is over. You have achieved absolutely nothing, but you are somehow more exhausted than you were on Thursday. 

At this point, I’ve just accepted my fate. My ideal Friday night used to be going out, seeing friends, being vibrant. Now, my ideal Friday night is aggressively canceling plans that I made on Tuesday, when I was a much more optimistic, naive version of myself. 

I just want to put on sweatpants that have completely lost their elasticity, eat a meal that requires zero chewing, and pass out. And if my forty-dollar weighted blanket happens to just quietly crush me in my sleep? 

Honestly... at this point, it sounds like a fair trade. 

Thank you, you’ve been great! 

*(Waves, steps back from the mic)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**(Walk to mic, adjust stand, pause, look around the room)**

**Opener: The "Good Evening" Lie**
So, the host said, "Give it up for a very funny comedian!" And I walked out here thinking, *"Okay, who is it? Where are they?"* Then I realized… *oh no. It’s me.* 

I hate that moment. That split second where the audience realizes, *"Oh. **This** is the guy. We paid for **this**."* You can see the buyer’s remorse in your eyes already. It’s the same look I get when I order a salad at a burger place. *Why did I do this? I could have had bacon. Now I’m eating kale and regret.*

**(Bit 1: The Smart Home Dumb Human)**
I tried to modernize my apartment recently. I bought all the "Smart" stuff. Smart bulbs, smart thermostat, smart lock. The only thing in my apartment that isn't smart… is me. 

I’m sitting on the couch, phone in hand, talking to a cylinder like it’s a god. *"Hey Google, turn on the lights."* Nothing. *"Okay Google, lights on."* Nothing. *" **Google. Lights. Now.**"* 

And from the other room, my girlfriend yells, *"The internet is down!"* 

So there I am. In the dark. Holding a $800 brick. I have to use the **flashlight on my phone** to find the **manual switch** on the **smart bulb**. That is the peak of human evolution right there. We invented fire, we invented the wheel, we split the atom… so we could use a flashlight app to turn off a lightbulb that requires a firmware update.

And the thermostat? It has "Eco Mode." Which is just a fancy way of saying, *"We’re going to let you freeze to death to save Amazon three cents on server costs."* I wake up at 3 AM, shivering, checking my phone: *"Nest has entered Eco Mode. Current temp: 58 degrees. Would you like to buy a sweater from Amazon Basics?"* **Yes! Yes, I would! Charge it to the account I can't access because the smart lock froze shut!**

**(Bit 2: The Grocery Store Checkout Gauntlet)**
Grocery shopping used to be simple. You put food in a cart, you gave money, you left. Now it’s a psychological obstacle course. 

First, the **Self-Checkout**. Which is just unpaid labor with worse benefits. I’m scanning a cucumber. *"Place item in bagging area."* I place it. *"Unexpected item in bagging area."* **It’s the item you just told me to place!** 

Then the machine starts screaming: *"PLEASE WAIT FOR ASSISTANCE."* A red light spins on top like a police siren. An employee walks over, types in a code *without looking*, and walks away. **She didn't check my bag! She didn't verify the cucumber!** She just reset the machine so I could keep working for free. I should get a W-2 from Kroger at the end of the year.

And the **Keypad**. "Do you want cash back?" No. "Are you sure?" Yes. "Select 'No' to confirm." Why is "No" the confirmation button? That’s gaslighting. "Do you hate yourself?" *Select 'No' to confirm you hate yourself.*

Then the final boss: **"Round up for charity?"** 
Look, I *want* to save the manatees. I do. But you’re asking me this while I’m buying generic bran flakes and a single yogurt. The screen says: *"Round up 43 cents?"* 
If I say **No**, the screen turns red. It doesn't just say "No." It says: **"DECLINED."** Like I just got rejected for a mortgage. The lady behind me hears *"DECLINED"* and thinks, *"Wow. That guy really hates manatees. He hates them so much he won't spare pocket change."* 

Next time, just add 43 cents to the yogurt. Call it "The Manatee Tax." I’ll pay it happily. Just don't make me look like a villain in front of the lady buying the family pack of toilet paper.

**(Bit 3: The Group Chat Mental Load)**
Can we talk about Group Chats? Specifically, the **"Planning a Dinner" Group Chat**. 

It starts innocent. *"Hey guys, dinner next Saturday?"* 
Then the **Availability Olympics** begin. 
*"I can do 7 but not 7:15."*
*"I’m gluten-free now."*
*"Does the patio have heaters? My knee acts up when the barometric pressure drops."* 

**Nobody decides anything.** We just exchange constraints until the heat death of the universe. 

Then—**The Silent Vote.** Someone sends a screenshot of a Yelp page. No text. Just the screenshot. That is the modern "I second the motion." 
Then the **Emoji Reacts** start. 
Thumbs up. Thumbs up. Heart. **Laughing face.** 
*Who laughed? What is funny about the chicken parm?* 

And there is always **One Guy**. Let's call him Dave. Dave doesn't reply for 14 hours. Then, at 11:45 PM, Dave texts: *"What's the vibe?"* 
**The vibe is we have a reservation for 8, Dave! The vibe is you're eating a salad because the kitchen closes in 15 minutes!** 

But we love Dave. Because without Dave, we’d have to admit we just want to sit in a booth, eat mozzarella sticks, and complain about our backs. Which brings me to my close.

**(Closer: The Reality of "Going Out")**
I’m 34. "Going out" used to mean: *Pre-game, Uber, Club, Late-night pizza, Sunrise, Regret.* 

Now? "Going out" means: 
*"Hey, you wanna go to that place with the good chairs?"* 
*"Yeah. Does it have parking?"* 
*"Street parking only."* 
*"...Pass. I'll make pasta. I have a new parmesan grater."* 

And that is the best night of my life. I’m in sweatpants by 7:30. I’m grating cheese directly into my mouth over the sink like a goblin. No cover charge. No bouncer judging my shoes. Just me, a carbohydrate coma, and the sweet, sweet silence of a phone on **Do Not Disturb**. 

That’s the dream, folks. Not the yacht. Not the mansion. **The parmesan grater.** 

Thank you, you’ve been great. My name is [Name]!

**(Drop mic / wave / walk off to upbeat music)**

content:
# "Adulting Is a Scam"

Hey, how's everybody doing? Good? Liars. Nobody's doing good. We're all just out here pretending.

So I'm at the age now where my body has started making announcements. Like, I didn't ask for updates, but my knees have opinions now. I stood up off the couch last week and made a sound like I was deadlifting a refrigerator. I was holding a remote control. The remote weighs four ounces. My body was like, "Brace yourself. We're going UP."

And nobody warns you that becoming an adult is just slowly turning into your parents one complaint at a time. I caught myself last week saying — out loud, to no one — "Why is everything so loud in this restaurant?" Alone. At a table for one. Complaining to the breadsticks.

You know what else nobody prepares you for? Grocery shopping as an adult. As a kid, the grocery store was magical. You'd ride in the cart, you'd beg for cereal with a cartoon tiger on it. Now I walk in and immediately have a crisis in the produce section. I stand there holding an avocado like I'm defusing a bomb. Is it ready? Is it ripe? There's a four-hour window between "rock" and "soup," and I have missed it every single time. I have never once eaten an avocado at the correct moment. Not once. I'm either chiseling it or drinking it.

And can we talk about how adults make plans now? Making plans with friends in your thirties is like negotiating a hostage release. "Okay, I'm free March 14th." "I can't do March, what about June?" "June's bad, my kid has a thing." "Okay, what about... never? Does never work for everyone?" And then we all agree on never, and we're genuinely relieved. We text "we should really get together soon!" and both of us know that's a lie. That text is just friendship maintenance. It's like blowing on the embers of a fire neither of us actually wants to build.

But the real betrayal? The real betrayal is sleep. When I was seven, I fought sleep like it was trying to rob me. I'd negotiate. "Five more minutes!" Now? Sleep is all I want, and sleep wants nothing to do with me. I get in bed exhausted, and my brain goes, "Hey. Hey. Remember that embarrassing thing from 2009?" Yes, brain. Thank you. Let's review the footage. Again. At 2 a.m. In high definition.

And then I wake up injured. From sleeping. I slept aggressively, apparently. I pulled a muscle dreaming. My doctor asked what happened and I said, "I was unconscious in a soft, padded environment, and I lost."

So yeah, that's where I'm at. My knees announce my movements, I'm losing battles to avocados, and my own brain runs a true-crime podcast about my life every night.

But hey — at least I'm not doing good honestly. Like the rest of you.

You've been great! Good night!

content:
*(The comedian walks onto the stage, adjusts the mic, and looks at the audience with an expression of mild exhaustion.)*

Hey, everyone. Good to be here. 

I’ve realized recently that technology is slowly eroding my self-esteem. Specifically, those CAPTCHA tests online. You know what I’m talking about—the little boxes you have to check to "Prove you are not a robot." 

First of all, why is the burden of proof on me? 

*(Points to self)* 

The computer is the one built of code! I’m sitting here in sweatpants, eating dry cereal out of a coffee mug at two in the afternoon. I am clearly a biological disaster. No machine would ever willingly live like this. 

But the computer doesn't trust me. So it makes me play its sick little game. "Select all squares with traffic lights." 

And instantly, I am cast into a deep existential crisis. I’m staring at these nine blurry photos, and there is a tiny, microscopic sliver of a traffic light crossing over into the bottom-left box. 

Does that count? Does the artificial intelligence count the pole, or just the light? 

If I click it, does the website think, "Aha! Look at this idiot, he thinks a metal pole is a traffic light. Access denied!" 

Now I’m sweating. I’m second-guessing my own eyesight. I am losing a cognitive exam designed by a toaster. I click "Verify," and the website just gives me a new picture of crosswalks. It’s basically saying, "Nice try, Terminator. Do it again."

*(Pauses, paces a step or two)*

And don't get me started on creating accounts. Secure passwords have gotten out of hand. 

It used to be simple. Your dog’s name and your birth year. Boom. Certified hacker-proof. 

Now, I’m trying to log into a website just to buy *one* pack of athletic socks, and they want me to come up with a password that can withstand a military cyber-attack. 

"Must contain a capital letter, a number, a punctuation mark, a hieroglyph, and the exact coordinates of where you lost your virginity." 

So I spend ten minutes crafting this masterpiece of cybersecurity. I type it in, and the website immediately flashes red and says: *Password: Weak.* 

*(Looks offended)*

Who are you to judge me, Nike.com? You sell shoes! You don't know my life! You think my password is weak? My *willpower* is weak. That's why I'm buying fifty-dollar sneakers instead of going for a run! 

*(Pauses for a beat)*

But the ultimate final boss of technology judgment is definitely Netflix. 

We’ve all been there. You’re on hour seven of a television binge. You haven't moved. You are practically part of the couch cushions. 

And suddenly, the screen goes dark, and a message pops up: *“Are you still watching?”* 

But they don’t say it like a question. They say it like a concerned intervention. It’s basically Netflix saying, "Hey… we’ve been tracking your eye movement. You haven't blinked in forty-five minutes. Go touch some grass." 

And the worst part? When the screen goes black, it doesn't just stop the show. It turns your TV into a mirror. 

For five agonizing seconds, you are forced to stare at your own reflection in the dark screen, holding a half-eaten slice of cold pizza, looking like a Victorian ghost haunting your own living room. 

And what do we do? We double down. We press "Resume." Because if we turn the TV off, we have to deal with the real world, and honestly, the real world doesn't even think we can recognize a traffic light. 

*(Smiles)*

Thank you guys, you’ve been great! 

*(Waves and exits stage)*
