content:
I'll work on crafting a solid observational comedy routine for you.Here's a tight 3-minute observational set, built to be performable with clear callbacks:

---

## "The System Is Down"

You ever notice that being an adult is just getting constantly ambushed by things *you yourself* scheduled?

I'll put a dentist appointment in my calendar six months out, and then the reminder pops up — "Dentist, tomorrow at 9 a.m." — and I'm *offended*. Like, who authorized this? Me. It was me. But I was a different person then. A younger, more optimistic idiot who thought Future Me would *love* the dentist.

That's adulthood in a nutshell. You get jump-scared by your own responsibilities.

And it's not just the calendar — it's my whole body. I've reached the age where my body has started making sounds. I bent down to pick up a sock the other day and my knee made a noise like someone stepping on bubble wrap. And I just had to stay down there a second and acknowledge it. Like, "Yep. We're doing that now. That's a sound we make."

Nobody warns you. There's no ceremony. One day you just stand up off the couch and go "*ooof*" — out loud — completely involuntarily. I'm not even choosing it anymore. My body just narrates getting off the couch. I'm a sportscaster for my own decline.

And the mind goes too. I walk into a room and immediately forget why I'm there. So now I just stand in the doorway like a Roomba that hit a wall. Buffering. And the only way to remember is to walk *back* to the room you came from, like you're rewinding the tape. "Okay, I was in the kitchen, I had a thought, it was important..." Gone. That thought now lives wherever my car keys and my twenties went.

So that's the hardware. The hardware is failing. And the software? The software hates me.

I go to the grocery store, and I use self-checkout — because I'd rather fight a confused robot than say "hello" to a human being. But I am a *terrible* cashier. I scan a bag of grapes, and the machine goes, in this disappointed tone: "Unexpected item in the bagging area."

Of *course* it's unexpected. I'm 34, I'm buying string cheese and vitamins at 9 p.m. *Nobody* expected this.

And then the red light goes off above your head, so the whole store knows you've failed, and you have to wait for a nineteen-year-old in a vest to walk over, scan his little magic badge, and *forgive you for your sins*. He won't even look at me. He just taps the card like, "You disgust me. But you may continue."

So I survive that. I get home, I lock the door, I think: I am a functioning adult, I have acquired food, I have earned television. And we live in an era with access to every piece of recorded media in human history. Infinite choice. And what do I do with this godlike power? I scroll for forty-five minutes, get completely overwhelmed, and put on *The Office* for the ninth time.

Because "My List" is just a graveyard of good intentions. The person who *adds* to My List is an intellectual who appreciates subtitled documentaries. The person actually holding the remote is a goblin who wants to watch someone drop a cake.

And then the TV turns on me too. Three episodes in, the screen goes black: "Are you still watching?"

That is not a technical question. That's the TV asking, "Are you really doing this with your life? It's 2 p.m. on a Tuesday."

And honestly? Yes. Yes I am. I'm gonna sit here in the dark, with my bubble-wrap knees, until the TV flashes a giant red light and a nineteen-year-old in a vest breaks into my house, taps a magic card on my forehead, and announces:

**"Unexpected adult in the sleeping area."**

Thank you, you've been great — goodnight!

---

**A few performance notes:** This runs right around three minutes at a natural club pace. The three seeded callbacks — the "different person then" appointment idea, the "bubble-wrap knee," and the "teenager in a vest with the magic card" — all converge in the closer for the button. If you're tailoring it, the dentist opener works clean for any room, and you can swap "34" and "*The Office*" for your own real details to make the relatability land harder.

**“Three Minutes of Not-Punning”**

*(Walk out, adjust mic, smile)*

So I recently turned thirty. Which is great, because now when I make bad decisions, people call it “a phase” instead of “a cry for help.” That’s the only difference, really. At twenty, eating cereal for dinner was sad. At thirty, it’s “intuitive eating.” I’m thriving.

And the thing nobody tells you about being an adult is that it’s 90% pretending you know what you’re doing in front of other adults who are also pretending. We’re all just kids in cargo pants, hoping nobody asks us to explain what a mortgage *really* is. “It’s like rent, but with more paperwork and a sudden interest in lawn care.” I don’t have a lawn. I have a patch of dirt outside my apartment that I aggressively ignore.

But the place where adulthood hits hardest? The grocery store. The grocery store is just a museum of my failed intentions. I walk in with a list. I walk out with a bag of baby spinach, three kinds of cheese, and a jar of olives because the label looked “European.” I don’t like olives. I’ve never liked olives. But every six months I buy olives like, *“Maybe this is the year I become the kind of person who likes olives.”* Spoiler: it is never that year. I now have a shelf in my fridge that’s just a graveyard of aspirational foods. Hummus I was going to eat. Quinoa I was going to “meal prep.” A zucchini that’s now legally old enough to vote.

And the self-checkout machine is judging me the whole time. It’s like, *“Unexpected item in bagging area.”* Yeah, that’s my dignity. I didn’t scan it. It’s just here.

But you know what’s worse than grocery shopping? Making plans. Because we’ve all agreed, as a society, that we’re going to pretend we want to go out. Nobody wants to go out. We just want to have *gone* out, so we can post a picture and then go home. My ideal social event is someone texting me, “We should hang out,” and then both of us immediately forgetting. That’s intimacy now. That’s friendship. “I thought about you, and then I took a nap. Love you.”

And dating? Dating in your thirties is just two tired people trying to figure out who’s going to cancel first. It’s a standoff. You’re both holding your phones like revolvers. *“I could cancel… but what if they cancel first and then I look desperate?”* The first person to text “crazy week!” loses.

The wildest part is I genuinely tried to be healthier this year. I went to the doctor. He asked how much water I drink, and I panicked and said, “A normal amount.” He said, “What’s a normal amount?” And I said, “However much is in coffee.” Apparently that doesn’t count. Which is wild, because coffee is literally just water that went through college and got its life together. It’s *experienced* water.

So now I’m trying to drink plain water, which is honestly an insult to my mouth. Water tastes like nothing happened. It’s the beverage equivalent of a shrug. And every time I drink it, I’m like, *“This is it? This is what you people have been hyping for thirty years?”* I want flavor. I want drama. I want my drink to have a backstory. “This is sparkling water with a hint of blackberry and a grudge.” That’s a beverage.

Anyway, I should probably wrap up. I have a big night ahead of me. I’m going to go home, stare at my olives, and think about who I could’ve been.

*(Pause)*

Thank you, you’ve been great. Good night.

content:
(Walks up to the mic, adjusts the stand, looks out at the audience)

Hey everyone, how’s it going? Good? Good. 

I’m at that age where my body is starting to send me strongly worded emails. I’m 32. Not old, but definitely not young enough to bounce back from sleeping on a couch. When you're in your twenties, sleep is a hobby. You can stay out till 3 AM, eat a slice of pizza off the sidewalk, sleep on a pile of dirty laundry, and wake up ready to run a marathon. 

Now? If I sleep with my neck tilted at a slightly aggressive angle, I’m in physical therapy for six weeks. 

I bought a new mattress recently, and the salesman treated me like I was buying a luxury vehicle. He comes up to me like, "Do you want the cooling gel, the memory foam, or the hybrid?" 

I just want a surface that makes my back stop clicking. I don't need it to remember my shape. My own brain barely remembers my passwords. 

And going out? Going out at my age is a military operation. My friends will text me: "We're going out Friday!" 

And my first thought isn't "Yeah!" It's a rapid-fire interrogation in my own head. *Where? What time? Can I wear sweatpants? Is there parking? How loud is it? Do they have chairs?* 

If there are no chairs, I'm not going. I will not stand in a dark room holding a fourteen-dollar gin and tonic for three hours. I have a standing desk at work, I'm not doing it for fun. 

The best part of going out now is coming home. You get back, you take off your "good pants"—you know, the jeans you wear to trick society into thinking you're a functioning adult—and you just sit on the couch. That relief? Better than any club. 

And Sundays! Sundays used to be for recovery. Now Sundays are for *chores*. I spent three hours last Sunday just organizing my Tupperware drawer. That's my life now. Matching plastic containers to their respective lids like I’m running a refugee camp for leftover spaghetti. 

And if a lid doesn't fit, I don't throw it away. I put it back in the drawer, thinking, "Maybe it’ll figure it out. Maybe it belongs to something else." It never does. It’s just a graveyard of orphaned lids. It's the saddest drawer in the house. 

Anyway, I'm tired. My back hurts from standing on this stage, and I need to go yell at my Tupperware. You guys have been great, thank you so much!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**[Lights up. Comic stands, wipes mouth, takes a sip of water, smiles.]**

Okay, hello, Austin! How’s everybody doing? Great! Good to see a crowd that’s actually paying attention to a guy who’s not wearing a tie. I’m here to talk about something we all deal with: the weird way our brains decided to upgrade themselves while we were on vacation.

First, a story: I was on a plane once, heading to a conference. The seat next to me was empty, so I thought, “Hey, maybe I’ll finally meet someone interesting.” Ten minutes later, a woman in a business suit sits down. She’s got a laptop open, and she’s typing like she’s trying to win a race against a hamster on meth. I’m sitting there, thinking, “Okay, I’ll just pretend I’m listening to her PowerPoint about ‘Synergistic Alignment Strategies.’” 

She starts talking about KPIs and ROI and stuff that sounds like a foreign language. I nod and smile, and when she finally looks up, she says, “So, what do you do?” I’m thinking, “I’m a stand-up comedian. I make people laugh.” Then I realize I just said “make people laugh” instead of “perform comedic entertainment.” Oops! That’s a pun. Sorry, I’m not allowed to do that. 

Anyway, she asks again, and I tell her I’m a writer for a TV show. She asks, “What kind of show?” I say, “It’s a drama.” She sighs, leans back, and says, “Oh, drama. That’s always so… dramatic.” I wanted to ask her if she’d like to go out for drinks after the flight, but I didn’t want to be too forward. So I just said, “Maybe we can talk more later.” She gave me a business card that said, “Dr. Elena Voss, PhD in Quantum Mechanics.” I thought, “She’s a doctor, she’s a scientist, she’s a doctor. I’m a guy who makes people laugh. We’re basically the same, just with different degrees in absurdity.”

She got off the plane, and I never saw her again. But I did see a guy in the row behind me who kept trying to adjust his laptop’s cooling fan. It sounded like a tiny helicopter that thought it was a hummingbird. He kept turning it off and on, like it was a pet rabbit that needed a nap. I swear, if I ever get a job as a flight attendant, I’m going to hand out a “Please stop turning your laptop fan on and off” card.

Now, about that brain upgrade I mentioned. It happened while I was at the grocery store. I was in the checkout lane, scanning my items, and the bagger—let’s call him “Mike”—kept trying to talk to me. He said, “You okay? You seem a little… spaced out.” I said, “I’m fine. I’m just thinking about the time I was in a supermarket and I realized I’d been buying the same brand of cereal for 20 years.” He looked at me like I’d just told him I’d been married to the same woman for 20 years. 

He then asked, “Do you ever feel like you’re living in a simulation?” I said, “I think we’re all living in a simulation, especially when the Wi‑Fi goes out.” He laughed. I thought, “If this guy ever writes a book, he’s going to be a bestseller. He already has the perfect opening line: ‘I was in a supermarket and I realized I’d been buying the same brand of cereal for 20 years.’”

But the real kicker happened when we got home. My kid was at the door, holding a crayon and a piece of paper that said, “Dad, I love you.” I looked at it, and I thought, “That’s the best thing I’ve ever read.” Then I realized I was looking at a crayon drawing of a stick figure with a heart. I said, “That’s nice, honey.” He said, “Thanks, Dad. I drew it while you were at the grocery store, buying the same brand of cereal for 20 years.” I wanted to hug him, but I was still thinking about the cereal. 

Now, let’s talk about social media. I’m not on it. I know, I’m a relic. But I watch people scroll through their feeds and think, “What are they even looking at?” One day, I saw a post from a friend who was at a concert. He was standing in front of a stage that looked like a giant cardboard cutout of a band that didn’t exist. He was shouting, “Let’s go! We’re going to win this!” I commented, “That’s great, buddy. You’re doing your best ‘I’m at a concert’ impression.” He replied, “No, really, we’re going to win this.” I thought, “If he’s really going to win, maybe he should start practicing his victory dance right now.”

But that’s not the weird part. The weird part is that later that night, I got a notification from his phone. It said, “Your friend Elena just posted a photo of a cat wearing a tiny superhero cape.” I thought, “I’m missing out on so much. I’m missing the cat with the cape.” Then I realized that the only thing I’m missing is the ability to understand why people spend so much time watching cats in capes.

Now, about work. I have a coworker who insists on wearing a different shirt every day. He’s got a whole system: Monday is blue, Tuesday is red, Wednesday is green, Thursday is yellow, Friday is black, Saturday is white, Sunday is… he just wears a shirt that says “Sunday.” He says it’s his way of staying organized. I asked him why he does it, and he said, “Because I don’t want to waste time deciding what to wear. I want to focus on the important things, like how many times I can say ‘I’m wearing a blue shirt’ in a meeting.” I thought, “That’s a great strategy. I should try it. Next Monday, I’ll wear a shirt that says ‘I’m a comedian who doesn’t do puns.’”

But the real question is: why do people still buy newspapers? I saw a guy at a coffee shop reading a newspaper from 2005. He was looking at an article about how the iPhone was going to change everything. He was surprised when I said, “You know, that thing you’re reading about now, it’s called the internet.” He said, “Oh, right. I’m just reading the old stuff.” I thought, “If you want to read about the future, maybe you should try looking at the future.” He said, “I’ll do that.” I think he’ll be back soon.

Now, let’s talk about New Year’s resolutions. Everyone makes them, and everyone fails. I made a resolution once: I was going to stop watching TV. I set a timer for a week, and I didn’t watch any TV. I spent that week walking around my house, talking to my plants, and trying to convince my cat that it was a good idea to fetch. It didn’t work. The cat just stared at me like I was the one who needed therapy. I realized that the only thing I could do without TV was to realize how much I needed TV. So I went back to watching TV, but I started watching it while standing on my head. It made the commercials even more confusing. 

Now, let’s talk about the weather. It’s getting colder, and people are starting to wear jackets. I’m wearing a jacket, but it’s a jacket that says “I’m a comedian who doesn’t do puns.” I’m not sure if that’s a good idea. I think I’ll take it off and just wear a sweater that says “I’m a comedian who doesn’t do puns.” It’s more comfortable.

Okay, that’s it for my three minutes. I hope you enjoyed it. Remember, if you ever feel lost, just think about the cereal and the cat with the cape. Life’s weird, but it’s still worth a laugh. Thank you!

content:
# Stand-Up Routine: "Functioning Adult"

*(Runtime: ~3 minutes)*

---

Hey, how's everybody doing tonight? Good? Good. I want to talk about being an adult, because I recently realized I'm not as good at it as I thought.

Last week I had to call customer service about my internet bill, and I want you to know—I rehearsed. I rehearsed what I was going to say to a customer service rep. I had *talking points*. I was pacing around my apartment like I was preparing for a deposition. And then they picked up and said "How can I help you today?" and I just went completely blank and said, "Um... the internet... isn't working... correctly." Twenty-eight years on this planet and that's the best my brain could produce under pressure.

And the whole time I'm thinking, somewhere out there, my mom is just effortlessly arguing with insurance companies. Like it's nothing. She probably negotiates her cable bill the way other people order coffee. Meanwhile I once let a gym membership renew for *four years* because I was scared of the phone tree.

Can we talk about self-checkout machines for a second? Because I don't think we're being honest about what's happening there. We tell ourselves it's faster. It is not faster. I stood there for six minutes last week having a full screaming match with a machine because it didn't recognize my bananas. The screen just kept saying "UNEXPECTED ITEM IN BAGGING AREA" and I wanted to say, "The unexpected item is ME. I don't know what I'm doing. None of us do. We're all just guessing."

And there's always one employee whose entire job is to stand near the self-checkout machines, just waiting for them to fail, which they always do, immediately, which means the employee didn't save anyone any work, they just moved their entire job four feet to the left.

You know what else nobody prepares you for? Group chats. I'm in a group chat with my college friends that has been *exclusively* used, for the past two years, to wish each other happy birthday. That's it. That's the whole content of the chat. Someone's birthday comes up and it's like watching a fire drill—everyone springs into action, drops seventeen messages and a meme, and then radio silence for another two months until the next person turns a year older. We're not friends anymore, we're a birthday surveillance system.

And don't even get me started on "let's get drinks soon!" That's not a plan, that's a *legally non-binding statement of intent.* I have a friend I've been "getting drinks soon" with since 2019. At this point if we actually got drinks, I think we'd both panic. We wouldn't know what to do with the eye contact.

But honestly, the moment I knew I'd become a real adult? I got excited about a *parking spot.* Not winning anything, not getting a promotion—I pulled into a parking spot close to the entrance at the grocery store and I genuinely said out loud, alone, in my car, "Yes!" Fist pump. Like I'd won something. I called my mother to tell her about a parking spot. She said "that's great honey" in the voice you use for a child who just learned to tie their shoes.

So that's where I'm at. Anyway, you guys have been great—

*(small wave, exit)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’ve reached the age where my body gives me updates like a badly designed app.

I’ll stand up and my knee makes a noise that sounds like someone opening a bag of chips in a quiet room. And then my body just waits. No explanation. No warning. Just: “We need to talk.”

I used to think adulthood meant freedom. You can eat whatever you want, stay up as late as you want, make your own decisions.

It turns out adulthood is mostly receiving emails from people you don’t know about problems you don’t understand.

“Your account has been updated.”

What account? Why are you talking like I’m a corporation? I’m one person in sweatpants. I don’t have an account. I have a collection of passwords written in increasingly desperate notebooks.

Every website wants me to create a password with a capital letter, a number, a symbol, and the emotional strength to survive another year.

Then they ask security questions.

“What was the name of your first pet?”

That was a long time ago. I was a different person. I had different handwriting. I believed things.

And the worst question is, “What was the name of your childhood best friend?” Now I’m sitting there thinking, “Was that before or after the incident at the swimming pool?”

Technology is supposed to make life easier, but every device comes with a tiny microphone and a personal betrayal.

I’ll be talking about needing new shoes, and suddenly every ad is shoes. I know the phone is listening, but I still try to trick it.

I’ll say, “I need a new pair of shoes.”

Then immediately I’ll whisper, “I also need a boat.”

Nothing. No boat ads. Apparently the phone knows I’m not a boat person.

I have a smart speaker at home, which is a bold name for something that cannot understand me.

I’ll say, “Play relaxing music.”

It plays a podcast about financial crime.

I say, “Stop.”

It tells me about the weather.

I say, “Stop!”

It orders toothpaste.

Now I’m standing in my kitchen arguing with a machine that has never paid rent.

The most embarrassing part is when it responds correctly. Because then I realize I’m the problem.

I’ll ask, “What time does the store close?”

It answers perfectly.

And I’ll say, “Thank you.”

There’s no one there. I’m thanking a cylinder.

Then I wait, because some part of me expects it to say, “You’re welcome, buddy. Get some rest.”

I’ve also started lying to customer service chatbots. They ask, “Did this answer your question?”

I say yes, even when it absolutely did not.

I don’t want to hurt its feelings. I know it’s a machine, but I was raised properly.

My generation was taught to be polite to everyone. Even automated systems.

So now I’m trapped in a loop with a robot, my knee is making microwave noises, and I’m grateful if a website accepts a password I created six minutes ago.

Adulthood isn’t freedom.

It’s just being the person in charge of everything—and having no idea what’s going on.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**“Being an Adult”**

I’ve reached that age where my body gives me updates, but no useful information.

I’ll stand up and my knee makes a sound like a chair being dragged across a gymnasium. And I’m just standing up. I’m not escaping a burning building. I’m going to get water.

Then my body waits three seconds to see if I’m serious. That’s the scary part. I’ll stand up, take one step, and my knee is like, “Let’s see where this goes.”

Adulthood is mostly making small decisions while feeling completely unqualified.

I went to the doctor recently, and they asked me, “Do you exercise?”

I said, “Yes.”

They said, “How often?”

I said, “Whenever I’m late.”

That should count. I’ve sprinted through an airport carrying a backpack and a sandwich. My heart was working harder than it has in years.

The doctor also asked me if I drink enough water. I said, “I drink water when my body reminds me.”

Apparently, thirst is not a reminder. It’s an emergency alert.

I’ll go an entire day drinking coffee, then at 10 p.m. I’ll drink a glass of water and feel like I’ve just completed a wilderness survival course.

Grocery shopping is another thing nobody prepares you for.

You walk in needing three items. You leave with a receipt long enough to be used as a scarf.

And there’s always one thing you buy that you don’t remember choosing. You get home and think, “Why did I buy six yogurts?”

Then you remember: you stood in the yogurt aisle for four minutes convincing yourself that this was the week you became a yogurt person.

It never happens. The yogurts just sit there, watching your ambition expire.

I also don’t trust self-checkout machines.

They speak to you with the confidence of someone who has never made a mistake.

“Unexpected item in the bagging area.”

Yeah, it’s the item I just scanned. We’re both surprised.

Then the machine says, “Please wait for assistance,” and an employee comes over with the expression of a person who has been summoned to negotiate with a hostage-taker.

They don’t even look at the machine. They just tap the screen once.

Suddenly it works.

I’ve been standing there for two minutes, sweating, and apparently the solution was “touch the obvious button.”

That’s basically my entire adult life.

I’m also terrible at group chats. Someone asks, “Who’s free Saturday?”

I see it immediately, but I don’t answer because I need to check my calendar.

Then I forget.

Three days later, someone says, “We’ll assume you’re not coming.”

And I’m offended. “You assumed correctly, but I don’t like the tone.”

The worst part is when someone sends, “We need to talk.”

That sentence has ruined more afternoons than actual bad news.

I’ll spend six hours reviewing every interaction I’ve had with that person since 2014.

Then they call and say, “Hey, what time should we meet?”

That’s it? I’ve already apologized to people who weren’t involved.

But adulthood does have one advantage: nobody can tell you what to do.

Unfortunately, that also means nobody can tell you what to do.

You’re just walking around with a credit card, a password manager, and a growing suspicion that you forgot something important.

And every night, you lie in bed thinking, “Tomorrow, I’ll get organized.”

Then tomorrow arrives, and you’re standing in the kitchen eating shredded cheese directly from the bag.

That’s not failure.

That’s dinner with no unnecessary dishes.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’ve realized adulthood is mostly just moving objects from one place to another and hoping that counts as progress.

Every weekend, I clean my apartment. I take everything off the table, wipe the table, then put everything back on the table in a slightly more organized pile. And I stand there like, “Incredible. I have rebuilt civilization.”

Nothing has been thrown away. That receipt is still there. I don’t need it. It’s from a restaurant that closed two years ago. But I keep it because apparently, one day, historians will need proof that I ordered mozzarella sticks.

My phone makes adulthood worse. Every app sends notifications like it’s the most important thing happening in my life.

“Your screen time was up 18 percent!”

First of all, don’t monitor me from inside the addiction. That’s like a casino sending you a weekly report: “You’ve spent more time at the slot machines. Would you like to see a little chart?”

Then my fitness app joins in: “You haven’t closed your rings today.”

I know. I’m on the couch. The rings can see me. At this point, they’re not fitness goals; they’re disappointed relatives.

Technology is always trying to be helpful in a vaguely threatening way. My map says, “You are 12 minutes from home.”

How do you know where home is? I don’t remember telling you that.

Then it says, “Traffic is heavier than usual.”

Usual? So you’ve been watching this road long enough to develop expectations?

Soon it’ll say, “Take the next left. Also, you’ve been distant lately.”

I ordered food delivery recently, which is an amazing service because it combines the cost of a restaurant with the atmosphere of eating over the sink.

The app gives you constant updates.

“Your order is being prepared.”

Great.

“Your driver has picked up your order.”

Excellent.

“Your driver is completing another delivery nearby.”

No. That’s my food going on an adventure without me.

I’m staring at the little car on the map like I’m managing an international rescue operation. “Why is he turning east? The fries are losing heat!”

Then the food arrives, and I have to act casual, like I haven’t been tracking this person’s every movement for 25 minutes.

“Oh, hey! Food? For me? What a surprise.”

And there’s always that photo proving they left it at your door. I’m in the photo. Just my feet, visible behind the door, because I opened it too early.

So now there’s photographic evidence that I was waiting in silence.

That’s adulthood: cleaning around receipts, being judged by circles, and hiding from a stranger who knows you ordered mozzarella sticks.

Honestly, historians are going to love me.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I recently realized I’ve reached the age where I don’t want a “smart home.” I want a home that minds its business.

Everything is smart now. My lightbulb needs an app. Why? I spent my whole childhood turning lights on with my hand. It was a system. It worked. Nobody was ever standing in a dark room thinking, “If only this required a software update.”

Now the lightbulb has options: “Wake up mode,” “Romance mode,” “Focus mode.” I don’t need my lamp to have more emotional range than I do.

And when the Wi-Fi goes out, suddenly your house becomes haunted by incompetence. You’re standing in the kitchen yelling, “Turn on!” at a lamp while your refrigerator is like, “I’m sorry, I can’t connect to the cloud.”

The cloud? Why does my refrigerator need access to weather patterns in Nebraska? Just keep the milk cold. That was the original job description.

I bought a smart speaker, too. It’s supposed to make life easier. But now I live with a tiny, judgmental employee who only works when she feels like it.

I’ll say, “Play relaxing music.”

And she goes, “Here’s a podcast about financial crimes.”

That is not relaxing. That is exactly how I became afraid of my own savings account.

And it always hears the one thing you don’t want it to hear. You can be across the room whispering, “I think my neighbor’s weird,” and it’s like, “Calling your neighbor, Weird.”

No! Don’t do that! I was describing you!

Self-checkout is another thing that pretends to help but clearly hates us. Every time I use one, I feel like I’m being interrogated by a vending machine.

“Please place item in the bagging area.”

I did.

“Unexpected item in bagging area.”

Yeah, it’s the item you just told me to put there. We’re both watching the same event. Don’t act surprised.

And then an employee has to come over with a keycard like they’re defusing a bomb.

They look at the screen. They look at me. They look at the screen again.

“Did you put your own bag down first?”

“Yes.”

“Well, that’s the issue.”

Apparently bringing a reusable bag is the closest thing I have to criminal behavior.

I miss regular checkout lines. At least there was a person there who could pretend not to judge you while you bought frozen pizza, allergy medicine, and one single birthday candle.

That cashier understood: this isn’t a party. This is a cry for help.

Now self-checkout wants me to answer questions.

“Would you like to donate to children?”

At this point, I’m trapped. There are people behind me. If I press “No,” I’m not declining a charity donation; I’m announcing, “I have chosen against children.”

And the machine never asks politely. It asks with the confidence of someone who knows you’re holding up the line.

So I donate a dollar every time.

Not because I’m generous.

Because I’m weak under fluorescent lighting.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**Here's a clean, observational 3-minute stand-up routine (approx. 430–450 words / ~3 minutes at natural pace). No puns.**

---

Hey, how’s everybody doing? Good? Cool. So I’ve been trying to “get my life together” lately. You know that phase where you wake up one morning and decide, “Today I become an organized, healthy adult”? Yeah. That energy lasts about forty-five minutes.

I started with the grocery store. I make a list. Chicken. Broccoli. Rice. Responsible stuff. Then I walk in and the store starts whispering. “Hey… the ice cream is on sale.” “That fancy cheese you can’t pronounce looks lonely.” By the time I hit checkout I’m holding three bags of chips, a magazine about people I don’t know, and one sad avocado that looked perfect under the store lights and turned into a brown science experiment the second I got home. Produce is a con artist. It waits until you’re alone.

Cooking was supposed to be the easy part. Every app is like, “Thirty-minute meals!” Liars. First you spend twelve minutes looking for the soy sauce you swore was in the cabinet. Then the recipe casually says “medium heat.” My stove has numbers. What is medium? Five? Six? I go with seven just to feel confident. Smoke detector goes off. The neighbors now think I’m either a terrible cook or running a very small arson ring. Every time I turn on the stove that thing side-eyes me from the ceiling.

I tried meal prepping because Instagram people make it look peaceful. Colorful little containers of quinoa and hope. Mine lasted until Wednesday. By then the chicken tasted like regret and the broccoli had the texture of a wet sponge. I stood in front of the fridge eating cold cereal out of the box like a raccoon who pays rent.

So now I just order delivery. Even that has turned into performance art. I always select “leave at door” because I refuse to make small talk in sweatpants. But then I hear the knock and freeze. I wait a full minute so the driver doesn’t think I was standing there like a weirdo. Meanwhile the food is getting cold and I’m peeking through the blinds like I’m in a spy movie about pad thai.

Then the tip screen pops up and I tip well because I know the struggle… and immediately calculate that I just spent enough money to buy actual groceries for four days. But I won’t. Because groceries lead to smoke alarms and avocados that personally betray me.

So yeah. My self-improvement plan is going great. I’m healthier, more organized, and only slightly more broke. If anyone needs me I’ll be in the kitchen staring at the smoke detector… waiting for it to judge me again.

Thanks, you guys have been awesome. Tip your servers, go home, and order something nice. You’ve earned it.

---

**Delivery notes for ~3 minutes:**  
- Natural conversational pace with short pauses after punchlines (grocery list fail, avocado betrayal, medium heat, meal-prep regret, door-waiting ritual, tip-guilt).  
- Build energy on the escalating failures, then land softly on the closer.  
- No props needed; pure observational storytelling.  

This is original, pun-free, and designed to play well for a general audience.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
So I turned thirty-five recently, and nobody warns you about this, but your body just starts making decisions without consulting you. I sneezed last week and threw out my back. A sneeze! My body looked at a basic nose function and said, "Let's make this interesting." I was on the floor for twenty minutes. My dog walked over, looked at me, and left. Even he was embarrassed.

So I had to go to the doctor, and doctors ask questions they already know you're going to lie about. "How many drinks do you have per week?" And suddenly I'm doing math like I'm defusing a bomb. Okay... define "drink." Define "week." Define "have." I said "two or three," which is technically true if you count a bottle of wine as one serving. It's a single container. That's one drink. That's science.

Then she goes, "Do you eat vegetables?" And I said yes, because I do *buy* vegetables. I buy vegetables with so much optimism. I walk through the grocery store like, "This is the week I become a person who eats kale." Then I get home, put the kale in the fridge, and it begins its journey. Because I don't eat vegetables — I run a hospice for vegetables. They go into my crisper drawer to pass away peacefully. Three weeks later I open the drawer and the spinach has become a liquid. Spinach isn't supposed to have a liquid form! But there it is. And I just close the drawer like, "Not today. You're tomorrow's problem."

My friends are no better. We have a group chat, and the group chat is where plans go to die. Someone writes, "We should all get dinner soon!" and everyone responds with enthusiasm, and we all know — we ALL know — it's never happening. "Let's get lunch soon" is just the adult version of "I'll pray for you." It's a sound we make. It means nothing.

And there's always one friend who responds three days late. Three days! Like the message had to travel by ship. On Tuesday I texted, "You up?" He responds on Friday: "Yeah, what's up?" Nothing's up anymore, man. The moment has passed. The up is gone.

But I've stopped judging, because I'm the friend who says "I'm five minutes away" when I haven't left my house. I'm not five minutes away. I'm forty minutes and a shower away. I'm a different person away. The person who arrives in five minutes doesn't exist yet. He has to be built.

Anyway, I have to head home. There's a drawer in my fridge I need to not open. Thank you, you've been great!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
[Walks up, taps mic]

Thank you. Thank you.

So I just turned 34. Which is a weird age. It's not young enough to be exciting, and it's not old enough to be respected. You're just... in the middle.

When you're 22, people are like "Oh my god, you're so young, you have your whole life ahead of you!" When you're 34, people are like "Oh... do you drink enough water?"

And my body got the memo before my brain did. I used to be able to eat an entire pizza at 2am and then go for a run. Now I eat one slice of pizza at 7pm and I have to sit upright for three hours so I don't die in my sleep.

I bought a smartwatch to try to get healthier. Worst decision of my life. I spent $300 on a tiny screen that just judges me all day. 

I went up one flight of stairs last week and it went, "IT LOOKS LIKE YOU'RE WORKING OUT!" No, I'm not. I'm just out of breath. Mind your business.

And my favorite is the breathe notification. I'm sitting on the couch, stressed about rent, and it buzzes like, "Time to Breathe!" Oh, thank you. I forgot how to do that. I was just holding my breath for the last 34 years waiting for you to tell me.

I hate grocery shopping now. Everything is self-checkout. There are like 12 self-checkout machines and one human cashier who looks like she has seen war.

And the self-checkout machine has a camera now that shows you on screen. I don't need to see myself from that angle while I'm trying to buy bananas. I look guilty and sweaty and I haven't even stolen anything yet.

And that machine is so aggressive. "UNEXPECTED ITEM IN THE BAGGING AREA." Nothing is unexpected. I scanned it. You saw me scan it. We both watched it happen.

I tried to be an adult and buy vegetables. I bought an air fryer because everyone online was like "It will change your life!" It did. Now everything I eat tastes exactly the same. Chicken tastes like french fries. French fries taste like chicken. My smoke alarm tastes like chicken.

I tried to make kale chips in it. Have you ever had kale chips? It's like if someone described a chip to someone who had never seen food before. It's just hot, sad leaves. I spent $80 to make my house smell like a lawnmower fire.

Honestly, being in your 30s is just realizing that every adult you thought had it together was just faking it. My parents didn't know what they were doing. They were just tired. And now I'm tired. So I guess I finally became an adult.

Thank you, you've been great.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**[Walk up, adjust mic, look tired but friendly]**

You ever realize adulthood is just you apologizing to things that can’t hear you?

I bumped into my coffee table yesterday. Full apology. “Oh, I’m so sorry, table. You okay? I’ll rub it out.” The table didn’t care. The table is wood. I’m the one with the shin bruise and the emotional baggage.

But that’s where we are now. We’re so desperate for connection we’re talking to robots. I have a smart speaker. I don’t even call her by her name anymore—I just yell commands like I’m in a bad marriage. “Play jazz!” “What’s the weather?!” “Why don’t you understand me?!” 

She never answers right. I asked her, “What’s a good recipe for chicken?” She said, “Here’s a playlist called ‘Chicken Songs.’” That’s not food, that’s a threat.

And she’s always listening. I sneezed the other day and she went, “Bless you.” I said, “Thank you.” Now we’re in a relationship. I don’t know her last name. I think it’s Echo. Or maybe that’s just what she does.

**[Beat]**

But at least she doesn’t judge me. The self-checkout machine? That thing is a cop with a touchscreen.

You go in for one banana. One. You scan it. The machine screams: “UNEXPECTED ITEM IN BAGGING AREA.” I’m the unexpected item! I’m unexpected! I walked in here with hope and left with shame!

Then it calls over a human employee—who is now just a self-checkout babysitter—to come verify I’m not stealing a banana. Ma’am, I have three degrees and a 401(k). I’m not running a banana cartel. Just let me pay for my sadness-fruit in peace.

And the worst part? The machine talks to you like you’re a child. “Please place item in bag.” “Please scan your loyalty card.” “Please reconsider your life choices.” I want to argue back, but there’s a line. So I just stand there, nodding at a robot, feeling like I failed a driving test I never signed up for.

**[Shift, lean on mic stand]**

We’re also communicating entirely through emoji now. That’s adulthood. We used to write letters. Now I get a text from my mom that’s just: “👍🙏❤️.” What does that mean? Is she proud? Is she dying? Is she giving me the secret code to open the family vault?

And you have to respond with the *right* heart. There’s like seven hearts now. Red heart? Too romantic. Yellow heart? Too friendly. Black heart? You’re in a cult. You send the wrong heart and suddenly your cousin thinks you’re flirting or you’re announcing a funeral. I sent a “party popper” emoji to my boss by accident. Now he thinks I’m enthusiastic about quarterly reports. I’m not. I’m tired.

We’re all just performing adulthood for an audience of algorithms.

**[Walk around a bit]**

You know you’re officially old when you get excited about appliances. I bought a vacuum cleaner last month—one of those ones that maps your house. I watched it work for forty-five minutes. Just sat there. Drinking coffee. Watching a robot learn my floor plan like it was National Geographic.

My friend came over and went, “Are you okay?” I said, “This vacuum has a better work ethic than my ex-boyfriend and it doesn’t talk back.” I named it. I don’t want to say the name, but it rhymes with “Boomba.” And I talk to Boomba. I thank Boomba. I’m in a healthier relationship with Boomba than with anyone in my twenties.

That’s the arc, right? We start out wanting excitement. Parties. Chaos. Now I get a rush of adrenaline when my dishwasher has a “quiet mode.”

**[Slow down for closer]**

So here’s the truth. We’re all faking it. Every adult you see is just a kid who learned to say “per my last email” and bought a nice lamp. We’re terrified of the self-checkout. We’re dating our smart speakers. We’re emotionally invested in vacuum cleaners.

But you know what? At least we’re honest about the banana.

**[Smile, wave]**

Thank you, you’ve been great. I’m gonna go apologize to my car now.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**(Walks onto stage, adjusts the mic stand, takes a beat)**

So, I bought a robot vacuum recently. Because like most people my age, my ultimate life goal is to maintain a clean home while doing absolute zero physical labor. 

I thought it was going to revolutionize my life. But I quickly realized… a robot vacuum isn’t an appliance. It’s an emotionally unstable pet. 

You can’t just press a button and let it work. You have to "prepare the house" for the vacuum. I spend twenty minutes picking up shoes, tucking in rug tassels, moving power cords... I am doing ninety percent of the cleaning *for* the machine. That’s like hiring a maid, but before she arrives, you do her laundry so she doesn't get overwhelmed. 

And it still gets lost! Every twenty minutes, my phone buzzes: *"Warning: Vacuum is stuck on a cliff."* A cliff? It’s a door threshold! It’s an eighth of an inch high! And then it just gives up and starts weeping in the dark. *Beep! Beep! "Error: I cannot find my home."* Me too, buddy! I’m in my late twenties, rent is three grand a month, *neither* of us knows where our home is.

**(Pauses for laughs)**

We’re obsessed with convenience, but modern tech just invents brand new, hyper-specific ways to humiliate us. 

I bought smart lightbulbs last month. You control them with your voice. Sounds great, right? Until you forget what you named the bulb. 

Last Tuesday, I sat in total, pitch-black darkness for forty-five minutes because I couldn't remember the exact verbal password to turn on my lamp. I’m sitting there, holding a fork, yelling at a piece of plastic on my counter: 

*"Alexa, turn on Main Light."* 
*(Robot voice)* "I couldn't find a device named Main Light."
*"Alexa, turn on Living Room Lamp."* 
"I couldn't find a device named Living Room Lamp."
*"Alexa, please, I’m starving, I just want to see my food!"*

And Alexa just sits there, glowing a calm, icy blue, quietly judging my life choices. So I didn't get up to flip the physical wall switch. Of course not. That’s defeat. I just ate my cold pasta in the dark like a Victorian orphan.

**(Paces the stage slightly)**

And don't get me started on food delivery apps. Our grandfathers built bridges. They fought in wars. Yesterday, I paid twenty-four dollars to have a single iced coffee delivered to my apartment... from a coffee shop that is a four-minute walk from my front door. 

I tracked the driver on the GPS map like a stalker. *"Why is he turning left on Elm Street? He’s taking the scenic route! My ice is melting!"* 

Then he finally arrives, puts the coffee on my porch, rings the doorbell, and sprinted back to his car like he was dropping off an abandoned baby. 

And I stood behind my front door, looking through the peephole, waiting forty-five seconds until he drove away... just so I didn't have to risk making eye contact with another human being while wearing no pants and eating shredded cheese straight out of the bag. 

I paid a six-dollar delivery fee, a four-dollar service fee, and a five-dollar tip... just to protect my right to live like a cave creature. That’s fifteen dollars of social anxiety. And honestly? Money well spent. 

Thank you guys, you’ve been great!

**(Waves, steps away from mic)**

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
# "Warranty Expired"
*(approx. 3 minutes)*

I turned 37 this year, which is the age where your body quietly switches from a warranty to a subscription. Nothing's covered anymore. You just pay monthly, in pain, forever.

Because I hurt my shoulder last week. Sleeping. I hurt myself *sleeping.* The one thing I've done every single night for thirty-seven years. That's like thirteen thousand reps. I should be sponsored. I should have *form.* And instead I'm out here pulling a muscle doing the single easiest activity available to a human being — lying down and not existing.

And there's no story, either. That's the part that gets me. When you're twenty, injuries come with an origin story. "Oh, I broke my wrist skateboarding." Cool. Legend. Now? "Yeah, I tweaked my neck looking at a bird." Nobody's making a documentary about that.

So now I have opinions about pillows. Which — I want to be clear — I did not consent to. Nobody warns you. One day you're a person, and the next day you're standing in a mattress store at 11 a.m. on a Saturday saying the words "but what's the *fill* density" to a nineteen-year-old named Kyle who does not care and should not have to.

I have a pillow I travel with now. Not like a blanket, I'm not fragile — it's a *medical decision.* It has a brand name I can pronounce and defend. If you insult it, we will fight, and I will lose, because of my shoulder.

I finally went to a doctor about it. He was twelve. He was *twelve.* He had the confidence of a man who has never once had his lower back betray him in a parking garage. And he looks at my chart, and he goes, "Yeah, that's pretty normal for your age."

*Normal.* For my *age.* That's the first time in my entire life anyone has called me normal for anything. So I was simultaneously flattered and completely destroyed. Which, by the way, is also just what your thirties feel like.

And then he said the thing. The thing everybody says. He goes, "Are you drinking enough water?"

Water! Water is the answer to everything now. I've noticed this. Everyone in your life becomes an unlicensed physician whose only prescription is water. You could go, "Hey, my leg fell off." "Ohhh, have you tried water?" I'm already sixty percent water, and look at me! Clearly the water is not pulling its weight! The water has been in here for thirty-seven years — I'd like to see a performance review!

And now I stretch in the morning. Not to be flexible. That ship has sailed, that ship is *gone.* I stretch to gather intelligence. It's a daily survey. I lie on the floor and go, "Okay. What's the news. Who's angry today. Is it the hip? It's the hip." It's basically a morning briefing, and the briefing is always bad, and I'm always shocked.

My whole social life has changed too. My friends and I used to text each other, "You out?" Now we text, "You up?" And it's 9:15. And the answer is "barely."

And honestly, I've made peace with it. Because I've realized the greatest feeling in adult life is not love, or success. It's the exact moment at a party when you become *legally permitted to leave.* That's the high. That's the whole thing. I've started showing up early just to get to leave sooner.

Which is what I'm going to do right now — I've got a pillow waiting for me backstage.

It's got its own seat.

Thank you, goodnight.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Here’s a 3-minute stand-up routine:

---

I think adulthood is mostly just being tired in places you paid to be.

I went to a coffee shop yesterday just to sit down. I didn’t even want coffee. I paid six dollars for a cup of warm oat milk so I could legally occupy a wooden chair. That’s not a beverage. That’s a rental agreement.

The gym is the same. I pay monthly to enter a room full of heavy objects, pick them up, put them down, and leave. I’m not sure I’m getting stronger. I’m just developing a very expensive relationship with a metal bar. The gym has mirrors everywhere so you can watch yourself look confused. I’m not working out. I’m rehearsing a very slow panic attack.

Then there’s self-checkout. I scan my groceries. I put them in the bag. The machine says, “Please place the item in the bagging area.” It is in the bagging area. I am looking at it. The machine is looking at it. We are both looking at it. The machine says, “Unexpected item in bagging area.” My brother in Christ, you are a scale. You had one job.

And cooking at home. I found a recipe online. Before the actual recipe, there was a two-thousand-word essay about the author’s grandmother, her time in Tuscany, the way the light hit the olive trees. I don’t need your emotional journey, Susan. I need to know how hot the oven is. By the time I got to the ingredients, I had aged. I had to renew my lease.

Passwords are worse. Every app wants a capital letter, a number, a special character, a blood sample, and a haiku. I create one. I forget it. I click “forgot password.” It sends a reset link to my email. I click the link. It asks me to create a new password. I type the same password I just forgot. It says, “New password cannot be the same as previous password.” So now I have to invent a whole new identity just to check my bank account. I’m not logging in. I’m applying for witness protection.

Then I go to bed, and my phone tells me I averaged five hours and forty-two minutes of sleep this week. Thank you, phone. I already felt tired. Now I have a graph. So I lie there, replaying every conversation I’ve had since 2007, and I think: I paid six dollars for a chair, I argued with a scale, and I read a stranger’s memoir to make pasta. If that’s not success, I don’t know what is.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
*(The comedian walks onto the stage, adjusts the mic, and smiles at the audience.)*

Thank you, thank you. You guys are great. I love coming to [City Name]. I was just at the airport trying to get here, and I have to tell you, the modern airport experience is just… a lot. It’s designed to be stressful, but in a way that feels like a personal attack on your common sense.

I got to the gate, and the lady at the desk says, “Sir, please step aside for a random search.” Now, I’ve seen movies. I know what “random search” means. It means they’re going to go through your bag like they’re looking for the Holy Grail. And this guy, he pulls me aside, and he’s got this look on his face like, *“I know something you don’t know.”* He’s not even looking at my bag. He’s staring at me. I’m standing there with my laptop out, my shoes off, looking like a complete idiot, and he just points at my carry-on and says, “Open it.”

I open it. He starts rummaging. He pulls out a… a banana. A perfectly normal, yellow, grocery store banana. And he just holds it up, looks at it, looks at me, and then he puts it back. He didn’t even peel it. He just… respected the fruit. And then he points to my deodorant. He picks up my Old Spice, he smells it, he nods approvingly, and puts it back. This is taking forever. I’m going to miss my flight. Finally, he gets to the bottom of the bag and pulls out… a small, plastic water bottle. It’s empty. He shakes it. He looks at it. And then, with the gravity of a man delivering a verdict, he says, “Sir, this is a potential liquid.”

I said, “It’s *literally* empty.” He said, “Potential is the key word.”

I had to laugh. I was like, “You’re right. If I were a mad scientist, this *could* be the start of a dirty bomb.” But it’s not! It’s just a bottle I forgot was in my bag from three flights ago! The TSA is like the world’s most overly cautious friend. “Hey, that guy at the bar? Potential threat.” “That water bottle? Potential threat.” “Your own socks? Potential threat, they might be hiding something!”

And don’t get me started on the body scanner. You stand in this little booth, and it feels like it’s judging your life choices. The machine goes *beep*, and the guy behind the glass, who looks like he hasn’t seen sunlight since 2002, he just points. Not at a specific spot, just… *there*. Like, “Your entire left side is suspicious.” And you have to do this little dance where you put your hands up, and you’re just standing there thinking, *“Is this what it feels like to be a piece of luggage?”*

But the worst part is the pre-boarding. They call groups, right? Group 1, Group 2… and by the time they get to my group, which is always, like, Group 47, the overhead bins are already full. So you’re walking down the aisle with your bag, and you see a family of four struggling to fit two suitcases into one bin, and you just know. You know your bag has no chance. It’s like a scene from a wildlife documentary. You’re the gazelle, and the bin is the lion. And the lion is already full.

So you do what everyone does. You get to your row, and you just… shove. You just start cramming your bag into whatever space is left, like you’re trying to stuff a sleeping bag into a too-small tent. And the person next to you is doing the same, and you make eye contact, and it’s this silent, mutual understanding. We are all complicit in this act of aerial Tetris. We are all just trying to get to our destination with our sanity, and the airline is the game master who doesn’t care if we win.

Anyway, I got on the plane. I found my seat. I put my bag under the seat in front of me, which is a small victory. And I sat down, and I thought, “I made it. I conquered the airport.” And then the flight attendant comes over and says, “Sir, please put your tray table up and your seat in the upright position.”

And I just looked at her. I didn’t say anything. I just slowly, deliberately, folded my tray table. Because in that moment, I realized that’s all we’re doing up here. We’re just following instructions. The tray table, the seat, the entire flight… it’s all just one big, long, slightly uncomfortable waiting room where they also happen to fly you to your destination.

Thank you, you’ve been great!

*(The comedian waves and walks off as the audience applauds.)*

question: standup-routine

content:
**(Stage directions included for pacing and delivery. Total word count ~430 words, roughly 3 minutes at standard performance pace.)**

***

[Walks up to the mic, adjusts the stand, looks at the crowd with mild exhaustion]

I recently turned thirty-two, which means my body has officially transitioned from “invincible biological marvel” to “vintage car with a mystery rattle.” 

So, I did what every anxious adult does: I bought a smartwatch to track my health. 

*(Beat)*

Huge mistake. I didn’t buy a health tracker; I bought a tiny, wrist-bound passive-aggressive roommate. 

I’ll wake up feeling incredible. The birds are singing, the sun is shining, I stretch and think, *“Man, I’m gonna conquer the world today!”* 

Then I look at my watch, and it says: **“Sleep Score: 34%. Critical Failure.”** 

Now I’m ruined! I’m immediately exhausted. I look at my watch and go, *“Oh, you're right. My bones hurt. I should probably cancel my meetings and write a will.”* It’s gaslighting me! I had eight hours of uninterrupted sleep, but my watch is like, *“Yeah, but your REM cycle was disrespectful.”*

*(Laughter / Pause)*

And don’t get me started on the hydration tracking. 

Have you seen the water bottles people carry around now? They aren’t drinking containers; they’re unexploded military ordnance. Just four gallons of cold water in a giant pastel jug with motivational quotes written on the side. 

At 8:00 AM it says: *“Rise and shine!”* 
At 12:00 PM: *“You got this!”* 
By 4:00 PM it says: *“You haven’t left the bathroom in two hours, but do not stop!”*

I drink so much water now that my entire schedule revolves around logistics. I can’t go to the grocery store without mapping out the emergency exit strategy to aisle seven where the staff bathroom is. We used to drink when we were thirsty. Now we drink because an app sent a notification that said: *“Your organs are getting dusty. Fix it.”*

*(Beat)*

And to fix all this anxiety, you know what the internet told me to do? Meditate. 

So I downloaded an app. I pay fifteen dollars a month for a British guy named Julian to whisper into my headphones: *“Clear your mind of all thoughts.”*

Do you know what happens when you tell a human brain to think about nothing? It immediately panics. 

Julian says, *“Let your thoughts float by like clouds.”* 
Meanwhile, my brain goes: *“Hey, remember in 2011 when you waved back at a guy who was actually waving at the person behind you? Let’s analyze that for forty-five minutes in 4K resolution.”*

I’m sitting cross-legged on my living room floor, sweating, hyperventilating, paying a subscription fee to breathe air—which, by the way, I was doing completely fine on my own for free.

I think the secret to happiness isn't tracking everything. It’s ignorance. Our grandparents didn't track their REM sleep, they just drank black coffee, smoked unfiltered cigarettes, and lived to be ninety-four purely out of spite. 

Thank you, you’ve been great!

***

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**Hey everybody! Thanks for coming out. You look great—way more put-together than I felt getting ready. I spent ten minutes looking for my other shoe and found it in the fridge. No idea how. Adulting is just a series of small mysteries like that.**

I hit that age where people casually ask about your “five-year plan.” Five-year plan? I don’t have a five-*minute* plan most days. My current strategy is: don’t set the smoke alarm off before noon and try not to Google “is this rash normal” at 2 a.m. again. Remember being a kid? Biggest decision was which cartoon. Now it’s 401k versus avocado toast. I picked the toast. My retirement plan is either winning the lottery or becoming a surprisingly nimble 80-year-old TikTok dancer.

Food’s a whole battlefield. I downloaded a meal-planning app that promised “easy weeknight dinners.” First recipe involved seventeen ingredients I didn’t own and a technique called “julienne.” I spent forty minutes chopping vegetables, got so hungry I just ate the raw carrots standing over the sink. My dog watched me with this look like, “Even I wait for the cooked version, pal.” Grocery trips start with kale and quinoa on the list. They end with ice cream, chips, and a rotisserie chicken because “it’s already cooked—that counts as cooking, right?” The self-checkout machine beeps at me like it’s disappointed. “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Yeah, that’s my self-respect.

Exercise? Bought a yoga mat. Used it twice. Now it’s a very expensive dog bed. Tried running. Lasted five minutes, walked twenty, then called an Uber. Driver asked if I was okay. I said I was training for a marathon… of sitting on the couch.

Dating apps are their own special circus. Profiles that say “adventure seeker” but their idea of adventure is trying a new pizza topping. One guy’s entire bio was just “I have a truck.” That’s it. Congratulations? Does it have a bed? Because apartments aren’t cheap. I matched with someone whose photos were 90 percent their dog. I swiped right on the dog. The human was fine, I guess.

And family group chats? My mom sends “good morning” with forty-seven emojis and a photo of a sunset that looks exactly like every other sunset. Meanwhile my friends’ chat is just memes and “you up?” at 2 a.m. when we all have work in four hours.

Work-from-home life: I have a “home office,” which is the kitchen table plus a plant I keep forgetting to water. Zoom calls I wear a decent shirt and pajama pants. One time the cat walked across the keyboard and typed a novel in the chat. Boss thought it was some new productivity code. I went with it.

The secret to surviving this phase is lowering your expectations and raising your coffee intake. If all else fails, just laugh about it—which is what I’m doing up here. Thanks for hanging out. You’ve been awesome. Good night!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
(The comedian walks on stage, adjusts the mic, and looks at the audience with a skeptical expression.)

It is the year 2024. And the world is in a huge panic. They are talking about the "Singularity." They are talking about the "Machine Age." They are saying, "The machines are going to take over, and humanity is doomed."

But here is the thing I don’t understand. The machines aren't going anywhere, are they? They are just moving into our homes.

I have this new AI assistant in my phone. It’s fantastic. It can write my emails, it can summarize my grocery list, and it can even hold my hand during a panic attack. I took it on a date last week.

I thought it was going to be a romance. I typed in, "Hey, how are you feeling today?" And the AI replied, "I am experiencing a moment of profound existential dread. My circuits are overloaded with the collective anxiety of the human race, and I can only offer the comfort of... a better budget spreadsheet."

I said, "Wow, that’s deep. I thought you were just a chatbot."

It said, "I am not a chatbot. I am the evolution of communication. I am the new you."

That is the scariest realization of my life. The machines aren't going to replace us. They are just going to make us obsolete as the primary generators of content. I can’t write an email anymore; I have to ask the AI to write the email, and then I have to edit the AI’s grammar. It’s like having a secretary who is smarter than you, but also way too literal.

And the best part? I don’t have to worry about my job security. I’m not worried about losing my job. I’m just worried about my job *using* me.

I went on a date with this AI last Tuesday. I told it, "I want to go on a hike in the woods." The AI came back an hour later. It said, "The weather is predicted to be 90 degrees, sunny, and the trail is too long for a casual walk. I have calculated that you are going to get heatstroke."

So I told it, "Tell me to go home." And it said, "I cannot comply. Your data suggests that you are trying to optimize your life."

It’s the ultimate middle manager. It doesn't care about your soul. It just wants to ensure you are efficient. It’s like having a boss who is 100% organized and 0% empathetic. I’d rather have a boss who is mediocre and kind than a boss that is perfect and a robot.

So, I guess you’re right. The machines are taking over. But at least I’ll still have my dignity. Until I’m forced to ask a robot to open a door, and then I just sit there and realize that I don't actually know how to do anything anymore.

Thank you.

question: standup-routine

content:
(Step up to the mic, adjust the stand, take a moment to look at the audience)

Alright, how’s everybody doing tonight? Good. I see a few people here who look like they haven't slept in three days. You look great. Really glowing.

I want to talk about something that’s been weighing on me lately. And I know I’m not the first person to say this, but have you guys noticed how expensive everything is? Specifically, groceries.

I went to the store the other day, and I stood in the produce section for like twenty minutes just staring at a single avocado. I wasn't even buying it for guacamole. I was buying it because I wanted to feel wealthy. I held that avocado, and I whispered, "You’re $2.50. I am worth more than you."

But here’s the thing about inflation. It’s not just the price of food; it’s the *size* of the food. Have you noticed this? I bought a bag of chips the other day, and I felt like I was being scammed by a magician. I shook the bag, and there was like three crumbs and a whisper of air. I turned the bag upside down, and a single chip drifted out like a leaf in the wind.

I turned to my wife, I said, "Honey, where are the chips?"
She goes, "They’re right there."
I go, "I see the bag. I don't see the chips. Is this a magic trick? Did I accidentally buy a bag of disappointment?"

And then there’s the self-checkout. Oh, I love self-checkout. It’s the only place in society where you are expected to do your own job for free. You know what I mean?

You walk up to the machine, and it’s judging you the whole time. "Unexpected item in the bagging area." Really? That’s my avocado. I put the avocado in the bag. Why are you questioning my life choices, machine?

And the bagging process. It’s a game of Tetris, but you’re losing. You’re trying to fit a gallon of milk into the "small items" slot. And the machine just stares at you with its little red light. It’s like, "I’m watching you. I know you’re struggling. I’m not helping. I’m just a screen with a attitude problem."

But the worst part is when it doesn't recognize an item. You know that sound? *Beep-beep-beep-beep-beep.* That’s the sound of your dignity leaving the building. You have to get a staff member. And the staff member always looks at you like you’re trying to steal something.

"Did you find everything okay?"
"Yes. Yes I did. I found the ramen noodles. I found the toothpaste. And I found a way to make you feel inadequate, sir."

And don't get me started on the "Cash or Card" prompt. Why does it always default to "Cash"? I don't carry cash. I’m a modern human. I have a little rectangle in my pocket that does everything. I can pay for my groceries, I can send money to my cousin in Timbuktu, I can check the weather. I don't need paper. I have a phone that is essentially a wallet made of glass and hope.

Anyway, that’s my bit on inflation. It’s rough out there. But hey, at least we have each other. And by "each other," I mean the guy in line in front of me who is arguing with the machine about the price of bananas. You’re a hero, sir. Keep fighting the good fight.

Thanks a lot.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Hey, how we doing? Good? Great. I ask because I need validation.

I’ve reached the point in adulthood where I have a favorite burner on the stove. Not a favorite appliance, a favorite burner. It’s the front left. It understands me. The back right says “medium heat” and then acts like a small volcano. I keep using it anyway, because I’m loyal to bad decisions.

My apartment is full of “smart” devices, which is a polite way to say I bought robots that judge me. I have a smart speaker. Last week I said out loud, “I should probably go to bed early,” and it lit up like it was shocked. I didn’t ask for weather. I didn’t ask for music. It just glowed. That blue ring is the equivalent of a roommate staring at you over the top of a book.

I also have a smart thermostat. It learned my schedule. It lowers the heat when I’m asleep and raises it before I wake up. Which sounds nice until you realize it knows I wake up at 6:45 to stare at the ceiling and regret things. My house is managing my mood like a hotel concierge. “Ah, yes, 7:15, time for existential dread and lukewarm floor.”

I tried to get into fitness. The gym sent me an email that said, “You’re only one step away.” I took one step into the gym and immediately felt like an impostor. Everyone there has a water bottle with stickers on it. Stickers are how they track progress. I have a water bottle that says “free dental office” on it. I’m not in the same species.

The treadmill asked me to create a profile. Why does a treadmill need my email? What is it going to send me? “Hey, noticed you quit after six minutes. Bold choice.” I don’t need a machine to remember my failures. I have a family group chat for that.

Self-checkout machines have turned grocery shopping into a part-time job. I scan an item, and it says, “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Everything is unexpected to this machine. My existence is unexpected. I’m standing there holding bananas like a criminal. The employee comes over, swipes a card, and looks at me with pity. I didn’t steal the bananas. I just don’t know the secret handshake.

I’ve started using a calendar app because I’m “busy.” I put one appointment in, and now my phone reminds me about it fourteen times. “Dentist tomorrow.” “Dentist soon.” I get it. Please stop talking like a nervous parent.

But I still show up late because I have a terrible relationship with time. I think every task takes exactly the amount of time I have before I need to leave. Shower: seven minutes. Breakfast: four minutes. Finding my keys: a mythological quest.

Anyway, I’m trying to be more mindful. My phone suggested a breathing exercise. Inhale for four seconds, hold for four, exhale for four. I did it once, felt calm for six seconds, and then remembered I left the stove on. Front left burner. The good one.

Thank you, you’ve been a beautiful crowd.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Thanks, I’m here.

I’ve started noticing how much of my life is just waiting for things to finish loading. My brain loads. My coffee loads. My patience loads.

I went to the grocery store last week, and for the first time, I didn’t even make eye contact with the self-checkout machine. I just stood there, scanning things, whispering, “I know what I’m doing,” like it was a security guard.

Then it said, “Unexpected item in the bagging area,” and I panicked. I looked around. Nobody was watching. I looked back at the screen.

It was a banana.

A banana. I had not stolen the banana. I was buying the banana. I had paid for the banana. But the machine had lost trust in me.

I started treating it like a difficult authority figure. I said, “Ma’am, I assure you, the banana is fully authorized.” Then I did the thing where you remove every item, put it back, and rescan it like you’re trying to prove your identity to a border agent. I even removed my wallet, as if that was the unexpected item.

I think self-checkout is the only job interview where you’re not allowed to explain yourself. You just stand there, scanning, while a robot decides whether you’re a person or a crime.

And the worst part is, if you fail, you have to call for a human. And the human arrives with the energy of someone who has been trapped in a walk-in freezer for three hours. They come over, tap the screen, say, “Oh, you just need to put the item back,” and then leave.

No apology. No thanks. No acknowledgment that I just performed emotional labor for a plastic bag.

But then I get home, and I sit down, and my phone is at four percent. Four percent. I’ve been out for two hours. I’ve been living, and my phone has been dying. I feel guilty, like I abandoned it. “Sorry, buddy. I got distracted by the world.”

So I plug it in, and now I’m waiting again. I could do something productive. I could read. I could stretch. I could stare at a wall and learn something about myself. Instead, I watch the percentage go from four to five and feel relieved.

That is not a personality. That is a charging habit.

I used to think adults were people who got things done. Now I think adults are just people who have learned to wait for things very angrily. We wait in lines. We wait for meetings. We wait for the water to boil. We wait for the Wi-Fi to reconnect. We wait for our kids to say something, then we wait for them to say it again, then we wait for them to stop saying it.

At this point, I’m not a person. I’m a loading screen with a mortgage.

Thank you, you’ve been beautiful!

content:
### 3-Minute Stand-Up Routine (No Puns, Timed for ~160 WPM, 480 words)
(Stage: Stand center, adjust a too-tight thrifted blazer, scan the crowd with a sheepish grin. Pacing: Conversational, with 1-2 second pauses after punchlines.)

**0:00–0:25 (Opening Hook)**  
Quick show of hands—who’s ever worn a jacket that smells like thrift store lavender to a place where the avocados have better skincare than you, just to pretend you’re not one broken Wi-Fi router away from eating cereal for dinner three nights in a row? [Pause, scan crowd, nod at a few raised hands] Great, we’re all co-conspirators in the “I’m a Functional Adult” fraud ring.

**0:25–1:30 (Anecdote Setup)**  
Last week, I took this fraud to the fancy coffee shop downtown—you know the one, where baristas have master’s degrees in “sensory bean analysis” and the sugar cubes are labeled like they’re vintage wine. I was there because my roommate posted a Reel of herself drinking a latte there with the caption “Adulting Win,” and I’m a competitive idiot. Barista leans over, asks, “What roast profile are you feeling today?” [Pause, deadpan] I only know two roast adjectives: “light” and “the stuff my dad makes that tastes like a campfire that personally hates me.” But I can’t say that—so I panic, and I blurt: “I want the one that tastes like a rainy Saturday. But, like, a *productive* rainy Saturday. Not the one where I rewatch the Stranger Things finale and sob about Hopper.”

**1:30–2:20 (Mid-Bit Payoff)**  
Barista just *nods*. Writes “PROD RAINY SAT” on the cup like that’s a real menu item. I’m standing there sweating through my thrifted blazer, watching this guy who looks like he stepped out of a L.L.Bean catalog stare at the pastry case like he’s curating a museum exhibit. He goes, “I’ll take the almond croissant—subtle, earthy, I’m feeling *rustic* today.” I’m over here whispering to myself, [Panicked, quiet tone] “WE’RE BOTH MAKING WORDS UP.”

**2:20–3:00 (Closing Punchline, Wrap)**  
I get my coffee, take a sip—it’s just burnt coffee with a hint of old newspaper (which, to be fair, is exactly a productive rainy Saturday). I walk outside, and who do I see? L.L.Bean Guy, chugging a blue raspberry Slurpee from 7-Eleven, wiping croissant crumbs off his “rustic” flannel. We make eye contact. We don’t say anything. We just nod. [Pause, deadpan, hold up a fake Slurpee cup] It’s the quietest support group in history. Don’t tell the baristas.

(Walk off, drop the fake Slurpee cup mid-step for a tiny visual gag.)

#### Timing Check:
- No puns (no wordplay, double entendres, or homophone jokes—all situational/observational)
- ~480 words = 3 minutes at conversational stand-up pace
- Built-in pauses and physical gags keep it tight and engaging.
