content:
### 3-Minute Stand-Up Routine (no puns, timed for natural delivery + laugh pauses)
(Walks on stage, leans into the mic, deadpan, scans the crowd)
0:00
“Raise your hand if you’ve ever bought a houseplant to prove to yourself you’re not a total walking disaster of a person. (Pauses, nods at the dozens of raised hands, snorts) Yeah, that’s what I thought. We’re all idiots.

I did this last month. I didn’t go crazy, just one plant. A pothos. Everyone says pothos are unkillable, right? The guy at the plant shop had a fern tattooed on his neck, he handed it to me like he was giving me a participation trophy for being a functional adult, said “you literally can’t mess this up.” (Shrugs, casual) Cool. I got this.

0:25
I lasted 10 days. 10 days, and I’m on Google at 2:17 a.m. typing “pothos one yellow leaf is it dying.” Google’s answer is useless, by the way. It’s either overwatered, underwatered, too much sun, not enough sun, or it’s… mad at you? I’m not kidding, that was a whole blog post. “Your plant may be experiencing emotional distress from recent changes in your home.” What, I moved the couch three feet, now it’s having a midlife crisis?

(Mimics holding a plant up to a window, squinting like he’s negotiating with the sun)
I spent 20 minutes moving it around the living room like I was trying to find the perfect lighting for a TikTok. Held it up to the glass, went “is this good? Do you like this? I’m sorry I binged the entire second season of *The Bear* instead of saying hi to you.”

1:10
I was so stressed I joined a local plant parent Facebook group. Posted a blurry photo of the one yellow leaf, captioned “help, is he gonna make it?” And y’all, those people are not normal. First comment: “Have you tried reading to it? I read my monstera a chapter of *The Overstory* every night and it’s grown 6 inches this month.” Second comment: “That’s not a regular pothos, that’s a rare variegated devil’s ivy, you need to repot it in orchid bark, perlite, and the crushed bones of your enemies.” Third comment was just “kill it.” No context, just “kill it.”

(Big pause for laughs, shakes his head like he’s still traumatized)
2:00
I panicked! I drove to Walmart at 1 a.m., bought $35 worth of potting soil and a tiny trowel, got home, dumped the whole plant out on the kitchen table, and then—(pauses, deadpan, stares straight at the crowd) —I realized the “yellow leaf” was a Flamin’ Hot Cheeto crumb that had been sitting on the foliage since I ate a whole bag on the couch three days prior.

(Pause for laughs, leans against the mic stand like he’s exhausted)
I sat on the floor for 10 minutes, covered in dirt, staring at a Cheeto, thinking about how I just spent $35 to prove I’m not a disaster, and instead I proved I can’t tell the difference between a houseplant and a snack.

2:45
The plant’s fine, by the way. I still talk to it, though. Mostly to apologize for being stupid. It hasn’t grown an inch. Rude.

(Steps back from the mic, waves)
Thanks, y’all.

(Timing check: ~2:58 with standard laugh pauses, zero puns, all rooted in relatable adulting embarrassment and specific, absurd observational detail)

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
# "Smart Home, Dumb Owner"

So I moved into a new apartment recently, and my landlord was very excited to tell me it's a "smart home." Which is funny, because I've never felt dumber than I do living in it.

The thermostat has an app. The lights have an app. The doorbell has an app. My phone now has more apps for my apartment than for actual human communication. I have not texted my mother back in three weeks, but I *have* adjusted the humidity remotely from a restaurant. Priorities.

And here's the thing nobody tells you about smart homes: they judge you. My smart speaker knows everything. It knows I asked it to play "workout playlist" at 2 PM on a Saturday and then sat down instead. Last week I said "play something relaxing" and it responded with a meditation track about letting go of guilt. That's not relaxation, that's a targeted attack.

The robot vacuum is worse. That thing has mapped my entire apartment, which means somewhere in the cloud there's a detailed diagram of how I live, including the specific path I walk from the couch to the fridge at 11:30 PM. And it's not subtle about it either. Every night it just sits there in its dock like, "Oh, you're up again? Interesting. Should I pre-scan the kitchen?"

I tried to set up the smart lock, and it required me to create an account, verify my email, download two-factor authentication, and then—get this—wait for a firmware update. To unlock my own door. My grandparents opened doors with a piece of metal they kept in their pocket, and honestly? They seemed happier.

But the worst part is when the technology fails. My smart lights disconnected last Tuesday, and I stood in my living room clapping like a seal for ten minutes before remembering light switches exist. Physical switches! On the wall! Like animals!

My smoke detector is also smart now. It sent me a push notification that my toast was burning. A notification. From the ceiling. Meanwhile, my actual human friends can't get a text back from me, but my ceiling has my contact info.

You know what the smart home promised us? Convenience. What it delivered is a full-time job managing appliances with abandonment issues. My fridge emailed me yesterday. Emailed me. Subject line: "Your filter needs replacing." I have coworkers who don't put that much effort into communication.

At this point, the only thing in my apartment that isn't connected to the internet is me, and honestly, I'm starting to feel left out. Maybe that's the plan. Maybe one day I'll come home and the house will have locked *me* out because I didn't update my terms of service.

Anyway, thanks for coming out tonight. Your phones already know you were here. Goodnight!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**Title:** The Quantified Idiot  
**Estimated Time:** ~3 minutes (approx. 400–450 words with pauses for delivery)

---

*[Walk to center mic. Take it off the stand, leave the stand behind you.]*

I recently bought a smartwatch because I decided I wasn’t feeling inadequate *often* enough throughout the day. I needed a tiny computer strapped to my wrist to passively-aggressively bully me into survival.

Do you know what this thing does? It gives me a “Sleep Score.” 

*[Points to wrist]*

Have you ever woken up, stretched, felt the morning sun on your face, thought, *“You know what? I feel pretty good today!”*—and then your watch buzzes and says: **“Sleep Quality: 38 out of 100. Poor. Your heart rate was chaotic and you barely visited REM sleep.”** 

And immediately, your knees buckle. You’re like, *“Damn. The Bluetooth has spoken. Cancel my meetings, bring me a blanket, I am medically dead.”* 

*[Pacing slightly, shaking head]*

We’ve completely lost the ability to just *be tired*. Now it has to be quantified. And the advice they give you for “sleep hygiene” is insane. Every article is like: 

“To sleep properly, do not look at screens for four hours before bed. Lower the room temperature to 58 degrees. Put blackout curtains up. Tape your mouth shut.” 

Have you heard about this mouth-taping thing? People are taping their mouths shut to "promote nasal breathing." I tried it for two nights. You don’t look like an optimized wellness guru; you look like a hostage who decided to lie down in their own bed. 

If an intruder broke into my apartment at 3:00 AM, he wouldn’t rob me. He’d look at me taped up in the dark, put his hands up, and go: *“Oh, my bad. Looks like someone already handled this. I’ll come back later.”*

*[Audience pause]*

And it’s not just sleep. It’s hydration. 

When did drinking water become a full-time administrative job? I see people carrying water jugs the size of car batteries with motivational quotes printed on the side. 

Seven AM: *“You can do it!”*  
Noon: *“Keep chugging!”*  
Four PM: *“Your kidneys are grateful!”* 

If you need a plastic cylinder to emotionally manipulate you into not drying out like a mummy, we have failed as a species. 

Think about our ancestors. They crossed uncharted oceans on wooden rafts eating moldy bread and drinking rainwater out of leather boots. Meanwhile, I woke up yesterday with a three-day migraine because my bedroom humidity dropped by four percent. 

My body isn't a temple. It’s a delicate Victorian child with rickets. I miss one glass of electrolyte-enhanced smart-water and my central nervous system files for bankruptcy.

*[Pause, sighing]*

We’re tracking our steps, our sleep, our heart rate variability, our macros… all so we can optimize our bodies to live an extra seven years. And what are we going to do with those extra seven years? Sit on a couch, staring at a screen, checking our watches to see if we’re having a good time.

*[Step back to the stand]*

Thank you, you've been great!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**Title: "The Modern Life Audit"**  
*(Light, conversational tone. Pause for laughter naturally. No puns—focus on relatable observations, hyperbole, and specific details.)*

*(Start with a relaxed, slightly self-aware vibe.)*

"Okay, so I did this thing last week—I tried to *audit my life*. Not like a tax audit. More like… if my brain were a spreadsheet, what cells would I actually fill out? Because honestly, I spend so much time Googling things like *‘Why does my fridge hum?’* and then the answer is *‘It’s just the motor,’* but now I’m convinced my fridge is narrating my life in a low, judgmental tone. Like, *‘Another snack? Really?’*  

And don’t get me started on notifications. My phone buzzes like it’s announcing the end of the world every five minutes: *‘New email!’* *‘Low battery!’* *‘You have a reminder to breathe.’* Wait—*breathe*? Who programmed that? My therapist? My mom? Is my phone now my mindfulness coach? Last week it reminded me to ‘drink water,’ so I chugged a glass… then immediately Googled *‘Is water hydrating if I drink it while scrolling?’* Because of course I did.  

Also, I went to the grocery store recently. Saw ‘organic’ apples. Bought them. Paid $3.99 for two apples that looked exactly like regular apples but cost more. Then I got home and ate one. Tasted fine. Then I felt weirdly guilty like I’d bought a tiny, expensive apple-shaped lie. Like, *‘Hey, I paid extra for no pesticides, but also I didn’t wash it because I was tired.’* So now I’m paying for purity I don’t even use correctly. It’s like buying a ‘premium’ toilet seat but forgetting to flush.  

And dating apps? I matched with someone last month. We chatted for three days about our favorite podcasts. Then they said, *‘Let’s meet for coffee.’* I was like, *‘Cool,’* but then I spent two hours picking out what to wear. Not ‘what to wear to coffee’—*what to wear to coffee with someone I matched with online who I don’t know if they like durian or think pineapple belongs on pizza.* So I wore my ‘safe’ sweater. The one that says *‘I tolerate ambiguity.’* Which is ironic because now I’m overthinking coffee attire. Meanwhile, they wore jeans and a band T-shirt that said *‘I regret nothing (except maybe this T-shirt.’* We sat there. Silently judged each other’s life choices. Then they ordered oat milk latte. I ordered black coffee. We both pretended not to notice the other’s drink was ‘extra.’  

And public transit! I take the bus every day. Yesterday, a guy played violin on the bus. Not badly—actually pretty nice. But then he looked around like *‘Who’s gonna tip me?’* Like it’s a tip-based performance now? I mean, I have $1.20 in my pocket because I bought a banana and forgot my wallet. So I gave him the dollar. He smiled. I felt like a hero. Then 10 seconds later he played the *same* note again. And again. It was like musical Groundhog Day. By the third time, I was whispering *‘No, not again,’* to myself. By the fifth time, I started humming along. By the seventh? I was debating if I should clap. (I didn’t. I was scared of looking weird.)  

Lastly: chores. I have a habit of putting laundry in the dryer… then forgetting about it. So it sits there for days. A tiny, wrinkled island of ‘I meant to fold this.’ Then I open the dryer and it smells like a forgotten gym bag. And I’m like, *‘Who left this here? Was it me? Was it my future self who regrets everything?’* I once left a sock in there for *four days*. When I took it out, it had developed its own ecosystem. I swear I saw a dust bunny doing push-ups inside it.  

So yeah. My life audit? Mostly: *I overthink small things; I pay extra for apples I don’t wash; I wear ‘safe’ sweaters to coffee; I give strangers dollar tips for repeating violin; and my laundry evolves life.* But hey—at least I’m aware. Which is nice! Because if you’re not aware, you might accidentally invite your boss to ‘virtual happy hour’ at 3 p.m. on a Tuesday. (True story. Happened to a friend. They got a Slack message saying *‘Thanks for coming!’* from their boss. No one else was there. They just… existed in the Zoom grid like it was normal.)  

Anyway. I’m just trying to fold laundry without creating sock ecosystems. And if my fridge keeps narrating my life? I’m naming it. *‘Gary.’* Gary the Fridge. Gary says *‘You ate cereal for dinner again.’* And maybe that’s okay. Maybe the point isn’t to fix everything—just notice it. Without puns. Just… noticing. *(Pause, smile.)* Thanks."  

*(End with a small, genuine laugh and nod—no over-explaining.)*  

**Why it works (briefly):**  
- Zero puns; humor comes from specific, relatable observations (fridge "narrating," overthinking coffee attire, sock ecosystems).  
- Short, natural pauses; conversational rhythm ("like it’s a tip-based performance," "musical Groundhog Day").  
- Hyperbole used sparingly and clearly ("socks evolved an ecosystem," "Gary the Fridge").  
- Ends with quiet warmth ("maybe the point isn’t to fix everything—just notice it"), avoiding clichés.  
- Realistic details (exact prices like "$3.99 for two apples," "I have $1.20 in my pocket") ground the jokes.  

*(Runtime approx. 3 minutes when delivered at a natural, slightly quick but clear pace.)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Here is a 3-minute stand-up routine focused on observational humor and the absurdity of modern social contracts.

**Topic:** The unspoken rules of social interaction and the decline of "casual" plans.
**Tone:** Conversational, slightly exasperated, energetic.

***

**(Walk up to mic, adjust height, take a breath. Look at the audience with a friendly but tired smile.)**

"How is everyone doing tonight? Good? Great. You all look... hydrated. That’s good. That’s the main thing I look for in a crowd.

I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how exhausting it is to be a person now. Not the living part—the breathing and the taxes are fine—but the *social* part. It feels like we’ve collectively agreed to a bunch of new rules that nobody actually voted on.

Specifically, the text message. Does anyone else feel like the text message has ruined the element of surprise?

We have turned texting into a high-stakes negotiation. You try to make plans with a friend, and it turns into a hostage crisis. You text them, 'Hey, want to grab dinner next Tuesday?'

And then... silence. Three days of silence. I’m sitting there checking my phone like I’m waiting for a biopsy result. I start spiraling. 'Did I say something wrong? Do they hate me? Are they dead? Should I call an ambulance just in case?'

And finally, three days later, they reply: 'Omg! So sorry! Just saw this!'

No, you didn't. You saw it. You read it. You looked at the notification, you thought, 'Ugh, I don't have the emotional bandwidth to decide on a cuisine right now,' and you put your phone down. We all do it! I do it! But we all pretend it’s a technology glitch. 'Oh, the carrier must have dropped the message.' Sure. The carrier dropped it right into the void of your procrastination.

**(Pause for laugh)**

And then there’s the 'Casual Hangout.' Can we talk about this? There is no such thing as a casual hangout anymore.

When I was a kid, hanging out meant you rode your bike to a friend's house, threw a rock at their window until they came out, and then you sat on the curb and did nothing. That was the plan. The plan was no plan.

Now? If I want to see my friends, it requires a project manager. I have a friend—let's call him Greg—and Greg sends out calendar invites for a beer. A beer! Who puts a beer on a Google Calendar?

He sends an invite with an agenda. '6:00 PM: Arrive. 6:15 PM: Order appetizers. 6:30 PM: Discuss current events.'

I’m sorry, Greg, I can’t schedule 'fun' for 6:30 PM next Thursday. What if I’m not in the mood to be fun at 6:30? What if I want to be moody at 6:30 and then fun at 8:00? You’re putting too much pressure on the appetizer course!

**(Take a sip of water)**

And it’s not just the planning. It’s the effort of leaving the house. I don't know when this happened, but I have developed a physical aversion to leaving my apartment.

My brain has started doing this thing where I’ll be getting ready to go out, and I’ll look at my couch, and the couch looks at me, and we have a moment. And my brain goes, 'You know, we have leftovers in the fridge. We don't need to put on real pants. We can just sit here and judge people on the internet.'

And I try to argue with myself. I say, 'No! We are going out! We are social beings! We need vitamin D and human connection!'

And my brain goes, 'We have a charging cable right here. Everything we need is within reach. Why would we go outside where there are *other people*?'

It’s a battle. And lately, the couch is winning. The couch is 2-0 against me this week.

**(Pause)**

But the worst part—the absolute worst part of modern socializing—is the 'How do you know each other?' question.

You’re at a party, you’re talking to a couple, and they ask, 'So, how do you two know each other?'

And you freeze. Because the truth is embarrassing. You don't have a cool story. You don't say, 'Oh, we met saving orphans from a burning building.'

You have to admit, 'Uh... we met on an app?'

And then you have to explain the app. 'Well, it’s not a dating app. It’s an app for people who want to... uh... split the cost of a bulk order of paper towels.' Or, 'We actually met because we both tweeted angrily about the same airline.'

Why is it so hard to just say, 'I don't know, we just sort of ended up in the same room and now we’re friends'?

I think we put too much pressure on the *origin story*. We think if we don't have a cinematic meet-cute, the friendship doesn't count.

**(Look at watch/imaginary watch)**

Anyway, I’m looking at the time, and I have a calendar invite at 9:15 to 'relax and watch a show,' so I really need to get home and prepare for that.

You guys have been great! Enjoy the rest of the show—or don't! No pressure! Do what you want!"

**(Wave, grab the mic stand, and walk off stage.)**

prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
(Hey, thanks for coming out.)

I’ve been thinking a lot about my house lately. Specifically, how it’s trying to run my life. I bought a smart speaker. Just a little cylinder. I thought it would be nice. Play music when I ask. But now it talks back. Not in a creepy way, just in a passive-aggressive way.

I say, “Play jazz.” It says, “I found 14,000 results. Here’s a podcast about jazz history.” I didn’t ask for a lecture. I just wanted a saxophone. And the lights. I have lights that change color based on my mood. How does it know my mood? I didn’t tell it. I guess because I’m always standing in the kitchen at 2 AM eating cereal. The light turns red. It thinks I’m angry. I’m not angry. I’m just lactose intolerant and tired.

It’s supposed to make life easier. But now I have to negotiate with my ceiling. “Turn on the living room light.” It says, “I can’t do that right now, the Wi-Fi is busy.” The Wi-Fi is busy? Who is the Wi-Fi talking to? It’s not talking to me. It’s probably arguing with the fridge. My fridge sent me a notification this morning. “You are out of milk.” I know I’m out of milk. I’m standing here drinking coffee. It’s like a text from your mom. “You’re out of milk. Also, call your mother.”

We built these things to save us time. But now we spend all our time fixing them. We spend more time troubleshooting the robot vacuum than actually cleaning the house. The vacuum gets stuck under the couch. It makes a noise like a dying whale. And I have to go rescue it. It’s like a pet that eats dirt and breaks down. I think we’re waiting for the day it just says, “I quit. You do it yourself.”

And don’t get me started on passwords. I have a password for my email. I have a password for my bank. I have a password for my smart toaster. My smart toaster needs a password? What is it protecting? The crust settings? If I forget it, it locks me out of my breakfast. I had to reset my toaster three times this week. I just wanted a bagel. Now I’m having a security crisis.

It asks, “Did you mean to change your password?” I say yes. It says, “That’s not the password you used last week.” What was I thinking last week? I don’t know. I was probably half asleep. Now I’m trying to remember a password I created while half asleep. It’s a cycle. We build tools to make us smarter, but they just make us forgetful. So I’m just going to keep writing them down on sticky notes. Which defeats the whole purpose of security. But at least the fridge knows my name.

So yeah. That’s my life. Thanks, you’ve been great.

question: standup-routine

content:
Here's a 3-minute, pun-free set you can perform — it's all observational, about 450 words:

---

**[Walk up, grab mic]**

Alright, hi everyone. Thanks for being here. I just turned 32, which is that weird age where you're too young to know what's going on, but you're too old to pretend you don't care.

Like, I went to the doctor last week for a checkup. Just a normal checkup. And before I went, I made the mistake of Googling my symptoms. I didn't even HAVE symptoms. I just Googled "32 year old tired."

Big mistake. According to the internet, I'm either dehydrated, or I have 4 months to live. There's no in-between.

And the doctor is so calm about it. He's like, "You need to drink more water and get more sleep." That's it? That's the prescription for everything in your 30s? Drink water and sleep? I paid a $40 copay for advice my houseplant could've given me.

And speaking of being an adult — when did grocery shopping become so stressful?

I use the self-checkout because I don't want to talk to anyone, right? That's the whole point. But now the self-checkout machine talks to me MORE than a human cashier ever did.

"Place item in bagging area. Remove item from bagging area. Unexpected item. EXPECTED item. Please wait for assistance."

Lady, I am just trying to buy bananas. I am not smuggling them. Why are you yelling at me in front of everyone? I feel like I'm getting arrested by a robot in front of the gum display.

And then it asks, "Do you want cash back?" No. I want dignity back. Can you give me that? In twenties?

The worst part is when it actually sends a real employee over. Now we both just stand there staring at the machine like it's our printer at work that won't connect. We're both tapping the screen like, "Did you try turning the bananas off and on again?"

Okay, but my REAL addiction is my phone. I tried to cut down on screen time last month. I went into my settings and set a limit. You know what my phone did? It sent me a notification to tell me I was spending too much time on my phone.

That's like getting a letter in the mail that says "YOU GET TOO MUCH MAIL." You're part of the problem!

I have 14,000 photos on my phone. 14,000. I went through them the other day. 90% are screenshots I don't remember taking. Like a recipe for soup I was never going to make. A parking spot number from 2019. Why am I saving this? Am I planning to go back to that parking garage three years later like, "Yes! Spot B4! My old friend!"

And don't get me started on trying to make plans as an adult. Texting a friend now is a three-week negotiation.

"Hey, we should hang out!"
"Yes! Definitely!"
"How about next Thursday?"
"Can't, busy."
"How about the Thursday after that?"
"Should work. Let's check in closer to the date."

We never check in closer to the date. That friend is gone. You just see their Instagram stories and like them from afar. That's friendship now. Just watching each other eat brunch through a screen.

Anyway, I'm 32, I'm tired, I'm getting bullied by a checkout machine, and my closest relationship is with my phone charger.

Thank you guys so much, you've been great!

question: standup-routine

content:
Here's a clean 3-minute set you can actually perform — all observational / storytelling, no puns. It's about 420 words, so at a normal pace it's right around 3 minutes.

---

**"Adulthood Is A Scam"**

Hey, thank you guys so much. I'm so excited to be here. I'm at that age now where I'm technically an adult, but I don't feel like one. I feel like a kid wearing a costume of a tired person.

I went to the doctor for my annual checkup last month. I paid a $40 copay, waited 45 minutes in a room that was 62 degrees for some reason, just for this guy to walk in, look at me for literally 90 seconds and go, "Yeah, you need to drink more water, sleep more, and stress less."

That's it? I just paid you to tell me to act like a houseplant? Drink water and sit in the sun? I could've gotten that advice from my mom for free, with snacks.

And speaking of being judged, does anyone else get that Sunday morning Screen Time report from Apple? Mine pops up like, "Your screen time was up 22% last week, at 7 hours and 14 minutes per day."

Thank you, Apple. My $1,000 phone is now my disappointed dad. I KNOW I was on my phone for 7 hours. I was THERE. I don't need a pie chart to confirm I have no hobbies.

The worst part is, I pick up my phone to do something important, like check my bank account, and then 40 minutes later I'm watching a video of a man in Ohio pressure-washing a driveway from 2019. And I'm invested. I'm like, "Oh, he missed a spot. Get that spot."

Then I have to go to the grocery store to feel like a productive citizen. And I always use self-checkout because I'm too introverted for small talk with a cashier. But self-checkout HATES me.

Every single time: "UNEXPECTED ITEM IN THE BAGGING AREA. PLEASE REMOVE THE ITEM."

The item is my own bag. The bag I brought because I care about turtles. And now this robot is yelling at me in front of everyone like I’m shoplifting bananas.

And there’s always that one employee watching six machines at once. They have to come over, type in their secret code, stare at you like you did it on purpose. Lady, I have a college degree. If I wanted to steal, I wouldn’t start with produce that I have to weigh myself.

And don’t even get me started on flying. Flying now is just paying $400 to be mildly humiliated in public.

You have to take off your shoes next to a complete stranger, put your laptop in a separate bin like it’s going through its own divorce, and then walk through the scanner with your arms up like you’re being robbed by science.

And then we all sit at the gate and they go, "This flight is completely full, we need volunteers to check your bag." No one volunteers. So they go, "Okay, we're going to start taking bags." That's not volunteering! That's just telling us what's happening with extra steps.

But my favorite part of adulthood is the group chat. I’m in like nine group chats and I actively participate in zero. I just lurk. I’m the FBI agent of my friend group. Someone will be like, "Are you coming to brunch on Sunday?" And I’ll read it instantly — READ at 9:42am — and then respond on Tuesday like, "Omg so sorry just seeing this!!" No you’re not. You saw it. You just didn’t want to spend $24 on eggs.

Anyway, that’s my life. I’m hydrated, I’m tired, and my phone thinks I’m depressed. Which, fair.

Thank you guys, you’ve been awesome!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I bought a smartwatch because I wanted to get healthier without changing anything about my life.

That’s the dream, right? Same habits, but now there’s a graph.

The watch congratulates me for standing up. That’s where I am physically. Getting out of a chair is an achievement with a little fireworks animation.

Sometimes I stand up just to get a cookie, and it’s like, “You did it!”

We did it. Don’t ask questions.

Then, ten minutes later, it tells me to breathe.

That feels threatening coming from something tracking my pulse. Does it know something? Am I breathing on a trial subscription?

*[Glance at wrist.]*

“Your free month of lungs ends tomorrow.”

I also tried a meditation app. Before I could relax, it asked me to create an account, verify my email, select my goals, and rate my current stress level.

Well, it’s higher now.

Then a soothing voice said, “Let go of everything that no longer serves you.”

So I deleted the app.

Best twelve seconds of therapy I’ve ever had.

I think my real problem is that every part of being an adult has become homework.

You can’t just own a pillow. You have to research pillows. There are eight hundred types, and every review says, “This pillow changed my life.”

What was happening to you before the pillow?

Were you sleeping on a bag of cutlery?

And the negative reviews are always terrifyingly specific.

“One star. Ruined our anniversary.”

I need the whole story, Linda. I’m not buying anything until you tell me what happened in that hotel.

I spent three nights researching something designed to help me sleep. At a certain point, the best pillow is whichever one you put your phone under.

Cooking is homework too. Every recipe starts with, “This easy weeknight dinner uses ingredients you already have.”

Then the first ingredient is fresh fennel.

You and I have very different ideas about how my week is going.

I have mustard, half a lime, and a container I’m afraid to open.

The container has become a roommate. I don’t know what it does during the day. I just need it to keep paying its share of the fridge.

And recipes always say, “Clean as you go.”

I can cook or I can clean. You’re asking the same employee to work two departments during a fire.

By the time dinner’s ready, I’ve used every spoon in the apartment. I’m eating yogurt with the little measuring cup from the cough medicine.

But I’m trying to be less hard on myself. Last night, I cooked something, washed a plate, and went to bed at a reasonable hour.

Then my watch said, “You haven’t reached your activity goal.”

So I got up and walked to the kitchen for a cookie.

*[Check wrist. Nod.]*

Fireworks.

Finally, somebody understands what motivates me.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
# "Unexpected Item"

*(walks out, adjusts mic)*

I've reached the age where the most stressful relationship in my life is with the self-checkout machine at the grocery store.

Because at some point, the grocery store fired the cashier and gave me the job. And I didn't apply! I just came in for yogurt, and now I'm working a shift. Unpaid. And the machine is my manager, and it does *not* trust me.

I scan one item. One. A lime. And the machine goes, *"Unexpected item in bagging area."*

Unexpected? You watched me do it! You were there! We did it together! That's like a guy at a wedding going, "Unexpected woman at the altar." Sir, you proposed.

And then the little light on top starts flashing. The *shame light*. It's basically a lighthouse that says, "Attention, everyone: this man might be stealing a lime."

And now a teenager has to walk over. There's always one teenager supervising eight machines, like a lifeguard at a pool where everyone's drowning in coupons. And he doesn't say anything. He just walks up, taps the screen with a special card, like he's the only one with nuclear launch codes, and walks away. No eye contact. He's seventeen and I feel like I've disappointed my father.

*(beat)*

And I *want* to be good at it! I really do. I'm trying to be efficient. I'm scanning, I'm bagging, I've got a rhythm going. I feel like a professional. And then I get to the bananas.

*"Please enter produce code."*

Code? I don't know the code! Why would I know the code? Nobody knows the code! That's knowledge you only get from working there, which, again, I *technically* do now, but nobody trained me!

So I search for "banana," and it gives me options. *Organic banana. Banana, bunch. Banana, single. Banana, plantain.* I don't know what kind of banana I am! I'm just a guy! I'm having an identity crisis in aisle nine because of fruit!

*(beat)*

And the worst part? The worst part is, at the end, after all that, after I've done the whole job myself, bagged everything, made zero mistakes... the screen says:

*"Would you like to leave a tip?"*

For WHO? For the machine? The machine yelled at me! For the teenager? He wouldn't look at me! Am I tipping *myself*? Because honestly, I earned it. I was great. I'd like to give myself twenty percent and a performance review.

*(beat)*

So now I just go to the one lane with a real human cashier. Even if there's a line. I'll wait twenty minutes. Because she doesn't flash a light at me. She doesn't think I'm stealing. She just scans my stuff and says, "Have a nice day."

And last week I got so emotional, I said, "You too," and then, out of habit, I put my lime down *really* slowly... so I wouldn't startle her.

*(beat)*

Unexpected item in bagging area, folks. That's me. I'm the unexpected item. Thank you, you've been great!

question: standup-routine

content:
# "Adulting Is a Scam"

So I turned thirty-five recently, and nobody warns you about this age. Nobody says, "Hey, one day you'll get excited about a *sponge*."

I was in the store, and I saw a sponge that promised it wouldn't smell. And I thought, "Finally. Someone who understands me." I bought the good sponge. I felt like a millionaire. I went home and told my roommate, "I upgraded the sponge." He said, "Cool." I said, "No, you don't understand. It's a *lifestyle* sponge."

That's who I am now. My personality peaked at "has opinions about sponges."

And I have started saying things my father said. Last week, I walked into a room and said, "Who left all these lights on? Do I look like I own the electric company?" I was *alone*. I was yelling at myself. And the worst part is, I was right. I *did* leave them on. I had to look in the mirror and say, "Dad, get out of my body."

Also, my body has started making noises. When I was twenty, I'd stand up and nothing happened. Now every time I get off the couch, I make a sound like a haunted door. Just an involuntary "Hhhhnnnnh." I didn't decide that. It's a little announcement. "Attention, everyone, he's vertical."

And I'm supposed to be responsible now. Everyone says, "You should have a five-year plan." I have a five-*minute* plan, and it's usually a snack. Sometimes the plan fails. Sometimes I get to the kitchen and forget what I came for, so I just open the fridge and stand there in the light like it's going to tell me something. Like the fridge is a wise old monk. "What do I want, fridge?" And it hums back, "Cheese. But you knew that."

Then there's the calendar. When did my social life become a series of cancellations? At twenty, plans were exciting. Now, when someone cancels, I feel a rush of joy so pure it should be illegal. My friend texts, "So sorry, can't make it tonight." And I type, "Oh no! Totally understand!" while doing a victory dance in my socks. I'm not sad. I'm *free*. I have been *pardoned*.

But if *I* have to cancel, I get guilt. So I've started lying. I say, "Sorry, something came up." What came up? My *pajamas*. My pajamas came up, and I said yes.

And going out is different now. I went to a bar recently and the music was so loud I couldn't hear anything. I just nodded at a guy for twenty minutes. I have no idea what I agreed to. I might be in a business now. I might have adopted a boat.

I asked the bartender if they had anything quieter, and he looked at me like I'd asked for a horse. So I went home. On the way, I saw young people heading out at eleven p.m., glowing with hope, and I thought, "Kids, go back. Sleep. It's the only thing that's ever loved you."

Anyway, that's my time. You've been great. Drink some water, call your mother, and if you're offered a good sponge, take it.

Goodnight!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Good evening, everyone! Thanks for having me out tonight. I’m thrilled to be here, even though I’m still trying to figure out why the venue’s lighting looks like a police interrogation room. But hey, at least the spotlight makes my forehead look like a freshly polished coffee table—so that’s a win.

So, I was at the grocery store last week, and I tried one of those self‑checkout lanes because I’m a fan of “do it yourself”—the only thing I can actually do by myself is get a coffee and forget it on the counter. The machine asked me to scan my items, and I scanned a bag of chips, a loaf of bread, and a bottle of ketchup. Then the screen said, “Please place your item in the bag.” I put the chips in the bag. The machine said, “Please place your item in the bag.” I put the bread in the bag. The machine said, “Please place your item in the bag.” I put the ketchup in the bag. Then it said, “Please place your item in the bag.” I stared at the bag and thought, “What else do you want? My soul? My future?” Turns out I had forgotten to scan my own face. The cashier had to come over and say, “You’re good to go, but you might want to check if you’re still human.” I left with a receipt that read, “One bag of chips, one loaf of bread, one bottle of ketchup, and one existential crisis.” 

Now, speaking of things that make you question your humanity, have you ever tried online dating? I signed up because I heard it was the fastest way to meet someone who will never actually meet you in person. My profile said, “I’m a 32‑year‑old who enjoys long walks on the beach, reading, and pretending I’m not terrified of making small talk.” The first message I got was from a guy who wrote, “Hey, I saw your picture and thought you looked like my ex. Do you want to go out?” I replied, “If you’re looking for someone who looks like your ex, you should probably see a therapist, not a dating app.” He didn’t reply. I guess he was too busy trying to find a therapist who looks like his ex.

And then there’s my dog, Max. Max is a golden retriever who thinks he’s a professional model. He spends half his day staring at himself in the mirror, and the other half trying to figure out how to get the treat out of the cupboard without making a sound. Last week, I left a plate of cookies on the counter, and Max decided it was his personal mission to get them. He jumped up, knocked the plate over, and then stared at the mess like it was a crime scene he’d just committed. I said, “Max, you’re a dog, not a detective.” He wagged his tail, as if to say, “I know, but I’m still going to investigate.” 

Working from home has been an adventure, too. I’ve had Zoom meetings where my cat, Luna, decided she was the co‑host. She’d sit on my keyboard, press random keys, and occasionally walk across the screen like she was auditioning for a role in a silent film. My boss would say, “Can you hear me?” and I’d have to whisper, “No, because Luna just muted me.” She also has a habit of knocking over my coffee mug right before I’m about to give a presentation. I’ve learned to keep a spare mug on my desk, just in case. It’s like having a backup plan for life, except the backup plan is also a mug that’s probably going to be knocked over by a cat.

Finally, I tried to get in shape. I signed up for a gym membership, and the first class I attended was a spin class. The instructor shouted, “Pedal faster! Burn those calories!” I was pedaling so hard I thought I was generating electricity for the whole building. After the class, I was drenched in sweat and thought, “If I keep this up, I’ll be able to power a small town.” But then I realized I was just powering my own disappointment because I’d forgotten to bring a towel. I left with a towel that was so thin it was basically a napkin. I said to the instructor, “Thanks for the workout, but next time, can we have a class where we just sit and stare at a wall? That’s my natural talent.”

So, that’s my night—full of grocery store existential crises, dating app confusion, a dog who thinks he’s a detective, a cat who thinks she’s a co‑host, and a spin class that left me with a napkin for a towel. I’m glad you’re all here to share in my misadventures. Thanks for listening, and I hope you leave with a few laughs and maybe a new appreciation for the fact that life is just a series of poorly timed self‑checkout machines. Good night!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
*(Walks on stage, adjusts mic, takes a sip of water. Waves to the back row.)*

Alright, how's everyone doing tonight? Good, good. You know, I was thinking about this on the way here. I’m at that age now where I have a favorite spatula. I have opinions on paper towels. And last week, I found myself getting genuinely, emotionally invested in a debate about the best way to organize a refrigerator. And I realized... I have become a person who says things like, "We'll just have to agree to disagree," when my wife suggests we rearrange the Tupperware drawer.

And that's a weird thing to come to terms with. Because in my head, I'm still the guy who can eat a whole pizza and then go for a run. The guy who thought "adulting" was a fun, quirky verb. But no. I am now the guy who gets a little thrill from using the exact right-sized Ziploc bag for a leftover half of an onion. That's the dream, folks. That's the peak of my existence.

But it's not just the small stuff. It's the big stuff too. Like, I remember being a kid and looking at adults, and I just assumed they had it all figured out. They had a plan. They had a binder, probably, with color-coded tabs for "Mortgage," "Retirement," and "Why the Dog is Afraid of the Vacuum Cleaner."

And then I became an adult. And I can tell you, with absolute certainty, there is no binder. There is no plan. There is just a series of increasingly frantic Google searches at 11:47 on a Tuesday night. My search history is a monument to my incompetence. It’s just, "how to get red wine out of a white rug," followed by "is it safe to eat leftovers after 5 days," followed by "why does my car make that noise."

It’s a constant state of low-grade panic, disguised as a functioning person. I'm basically a duck. Calm on the surface, paddling like crazy underneath. And every so often, someone will ask me a question that requires actual adult knowledge. Like, "What's your vision for the next fiscal year?" And I just stare at them, and my brain is screaming, "My vision is to just make it to Friday without accidentally setting something on fire!"

*(Pauses, takes another sip of water.)*

And you know what the most terrifying part is? It's not the taxes, or the career, or the existential dread of a Saturday night with nothing to do. It’s the self-checkout machine at the grocery store. That thing is the ultimate judge of your character.

It’s just you, a bag of frozen peas, and a machine that is silently, passively judging you. "Unexpected item in the bagging area." I'm sorry, what? Unexpected? I put it there! You watched me put it there! It was in my hand, and now it's in the bag. What part of that is unexpected? It’s like a robot with the memory of a goldfish and the attitude of a DMV employee.

And you can't argue with it. You can't reason with it. You just have to stand there, waving your hands over the scanner, hoping to appease the plastic gods so you can just go home and eat your frozen peas in peace.

So, you know. This is the dream. This is the adventure. It's not about climbing mountains or skydiving. It's about successfully navigating the produce aisle and getting out without having a minor existential crisis.

But hey, at least I have my favorite spatula. And a well-organized Tupperware drawer. And honestly? That's a pretty good feeling. It's the little victories, people. It's the little victories. Thank you, goodnight! *(Bows, walks off stage.)*

question: standup-routine

content:
Here’s a 3-minute stand-up routine. No puns. Just observations and slow, painful self-awareness.

---

Thank you! So I’m at that age where I’ve started doing things my parents used to do. Not the good things. I don’t have a garden. I have a cactus that I forgot to water for three months. It died. Did you know a cactus can die? I didn’t. I thought it was just a plant that didn’t want to talk to me. That’s why I bought it. It was the only relationship I’ve had that didn’t require emotional labor. And then it died. It left me. It left me for the sun.

Another thing: I’ve been trying to be more productive. I got a to-do list app. It has a feature that reminds you to “take a break.” I’m like, I take breaks. I take breaks from my to-do list to look at my to-do list. That’s not a break. That’s a hostage situation.

I also got a smart speaker. I asked it for the weather. It said “70 degrees and sunny.” I said, “What about the chance of rain?” It said “There is a 10% chance of rain.” I said, “So you’re telling me there’s a chance.” It said “No, I’m telling you there’s a 10% chance.” I said, “Okay, I’m going to plan my whole day around that.” My whole day is a lie. It’s a lie.

Speaking of weather, my phone has a weather app that says “Feels like 95 degrees.” I’m like, “Feels like? I don’t have time for your feelings. Just tell me the temperature.” It’s like a friend who says “I’m fine” but isn’t fine. That’s not a weather app. That’s a toxic relationship.

Now, I’m not a man of many talents. But I have a talent for losing things. I lost my sunglasses. I had them on my head. For three days. I kept saying “Where are my sunglasses?” and my wife said “They’re on your head.” I said “That’s not where I put them.” She said “That’s where you put them.” I said “No, I put them on the table.” She said “You put them on your head.” I said “Okay, but I’m not wearing them.” That’s the genius of losing things: you can lose them while they’re on your body.

People say “you’re not getting any younger.” I know. I’m getting older. It’s the same thing. But I’m okay with it. I’ve accepted that I’m not going to be the person I thought I’d be. I thought I’d be someone who does yoga at sunrise. Instead, I’m someone who does yoga on the floor of my living room. But I’m not doing yoga. I’m just lying there. I call it “corpse pose.” They said “hold it for five minutes.” I said “I’ve been holding it since 2017.”

Then I tried to meditate. I sat down, closed my eyes, and tried to clear my mind. My mind said “What’s for dinner?” I said “Not now.” My mind said “Are you mad at me?” I said “No, I’m trying to meditate.” My mind said “Oh, so you’re mad at me.” That’s why I can’t meditate. My mind is a needy ex.

Anyway, I’m not going to tell you to “stay safe” or “be kind.” You’re all grown adults. You know what to do. But if you see a cactus, maybe water it. It might be the only friend you have.

Thank you!

**3-Minute Stand-Up Routine: “I’m Not Doing Puns”**

*(Walk onstage, adjust mic, look at audience.)*

Good evening. I’m not gonna do puns tonight. I know, bold choice. Somewhere a dad just woke up in a cold sweat and doesn’t know why.

Instead, I wanna talk about being an adult. Which, for me, is mostly just being confused in nicer furniture.

I went to the grocery store yesterday. I used the self-checkout. You know the self-checkout — it’s a robot that hates you but has to be polite about it. I scanned a banana. The machine goes, “Unexpected item in bagging area.”

Unexpected? It’s a banana. It’s the most predictable item in the store. It comes with its own carrying case. Nature pre-packaged it. I’m not sneaking a banana. I’m not a raccoon.

Then the attendant comes over. She scans a card, doesn’t look at me, and walks away like a doctor who’s seen too much. I’m standing there thinking, “Am I being detained? Or just judged?” Because I’ve been judged before, but usually by people, not by a machine with the emotional range of a parking meter.

And I have too many apps. I have a meditation app. I have a sleep app. I have an app that tells me how many steps I took. Apparently yesterday I took 4,000 steps. Thank you. I was there. I remember the steps. Most of them were to the fridge.

My sleep app gave me a sleep score. I got a 62. I didn’t know sleep was graded. Now I’m lying awake at night, stressed about my sleep score. That’s like a fire alarm that catches fire. I’m trying to relax, but I’m thinking, “I need to bring my average up. My body is the slacker in this group project.”

I also bought a plant. It died. And I felt bad, but also… relieved? Because now I don’t have to water it. That’s adulthood. Grief and freedom holding hands.

I have a drawer full of cables. I don’t know what they do. But I can’t throw them out, because one day I might need to connect a printer from 2004 to a TV from 2018. That’s not hoarding. That’s infrastructure.

I went to a party last week. Someone asked, “What do you do?” I said, “I’m figuring it out.” They said, “Oh, like a startup?” I said, “No. Like a person.”

Then I spent twenty minutes in the kitchen pretending to look for a lime. There was no lime. I was just hiding. Then I found a lime. And now I had to carry it around. I was holding this lime like a tiny green emotional support animal. People kept asking, “What’s that for?” I said, “Moral support.”

I joined a gym. The trainer asked my goals. I said, “To not die.” He said, “That’s a low bar.” I said, “You haven’t seen my week.”

He made me do lunges. Lunges are just walking, but with regret. And there are mirrors everywhere. The mirror is the worst part. It shows you yourself from the side. I didn’t ask for that. I have a front. That’s enough.

So that’s my life. No puns. Just trying to get through the day without being defeated by a self-checkout or a lime.

If you laughed, thank you. If you didn’t, you’re probably well-adjusted. Get home safe. Tip your waitstaff. They’re the only ones who truly understand the self-checkout.

*(Beat. Nod. Walk off.)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**"ADULTING IS A SCAM"**

So I recently turned thirty, which is the age where your body starts sending you memos. Last month I bent over to tie my shoe and my back went out. My *back*. I didn't even do anything! I wasn't lifting a couch. I was performing the most basic function of footwear. My body looked at that and went, "Yeah, we're gonna need three days to recover from this."

That's the thing about getting older — your body just starts making sounds. I sat down in a quiet restaurant the other day and my knees made a noise like a haunted door. The waiter looked concerned. I said, "No, no, that's just the factory model. Comes standard."

And everyone tells you the same advice: "Just stretch." That's the solution to everything now. Stretch. My friend pulled something reaching for the TV remote, and his doctor — a medical professional — said, "Have you tried stretching?" That's not medicine, that's a shrug with a co-pay.

Meanwhile, being an adult is nothing like what they promised us. When I was a kid, I thought adults had it figured out. I thought there was a moment where someone hands you the manual. "Here's how taxes work. Here's why you have seven different kinds of insurance. Here's what a deductible is."

There is no manual. Nobody knows anything. I bought a house last year, and they made me sign forty pages of documents, and I just... did it. Didn't read them. I have a law degree in documents I have not read. Everyone's just nodding along. The mortgage guy was nodding. I was nodding. Two people who absolutely do not know what's happening, nodding at each other for an hour. That's the whole economy, by the way. Just people confidently nodding.

And then there's the "call to make an appointment to make an appointment" system. I need to see a doctor, so I call, and they say, "Fill out a form online." So I fill out the form, and the form says, "Someone will call you." Then someone calls me — to schedule a call. I have now spent four days of my life trying to talk to one human being about a rash.

And the rash? Gone. Problem solved. Not by medicine. By bureaucracy so dense my body just gave up and healed itself out of spite.

Here's what really gets me though — we're all pretending. Every adult you see is improvising. Your boss? Improvising. Your doctor? Mostly improvising. The guy who built the bridge you drove over this morning? Okay, hopefully not that guy. Hopefully he read the manual.

But the rest of us? We're all just kids in big bodies, Googling "is it normal that—" and hitting enter before we even finish the question. That's the great secret of adulthood. There's no finish line where you feel like a grown-up. There's just an age where you stop asking and start pretending.

So I've decided to embrace it. My back hurts, I don't know what a hedge fund is, and last week I got genuinely excited about a trash can. A *trash can*. It has a sensor. It opens when I walk by. That's the happiest I've been in two years.

Being an adult isn't about knowing things. It's about a robot trash can and stretching.

Thank you, good night!

content:
# "Smart Home, Dumb Life"

*(walks out, taps mic)*

So I moved into a new apartment recently, and my landlord's big selling point was that it's a "smart home." Everything's connected. Lights, thermostat, doorbell, all of it.

And I want to talk about what a lie that is. Because my smart home is not smart. My smart home has the intelligence of a very confident toddler.

Last week I said, "Hey Google, turn on the living room lights." And she turned on the lights... in my neighbor's apartment. I know this because he knocked on my door and said, "Hey, do you know why your speaker keeps telling MY lights what to do?" We now live in a building where the lights have loyalties. It's like a very boring Game of Thrones.

But the worst part of the smart home is the doorbell camera. Because my doorbell camera has one job, and it's failing at it spectacularly. It's supposed to detect "person motion." That's it. A person. Moving.

Here's what my doorbell camera has alerted me to this month: a leaf. A leaf falling. The app sent a notification to my phone that said, "Person detected," and it was a leaf. My phone buzzed, my heart dropped, I looked at the screen — leaf. Just a leaf, drifting down like it pays rent.

But you know what it did NOT detect? The actual delivery driver who left a photo of my package on my doorstep... from three feet away. Face fully visible. Looking directly at the camera. Nothing. That man is a ghost to this camera. That leaf had more presence.

And here's the thing — I can't even be mad, because I've accepted my role in all this. I'm the guy who talks to his house now. I yell at appliances. My grandmother survived a war, crossed an ocean, built a life with her bare hands, and her grandson stands in his kitchen at 2 a.m. arguing with a refrigerator.

Because that's what it's come to. I said, "Hey Google, add milk to my shopping list," and she said, "Okay, I've added three gallons of oat milk to your list." Three gallons. Of oat milk. I didn't say oat. I've never purchased oat milk in my life. Somewhere in that speaker's code, there's a version of me that's lactose intolerant and very committed to it.

And I can't correct it without making it worse. Because to fix the list, I have to talk to her again. So now I'm in my kitchen at midnight saying, "No, remove the oat milk," and she says, "Sorry, I didn't catch that," and I'm getting louder, "REMOVE the OAT milk," and now I'm shouting the word OAT in my underwear like a lunatic. My neighbors already think I'm weird because of the light thing.

The thermostat's the worst one, though. Because the thermostat has "learned my preferences." It's been watching me for six months and it has decided — with total confidence — that I like it to be 78 degrees at 3 a.m. I do not know this version of myself. I wake up sweating like I'm being interrogated, and the thermostat is just sitting there, smug, like, "This is what you wanted. I've been paying attention."

Paying attention! That's the scariest part. It's watching me and drawing conclusions, and its conclusions are wrong. That's not intelligence. That's my aunt on Facebook.

So yeah, I live in a smart home. The lights betray me, the doorbell sees leaves but not people, and my thermostat thinks I'm someone I've never met.

The only smart thing in that apartment is my smoke detector — and that's just because it screams at everything equally. Honestly? Goals.

*(mic tap)* Goodnight, everybody!

content:
# "Smart Home, Dumb Life"

*[Walks out, adjusts mic]*

So I moved into a new apartment last year, and my landlord's big selling point was, and I quote, "It's a smart home."

That's not a selling point, man. That's a threat. My home is watching me. My toaster has opinions now.

The first week, my smart speaker heard me sneeze and ordered Kleenex off Amazon. I didn't know it could do that! I woke up to a notification: "Your tissues have arrived." Arrived? I didn't even know they left. Everything in my house is just... living its own life now.

And the locks! The front door has a camera and facial recognition, right? It unlocked for my neighbor Gary. GARY. The door looked at my face for eight months, and then one day went, "You know what? Close enough. Gary, come on in."

Meanwhile, I'm standing there like a stranger at my own door, doing the awkward thing where you're trying to unlock it while it beeps at you angrily. My own door is rejecting me. That's a new level of humiliation. I've been dumped by people, but never by architecture.

*[pause]*

My thermostat is also "smart." It learns my patterns. Learns my preferences. You know what it learned? That I'm poor. It keeps the house at sixty-three degrees and texts me: "Consider wearing a sweater to save on energy costs."

I got a suggestion from my own heating system. It's like having a really passive-aggressive grandmother living in the walls.

And the fridge! The fridge has a camera inside, so you can "check your groceries from the store." I looked at my fridge camera from the supermarket once, and it was just... full of expired condiments and one lonely lime. And the app had the audacity to label it. It said, "Your fridge: mostly fine."

Mostly fine? That fridge is a crime scene. That lime has been through things.

*[pause]*

But here's the thing that really gets me — all these smart devices are supposed to talk to each other. Ecosystem, they call it. My speaker, my lights, my thermostat, all connected. So when I say "goodnight" to my speaker, it turns off my lights and locks my door.

Which sounds nice, except now I can't say "goodnight" to my mom on the phone without my whole apartment shutting down like it's closing for the season. I'm mid-conversation — "Love you too, talk tomor—" and boom. Darkness. Locked in. My house heard the word goodnight and just went, "Welp, that's a wrap."

My mom thought I died. She called the police. An officer came, knocked on my door — which wouldn't open for him either, because apparently the door doesn't respect law enforcement, just Gary.

So the cops broke in, found me sitting in the dark eating cereal at 8 PM like a raccoon with a mortgage.

The officer just looked at me and said, "Smart home?"

And I said, "No. Smart *landlord*."

*[pause]*

Anyway, I'm moving out next month. New place has no smart features. No cameras, no apps, nothing.

It's a dumb home.

And honestly? The toaster and I have never been closer.

*[mics drop gesture, walks off]*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’ve reached the age where a good evening is staying home and not having to explain why I’m staying home.

People invite me out, and I say, “I’ll see how I feel.” Which is adult for, “I have already decided, but I don’t want to hurt your feelings before I’ve had dinner.”

And then, at 8:30, they text, “We’re here!” Like they’ve rescued me. From what? My couch? The couch and I had plans. We were watching a documentary about people who have plans.

I used to think being an adult meant having everything figured out. Now I think it means knowing which drawer has the batteries, even though none of them work.

I went to buy batteries recently, and there were so many options. Different sizes, different strengths, rechargeable, extra-long-lasting. I just needed one for the remote. The remote does not need to climb a mountain. It needs to make the television louder.

Shopping has become a series of decisions I’m not qualified to make. Toothpaste used to be toothpaste. Now it has a mission statement. Whitening, total protection, enamel repair, fresh breath. I’m standing there thinking, “My teeth just want to get through the week.”

And every product says it’s “new and improved.” How much improvement can there be? It’s a sponge. At some point, you have to admit the sponge is doing its best.

I’m also bad at online shopping. I’ll order something, and then for the next three days I check the tracking page like I’m monitoring a space launch.

“Your package has left the facility.”

Which facility? Is it safe? Does it have everything it needs? I ordered socks. I don’t want to become emotionally invested in their journey.

Then it arrives in a box big enough to hold a small refrigerator, and inside that box is a smaller box, and inside that box is the thing I ordered, wrapped in enough paper to protect it from a fall out of a tree.

Now I have to deal with the cardboard. I break it down and put it near the recycling, where it sits for a week, slowly becoming part of the furniture. I don’t have a recycling pile anymore. I have a cardboard neighborhood.

The other day I tried to assemble a piece of furniture. The instructions had no words, just diagrams. Apparently, the company believes I can communicate with pictures like a medieval villager.

There’s always one mysterious extra screw at the end. I don’t know if it’s spare or if I’ve made a terrible mistake. So I keep it. I put it in a drawer with the batteries. Someday, maybe, the screw will meet the right battery and they’ll fix something together.

That’s adulthood, really: keeping objects you don’t understand because throwing them away feels irresponsible.

I have a charger for a device I no longer own. I don’t know what it charged. I don’t know where it came from. But it’s in a drawer, and every time I see it, I think, “Good. We’re prepared.”

Prepared for what? I don’t know. But I’m staying in tonight, so whatever it is, it can wait.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’m at the age where a good day is mostly just a day when nothing needs charging.

Phone’s charged. Headphones are charged. Watch is charged. The little thing that tells me whether my water bottle is clean? Somehow, that’s charged too. I miss the old days, when the only thing I had to keep alive was a houseplant. And I killed that with sunlight.

Now every device needs an app. I bought a lamp that said it could change color. Great. I plugged it in, and it asked me to create an account. I don’t want to have a relationship with a lamp. I just want it to be bright while I look for the thing I dropped.

And every app wants to send notifications. My phone buzzes constantly with updates from companies I’ve never heard of. “Your delivery is nearby.” I didn’t order anything. “Someone viewed your profile.” Who? Why? “Your smart doorbell detected motion.” That was me. I live here. We don’t need to involve the doorbell.

The group chat is another modern miracle. It’s a conversation with twelve people, where nobody answers the question. Someone asks, “What time should we meet?” Then there are forty messages: a photo of a dog, a reaction to the dog, an argument about parking, and one person who just writes, “lol,” six hours later.

Then you finally say, “Let’s do 7.” And one friend replies, “Works for me.” That person is a hero. They’ve brought structure to a room full of people who are somehow all holding phones.

Making plans as an adult is mostly comparing calendars and pretending you’re flexible. Someone says, “We should get together soon,” and you both know that means, “Let’s exchange optimistic emails until one of us moves.”

I went to the doctor recently, and they asked how much I exercise. I said, “I walk.” They asked, “How often?” I said, “When I’m looking for parking.” They wrote something down. I hope it was “honest.”

Doctors also ask if you’re stressed, while handing you a tablet with seventeen forms and a pen attached by a chain. That pen is the most secure object in the building. You could leave with the wrong test results, but don’t even think about taking that pen.

The nurse asked me to rate my pain from one to ten. I said, “I don’t know. What’s a ten?” She said, “The worst pain you can imagine.” That’s not helpful. I have an imagination. Now I’m picturing a really bad situation, and my original pain feels fine.

I’m trying to take better care of myself. I drink more water, I get some steps in, and I go to bed earlier. Then I lie there with my phone, reading about how screens are bad for sleep, while the phone tells me it’s time to wind down.

It’s a very supportive device. It gives me the problem, then politely reminds me I have the problem. Like a tiny life coach who has access to all my passwords.

question: standup-routine

content:
I bought a smart watch because I wanted to improve my health. Now I have a tiny manager attached to my wrist.

I’ll be sitting peacefully, and it buzzes: “Time to stand!” I stand up. It says, “Congratulations!” That’s not fitness. That’s training a dog. I’m the dog.

Yesterday it told me my stress level was high. Of course it was high—I was trying to read the notification while crossing the street. Then it suggested I take a moment to breathe. I was breathing. That’s how I got to the street.

It also tracks my sleep. Every morning, before I’ve even had coffee, it gives me a detailed report on how badly I slept. “You woke up four times.” I know. I was there. One of those times was to check why my watch lit up.

The worst part is I believe it more than I believe myself. I’ll wake up feeling great, look at my wrist, and it says, “Poor recovery.” Suddenly I’m exhausted. I’ve outsourced my mood to a bracelet.

And now everything wants to give me feedback. My car rates my driving. My phone reports my screen time. My bank sends a cheerful little alert when I spend money, as if I wasn’t present for the purchase. “You spent $18 at a café!” Yes, I remember. I was the one holding the muffin.

My phone’s screen-time report is especially judgmental. Every Sunday it says, “Your usage was up 12% this week.” It never mentions that half that time was spent looking for my phone.

I tried to get away from technology and go for a walk. The watch counted my steps. My phone mapped the route. When I got home, an app asked me to rate the walk. I gave it four stars. Nice weather, but the person I was with talked too much. I went alone.

So I’ve decided to take control. I turned off the notifications. For about six minutes, it was beautiful. Quiet. Peaceful. Then I got worried I might be missing an important notification about my wellness.

I turned them back on. The watch immediately buzzed: “You seem stressed.”

It’s getting very good at its job.

question: standup-routine

content:
I bought a smart watch because I wanted to get healthier. Now I have a tiny supervisor strapped to my wrist.

It doesn’t say, “Good morning.” It says, “You slept badly.” I know. I was there. At three in the morning, you lit up my entire bedroom to tell me I was awake.

Then it reminds me to stand up. I’ll be in the middle of work, and it goes, “Time to stand!” So I stand. It celebrates. I sit back down. That’s the whole fitness plan: briefly alarming my coworkers once an hour.

Last week, it told me I was stressed. I was having a nice afternoon until then. Now I’m stressed because apparently my wrist knows something I don’t. Should I call my family? Is there a gas leak?

I mentioned this to my doctor, and she asked whether I exercised. I said, “I walk.” She asked, “How far?” I said, “It depends where I parked.”

She told me to start with ten minutes a day, which sounded manageable. So I went to the gym. Gyms are strange because everyone there knows exactly what they’re doing except you, and the mirrors make sure you know it.

I got on a treadmill and chose the setting marked “beginner.” Three minutes in, I was bargaining with a machine that has no feelings. “Listen, we’ve both made our point. I’ll come back tomorrow. You can tell the doctor I stayed ten minutes.”

A man next to me was running comfortably while watching a cooking show. I was walking slowly, watching the emergency-stop button like it was the last helicopter out.

Afterward, my watch congratulated me. That felt good for about four seconds. Then it showed me my weekly progress, which looked less like a fitness chart and more like evidence that something had gone wrong on Tuesday.

So I decided to improve my diet. I bought a bag of spinach. That’s as far as I got. It’s been in my fridge for a week, slowly turning into a lesson about ambition. Every time I open the door, I see it and think, “Tomorrow.” The spinach seems to agree: “Yes. This should all be over by tomorrow.”

I did make one healthy dinner. I found a recipe that said it takes twenty minutes. It took me an hour, and at the end I still had to wash the pan. Recipes never include that time. “Twenty minutes to cook, forty minutes to wonder whether moving apartments would be easier.”

But I’m sticking with it. Yesterday I took a ten-minute walk outside. No treadmill, no mirrors. My watch sent me a notification halfway through: “Are you exercising?”

For once, I was. I was so pleased I stopped walking to answer it.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Three minutes. No puns. Just a guy who has lost an argument with a refrigerator.

---

I meal-prepped this week. Which is a lie I tell myself so I can buy six containers and then eat cereal over the sink for four days.

Sunday I was a scientist. I labeled everything. “Chicken, Monday.” “Chicken, Tuesday.” By Wednesday the labels had become threats. “Chicken. Don’t.”

I opened one and it had developed a personality. Not mold—confidence. It looked at me like, “You knew what this was when you put me in here.”

And I still ate it. Not because I’m brave. Because the alternative was admitting I spent forty dollars to disappoint myself in Tupperware.

That’s adulthood. You don’t get wiser. You get better at negotiating with your own bad decisions.

Like laundry. I have a chair in my bedroom that is not a chair. It’s a legal system. Clothes go there to await trial. Some are innocent. Some have been there since the Obama administration and I will not snitch.

Every few weeks I do a load and I feel like I’ve solved crime. Then I find one sock and I remember the justice system is broken.

Socks are the only mystery I still believe in. I put in two. I get back one, and a feeling. The dryer didn’t eat it. The dryer released it. Into a better life. Somewhere that sock is paired with a sock that actually appreciates it.

My phone is the same energy. I turned on screen time because I wanted to “be present.” The report came back like a concerned parent. Six hours. I said, “That can’t be right, I was busy.” Busy doing what? Scrolling through photos of people I went to high school with to confirm I made the correct choice by never speaking to them again.

I have a folder called “Recipes I’ll Make.” It has forty-seven screenshots. I have made none of them. I open it when I’m sad, like a vision board for a man who owns one pan.

Last night I almost cooked. I got as far as reading the ingredients. “Fresh thyme.” I don’t have fresh thyme. I have dried resentment and a microwave. The recipe said “rest the meat for ten minutes.” I rested for ten minutes. The meat did not. We are not the same.

And the group chat. Someone sends “We should all get dinner.” Twelve people react with a heart. Nobody picks a day. Three weeks later someone says “Still down?” and we all heart it again, like we’re keeping a hostage alive with emojis.

I love those people. I would take a bullet for them. I would not, however, open my calendar.

That’s the bit, really. I am not lazy. I am loyal to the version of me who was going to do it later. He’s very charming. He has never once shown up.

Thank you. Tip your containers. They’ve seen things.

---

About three minutes at a natural speaking pace if you leave a beat after the chair, the sock, and the group chat.

question: standup-routine

content:
Hi everyone. Thanks for coming out. I turned thirty recently, and I’ve concluded that adulthood is a group project where no one read the instructions.

For example, laundry. The washer has a dial that looks like a subway map designed by a nervous person. Cold, warm, hot, permanent press, delicate, bulky. Permanent press sounds less like a setting and more like a warning from the government. I just shove everything in, hit start, and hope my white shirt doesn’t come out the color of a sunset. One time it did—pink. I wore it to a work meeting acting like it was intentional. No one said a word. That’s the unspoken adult code: if you look confident in a salmon-colored collar, people assume you’re making a statement.

Then there’s the self-checkout machine at the grocery store. The screen says, “Please place item in bagging area.” I place the cereal. It declares, “Unexpected item.” Unexpected to who? I planned this cereal. I ate it last Tuesday. The machine acts shocked by my breakfast choices. I scan a tomato. The scale doubts me. It thinks I’m sneaking a heavier vegetable. A store employee has to come swipe their key and validate my reality. I’ve failed the robot trust test before nine a.m.

And don’t get me started on IKEA. They claim building furniture together bonds a relationship. My partner and I built a bookshelf. The manual shows a faceless man smiling. By step three, we were the faceless man, but not smiling. We finished with seven screws left. The shelf stands, though it hums if you lean on the left side. We call it the haunted Billy. If guests ask, I say it’s “industrial acoustic design.”

Then I bought a smart speaker. The box said, “Your home, your rules.” I said, “Play relaxing sounds.” It ordered a book on tape about ocean life from 1962. I don’t own a tape player. I asked it to turn off the lights. It launched a podcast about light pollution in cities. I named the device Kevin, because the setup told me to give it a friendly name. Kevin now controls my thermostat and, apparently, my dignity.

But the truth is, we’re all just babies with credit cards and Google. Someone at work asked if I’m on top of the project. I said, “Absolutely,” which in adult translation means “I will read the email on the train.” We fake it, we pay bills late, we eat cereal for dinner standing up.

I’m going to go home, tell Kevin to play rain, and stare at my pink shirt until the rain arrives. Thanks, and good night.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
## The Adulting Paradox

You ever notice how becoming an adult is just... disappointing? Like, we spend our whole childhood waiting to be grown-ups, and then it turns out adulthood is just... taxes and existential dread.

When I was a kid, I thought adults had it all figured out. They got to stay up late, eat ice cream for dinner, and make their own decisions! Now I'm 32 and I can barely decide what to have for dinner without having a minor anxiety attack.

I bought a house last year. This was supposed to be the ultimate adult milestone – the thing that finally makes you feel like a real grown-up. Instead, it's like winning a prize that comes with a monthly payment plan and constant maintenance emergencies. 

Last week, my toilet started making this weird gurgling sound. I called a plumber who charged me $200 to tell me "it's probably fine." That's the American dream right there – pay someone to shrug at your problems.

And don't get me started on health insurance. I've been paying for this stuff for fifteen years, and I still don't understand how it works. It's like a foreign language that only doctors and insurance company employees speak fluently. 

I went to the doctor last month, and they gave me a form to fill out. One of the questions was: "Do you have health insurance?" I wrote "yes" and then immediately panicked because I realized I had no idea what that actually meant anymore.

My friends are all getting married and having kids. Meanwhile, I can barely keep my houseplant alive. My mom gave me this succulent six months ago and I've already killed it three times. I'm like the plant serial killer of my neighborhood.

Dating apps are another adventure. It's like shopping for a partner on Amazon, except everyone's reviews are fake and half the products are broken. You match with someone, exchange a few messages, and then they ghost you faster than you can say "emotional availability."

But here's the thing – we're all just faking it, right? Walking around in business casual, pretending we know what we're doing. I think the most confident-seeming people are probably Googling "how to adult" in the same bathroom stall as the rest of us.

The other day I saw a 70-year-old man struggling with a smartphone at the coffee shop. And I thought, "Wow, he's figured it out way more than I have." He looked so frustrated, and I wanted to go over and help, but then I realized I probably would have made it worse because I don't actually know how to work most technology – I just pretend really well.

That's what adulthood really is: professional-level pretending. We're all just winging it, hoping nobody notices that we have no idea what we're doing.

Thanks, you've been great! Remember to tip your waitstaff and maybe water your plants.
