**[Opening]**  
*Walks on stage, adjusts mic*  
"So, I’ve been trying to disconnect from technology lately. Which is funny, because my phone is literally trying to disconnect from me. It keeps showing me this little red badge that says, ‘Battery at 5%.’ And I’m like, ‘Buddy, you’re the one who’s been streaming cat videos for six hours straight. We both know what’s happening here.’"  

*Pause, shake head*  
"And don’t get me started on apps. I downloaded an app that tells me what apps I need. It said, ‘Based on your usage, you should try meditation.’ I opened the meditation app, and it immediately asked me to watch another app called ‘How to Stop Staring at Apps.’ It’s like the tech industry is gaslighting us into a recursive nightmare."  

---

**[Bit 1: Passwords]**  
*Leans into mic*  
"Passwords are the ultimate prank. We’re supposed to create these ‘strong’ passwords, but they’re always something ridiculous like ‘ILuvKittens123.’ Then websites give you security tips like, ‘For maximum security, use a password manager.’ Which is just tech speak for, ‘Let’s make this problem someone else’s.’  

I tried a password that’s literally impossible to guess: ‘123456.’ It worked! For like, five seconds. Then the hackers won and took my Netflix account hostage. They made me watch *The Office* again until I gave in. That’s when I realized, ‘123456’ is the new ‘password.’ It’s not a password—it’s a cry for help."  

---

**[Bit 2: Relationships]**  
*Paces, acting out a scenario*  
"My relationship with my partner? It’s like a Shakespearean drama meets a Home Depot commercial. Last week, I walked into the bathroom and the toilet seat was up. I said, ‘Why is the seat up?’ And they said, ‘Because you never put it down.’ And I’m like, ‘That’s because you never—’ *Cut myself off, mock-dramatic gasp* ‘—*put the seat down!*’  

We’ve reached a stalemate. I put a sign on the toilet: ‘If you’re reading this, you’re the problem.’ They put a sign on my side of the bed: ‘If you’re reading this, you’re the problem… and also a terrible husband.’ At this point, we’re just arguing over who’s more dramatic. Spoiler alert: It’s me. I once cried during a car commercial."  

---

**[Bit 3: Remote Work]**  
*Imitates typing on a laptop*  
"Remote work is great until your ‘home office’ becomes a crime scene. My kid walks in mid-meeting and asks, ‘Dad, why is the sky blue?’ And I’m supposed to be explaining ‘synergy’ to a Zoom call. I tried to pivot: ‘Because it’s a metaphor for how our company’s future is bright.’ *Kid nods like a tiny CEO.*  

And don’t even get me started on ‘Do Not Disturb’ signs. My neighbor once hung one on my door. I’m like, ‘How do you—? Oh wait, I forgot I live in a horror movie. Next thing you know, I’ll be hiding in a closet while my own kid texts me: ‘Mom, where are you?’"  

---

**[Bit 4: Social Media vs. Reality]**  
*Pulls out phone, pretends to scroll*  
"Social media is the only place where people live in a universe where their lives are perfect. ‘Look at my vacation!’ Meanwhile, I’m sitting here eating cereal for dinner and trying not to cry because my plant died. And don’t even get me started on filters. My face is so filtered, my eyelashes have their own LinkedIn profile.  

I tried posting a ‘real’ photo once: Me with pizza stains on my shirt and a ‘World’s Best Dad’ mug. The comments were like, ‘Aww, so relatable!’ and ‘Can I adopt you?’ I’m like, ‘This isn’t a dad bod—it’s a ‘I-ate-the-entire-bag-of-cheetos-and-now-I’m-sorry’ bod.’"  

---

**[Closer]**  
*Walk back to mic, softer tone*  
"But here’s the truth: Life’s messy, and so are we. We’re all out here trying to figure it out, faking it better than anyone else. And if you’re wondering, ‘Is this my life?’ the answer is yes. But hey, at least we’re not alone in the chaos.  

*Pause, grin*  
And if you see my phone battery at 5% tonight, just remember: It’s not a warning. It’s a lifestyle choice. Thank you, you’ve been a great audience. *Exits stage left, hobbles slightly as if lugging a dead phone*"  

---  
**[End]**  
*Total runtime: ~3 minutes. Delivery focuses on timing, physicality, and relatability without relying on wordplay.*

content:
# "I Am Functioning"

*(walks up, looks at mic)*

So I turned thirty last month. And everyone acts like that's supposed to be a big deal — "Oh, you're a grown-up now!" No. I'm not a grown-up. I'm a child who pays rent. That's it. That's the whole difference.

I used to think adults had it figured out. You know, I'd watch my parents and think, "One day I'll be that person who owns a plunger and isn't afraid to use it." *(beat)* And here I am — I own three plungers, and I still Google "how to unclog a toilet" every single time.

The worst part is the little things. Like, I went to the doctor last week and he said, "You need to watch your cholesterol." And I said, "Doc, I'm trying, I'm really trying." And he looked at me like I'd just told him my biggest failure. And it WAS my biggest failure. I ate an entire sleeve of Oreos at eleven at night while watching a documentary about heart disease. That's not a snack. That's performance art.

And relationships — don't get me started. My friend told me the secret to a good relationship is communication. So I started communicating more. My girlfriend said, "We need to talk." And I said, "Great! I've been really looking forward to this." And then she told me she was leaving, and I said, "Okay, great communication!" I'm not good at this stuff. I'm the guy who says "I understand" when he absolutely does not understand anything.

You know what else is crazy? How much of adult life is just pretending. Pretending you know what you're doing at work. Pretending you're fine when your back goes out picking up a grocery bag. *(mimics wincing)* I threw out my back reaching for a cereal box. A CEREAL BOX. I have the back of a sixty-year-old accountant and the diet of a raccoon.

But honestly? I think I'm getting the hang of it. Last week, I cooked a whole meal. Chicken, vegetables, rice — the works. And my neighbor knocked on my door and said, "That smells amazing, what are you making?" And I said, "I don't know, I bought it all at the store and hoped for the best." She smiled and walked away. That's love, man. That's love.

*(pause)*

I'm thirty now. I have a plunger, a bad back, and a neighbor who thinks I'm a good cook. I think I'm doing pretty well.

*(bows, exits)*

content:
# "The Invisible Curriculum"

*(3-minute stand-up routine)*

---

Nobody tells you what adulthood actually is. You go through twelve years of school, you graduate, you get a diploma — and nobody says, "Congratulations! Now you're just going to be mildly anxious forever."

I turned twenty-five and realized I'd been handed a life with no instruction manual. It's like buying a piece of furniture from IKEA. You get forty-three pieces of wood, an Allen wrench the size of a toothpick, and a diagram that's just... arrows. There's no picture on the box. You just have to *feel* your way through it, and somewhere around step twelve you're crying on the floor, and you've built a shelf that leans seventeen degrees to the left.

That's my life. That's every week.

I tried to be an adult last month. I sat down and made a budget. I listed my expenses — rent, groceries, electricity, phone. Then I got to the end of the list and there was a line item I didn't even know existed: "Miscellaneous." I'm like, what is *miscellaneous*? What does that even mean? That's not a category, that's a confession. "I spent forty dollars at Target and I don't even know what I bought." That's not miscellaneous, that's a crime scene.

And then there's the medical system. I went to the doctor recently for a thing that wasn't even that serious — it was just a mole, it was fine. The doctor looked at it, looked at me, and said, "We should just... monitor it." Monitor it. That's not a diagnosis, that's a dare. You're just like, "Cool, I'll go home and stare at it every night and convince myself it's getting smaller."

The worst part is everyone pretends they have it together. You go to a dinner party and someone says, "So, how's life?" and they just... nod like they understand what they're doing. They don't. We're all just winging it. We're all just pretending the shelf isn't leaning.

I think the real lesson nobody teaches you is this: adulthood isn't a destination. It's just a long hallway with a lot of locked doors and a buzzing fluorescent light, and you're just walking down it hoping nobody asks you what you're doing with your life — because you genuinely don't know.

But hey — at least I built that shelf. It holds books. It leans. It's perfect.

*(bow)*

---

*Approximate runtime: ~3 minutes at natural conversational pace.*

# 3-Minute Stand-Up Routine: "Adulting Is a Scam"

So I turned thirty last week. And nobody warned me that adulthood is just choosing between two mildly unpleasant options for the rest of your life. *"Do I do my taxes or do I let the IRS find me?"* That's not a decision — that's a horror movie.

My phone has more passwords than I have close friends. I have a password for my password manager. I have a password to log into the app that stores my passwords. And every six months, it makes me change it, so I just write it on a sticky note. I put the sticky note *on* the password manager app. I'm not hiding it. I'm displaying it. I've accepted my fate.

And don't get me started on grocery shopping. You go in for milk, you come out with four things you didn't need, a candle that smells like "ocean breeze" — which is just salt water and regret — and somehow you've spent sixty dollars. Sixty dollars on food I'm going to eat while standing over my sink in the dark. That's the whole meal. I'm just a person hovering over a garbage can with a leftover burrito.

Social media is another thing. Everyone's living their best life online. Meanwhile, I'm on my couch at 11 PM eating peanut butter straight from the jar with a spoon like a raccoon. And I'm not even upset about it — I'm at peace with the raccoon. *The raccoon is me.*

But honestly? The weirdest part is how we all just... agreed to this. Nobody voted for this. There was no referendum. One day you're a kid eating chicken nuggets without a care, and the next day you're in bed at 2 AM googling *"is it normal to be tired at 3 PM"* and the search engine just stares back at you like, *"Buddy, it's not 3 PM for anyone. That's just your life now."*

And the scariest thing? It works. I pay my bills. I show up. I put on pants that aren't sweatpants sometimes — well, *joggers*, which are basically sweatpants with better marketing. But I function. I'm a functioning adult. Which is just a kid with a credit score and a therapist.

Thank you, you've been a great audience.

---

**Word count:** ~380 (≈3 minutes at performance pace)
**Techniques used:** Observational humor, exaggeration, self-deprecation, misdirection, callback (the raccoon)
**No puns used** — all laughs come from relatable premises and escalation.

content:
( walks to the mic, adjusts the stand)

Hey everyone, how we doing? Good?

So, I realized something recently. We are living in the future, but we’re acting like we’re still stuck in 1998.

Think about it. We have phones in our pockets that can calculate the speed of light, translate any language, and tell us exactly where the nearest sushi place is. And yet, I still spend ten minutes trying to plug a USB-C cable into a charging port.

I’m serious. I have this phone. It costs more than my first car. And every time I need to charge it, I do the flip test. Flip it once. Doesn’t go in. Flip it again. Still doesn’t go in. Flip it a third time. Finally clicks in. And I feel like I’ve won a small victory. Like I just hacked the matrix.

It’s the only time I feel powerful in my life.

And it’s not just the cable. It’s the passwords. Everyone has a password policy now. “Must contain a capital letter, a number, a special character, and the name of your pet’s first vet’s middle name.”

So I set this password. And I type it in. It says, “Incorrect.”

So I try again. It says, “Incorrect.”

Then I remember. I changed my email address three months ago. So now I have to reset the password to reset the password. I’m locking myself out of my own life just to prove I remember the code to the code.

I finally get back in, and I write the new password down on a sticky note. And I put the sticky note on the front of my laptop.

Security is an illusion, people.

But the weirdest part of modern life isn’t the tech. It’s the way we treat each other. Or specifically, the way we treat a stranger.

Like, I went to the grocery store yesterday. I was just minding my own business, buying bananas. You know, the basic things. And I got stuck behind a lady in the checkout line.

She was doing the full scan. Bagging her own groceries. And she had this attitude like she was defusing a bomb.

She puts the milk down. Then the bread. Then the eggs. And she’s moving her arms like she’s conducting an orchestra. I’m just standing there with my basket, looking like I’m in the way.

I wanted to say, “Ma’am, it’s okay. We all have problems.” But I didn’t. Because that’s the thing about being polite now. We’re terrified to say anything.

We’d rather stand in silence for four minutes than ask, “Hey, could you move the eggs to the left?”

We’re all walking around with this invisible shield. Just hoping nobody talks to us. If someone makes eye contact, we look down immediately. We pretend to be checking our phones.

But nobody is checking their phones. Nobody has anything on their phone. We’re just standing there, looking at the black screen, pretending to be busy.

I saw a guy like that in line yesterday. He’s staring at his screen. I look down at mine, I’ve got a calculator app open. I haven’t done a calculation since Tuesday. I’m just tapping random numbers.

I thought about asking him, “Hey, what’s two plus two?” Just to break the tension. But I didn’t. Because then he’d have to look up, and then we’d have to make eye contact, and then we’d have to smile, and then we’d have to talk.

No thank you. I’ll take the silence. I’ll take the USB struggle. I’ll take the password reset.

At least when the computer says “Access Denied,” it’s being honest. It’s not pretending to be my friend.

So, yeah. That’s my life. I’m just a guy with a phone, a password, and a lot of patience.

Thank you guys, I’m (Your Name)!

(Waves, walks off)

content:
# "The Modern Human Experience"

---

So I got a smart watch last year. You know what a smart watch tells you? It tells you everything you're doing wrong. Every single day, this thing is judging me.

"You haven't moved in three hours." That's because I'm *working*, watch. I'm not a Labrador retriever. I don't need to be exercised.

Then it tells you to breathe. *Breathe.* I've been breathing. I've been breathing for thirty-four years. I'm pretty sure I've got it. But the watch is like, "No, no — do it *mindfully*." I've never once breathed mindfully. I just breathe. And apparently that's a mistake now.

---

And speaking of things that judge you — my phone is always trying to sell me stuff I already bought. I bought a couch two months ago, and now every app I open is like, "Still looking for the perfect couch?" No! I found it! I'm sitting on it! Stop following me around the internet like a bad ex.

Last week I Googled one thing — *one thing* — a camping tent. Now my entire identity to the algorithm is "person who might like the outdoors." I'm getting emails about hiking boots. I haven't left the house in three days. I ordered DoorDash twice today. I am not a hiker. I don't even know what a trail is.

---

You know what else is a scam? Grocery stores.

They've got you at the register, right? And there's that moment where the cashier asks if you want to round up for charity. And everyone in line is watching. You can't say no. You can't be the person who's like, "No, I'm keeping my four cents." So you say yes, you round up, you feel like a saint — and then you get home and realize you just spent $87 on groceries and you don't know what any of it is.

I bought a whole bag of something last week. I still don't know what it was. It's just sitting in my pantry, judging me, waiting for me to figure it out.

---

And can we talk about how nobody actually knows how to use a printer?

We've had printers for like forty years. We put a man on the moon with less technology. But every single time — every single time — you hit print and the machine just… *thinks* about it. It makes this noise. It's like it's deciding whether you're worthy. And then it says "Paper jam." There is no jam. I checked. There's no paper. There's no jam. The printer is just upset with me.

My printer and my smart watch are in cahoots. They're both just sitting there, whispering about how lazy I am.

---

Anyway, that's my life now. Just a man, being judged by his own possessions. And if you think about it — isn't that just what your parents always said would happen?

*"One day, your stuff will be the one telling you what to do."*

Thanks, you've been great. Good night.

---

*(Approximate delivery time: 3 minutes at a natural pace)*

content:
# "Adulting Is a Scam" — A 3-Minute Stand-Up Set

---

*(Walks up to the mic, adjusts it, looks at the audience)*

So I bought a house last year. That's supposed to be like... the American Dream, right? The real estate agent was like, "Congratulations, you're a homeowner now!" Yeah, thanks. I'm also a prisoner. I used to call one person when something broke. Now I am the person. Last week my garbage disposal stopped working, and I just stood over the sink staring at it like it owed me money. I went on YouTube and watched a twelve-minute video about garbage disposals. Twelve minutes! I could have learned an entire language in that time. Instead I now know what a "hopper pipe" is, and I don't want to.

*(Beat)*

And the thing is — owning a house doesn't make me feel grown up. It just makes me feel tired. I recently got excited about a new mop. A MOP. My twenty-year-old self would be disgusted. My twenty-year-old self also thought gas was expensive at two dollars, so honestly, screw that guy.

*(Beat)*

You know what's wild? Grocery shopping. I used to walk into a grocery store with no plan and just... wing it. Now I go in with a LIST. I plan meals. I buy "staples." Who even am I? Last week I found myself standing in the spice aisle for five minutes debating between paprika and smoked paprika like it was a *moral* decision. And then I got home, used neither of them, and ordered pizza.

*(Beat)*

And dating as an adult is a whole different level of chaos. You can't just "meet people" anymore. Oh no. You have to go on an APP. You create a profile where you pretend to be interesting. I put "I love hiking" on mine. I don't love hiking. I've been on two hikes, and both times I was miserable by the ten-minute mark. But apparently "I love sitting in a dimly lit apartment rewatching The Office for the ninth time" doesn't test well.

*(Beat)*

My girlfriend and I moved in together, by the way. Which is great. Love her. But sharing a bathroom with someone is the real compatibility test. Forget love languages. It's about who cleans the hair out of the drain. And it's ALWAYS you. You just know it's you. You can never catch them in the act. It's like the hair just appears. Every time I pull that hair out of the drain, I look at it and think, "This is what love is. It's gross and it's on my hands."

*(Beat)*

And nobody tells you how weird it is to still feel like a kid when you have actual responsibilities. Like, I have a mortgage. I have health insurance. I have a retirement fund I don't understand. But I still can't eat cereal without watching cartoons. I just balance my checkbook now while doing it.

*(Beat)*

Here's my theory: being an adult is just doing kid stuff with worse knees and way more bills. Thank you, you've been great!

---

*⏱ Approx. delivery time: 3 minutes at a natural pace*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I started therapy last year because I realized I was spending too much time worrying about things that hadn't happened yet.

My therapist was great. First session she says, "Tell me what brings you in." And I’m like, "I’m anxious." She says, "Okay, about what?" And I just start listing.

I’m anxious about my retirement. I’m 34. I’m anxious about my kids’ college fund. I don’t have kids. I’m anxious about my dog getting old. I don’t have a dog.

She just nods. She’s taking notes. I’m spiraling and she’s like, "That’s a lot." I said, "Yeah, I know, I’m a lot."

After about 20 minutes she stops me and says, "Can we just focus on one thing that’s actually happening right now?" And I said, "Okay, I’m anxious that you’re judging me for being anxious about things that aren’t happening."

She didn’t even blink.

That’s when I knew she was a professional.

The thing is, modern anxiety is just really efficient. It used to be like, "Oh no, a bear is coming." Now it’s, "Oh no, what if my Wi-Fi goes out during a Zoom call in three years and my boss thinks I’m unprofessional and then I get fired and then I have to move back in with my parents who still think I’m a disappointment."

We’ve upgraded.

I also have this new fear of being left on read. Not by a crush, by my own bank. I’ll get a notification that says "Payment processed" and I’ll sit there waiting for the confirmation email. It never comes. I start refreshing. I start Googling "is my bank ignoring me." I’m 34, I have a mortgage, I am being ghosted by Chase.

And don’t even get me started on grocery shopping. I used to go in, get what I needed, leave. Now I go in with a list and I leave with a crisis.

I’m standing in the cereal aisle for 12 minutes because I’m trying to decide if I’m the kind of person who buys the healthy cereal or the kind of person who lies to themselves. I pick both. I’m now the kind of person who buys two boxes of cereal and eats neither.

The self-checkout machine is my therapist now. It asks me, "Did you find everything okay?" And I want to say, "No. I found oat milk, and now I’m questioning all my life choices."

I think the hardest part about being an adult is that nobody tells you when it’s over. You just wake up one day and you’re Googling "how to unclog a garbage disposal" at 2am and you’re not even mad about it. You’re just... resigned.

My dad called me the other day and said, "You’re doing great." And I said, "Thanks, Dad." And he said, "No, seriously, you’re doing great for someone who’s 34 and still can’t assemble IKEA furniture without crying."

He’s right. I built a bookshelf last weekend. It took me four hours. It’s crooked. It’s wobbly. It holds books. It also holds my entire sense of self-worth, and it’s about to collapse.

That’s adulthood. You’re just trying to keep things from falling over while pretending you meant for them to be crooked.

Thanks, I’ll be here all week. Try not to worry about it.

content:
**[Spotlight hits, the comic walks up, adjusts the mic]**

Hey everybody, great to be here. I’m gonna talk about something we all know too well—being an adult in the 21st century. You know that feeling when you’re standing in the grocery aisle and you realize you’ve been shopping for the same thing for ten minutes and still can’t decide whether to buy the name‑brand cereal or the “just as good” one? It’s like a mini‑courtroom, and the judge is a 30‑year‑old dad who’s already decided he’ll just get the cheap one and pretend it’s a “budget lifestyle choice.”  

And the cereal box? It’s got a picture of a smiling family on it, all bright and happy, while the actual cereal looks like tiny, sad little rocks. You’re standing there, holding a box that says “100% Whole Grain” and you think, “Whole grain for what? My whole day? My whole diet? My whole existence?”  

Then there’s the whole “organic” thing. I saw an organic carrot once. I asked the clerk, “Is it organic because it’s grown without chemicals, or because it’s grown without… personality?” She looked at me like I’d asked whether the carrot has a social security number.  

Speaking of numbers, let’s talk about passwords. Remember when we used to pick a simple word like “password”? Now the requirements are ridiculous. You need a capital letter, a number, a symbol, a hieroglyph, and a blood sample. I wrote a password once that was just a string of emojis. The IT department sent me a notice: “Your password is too pictorial.” I’m like, “What’s the point of a password if I can’t just show you a picture of a cat and a taco?”  

And the two‑factor authentication. It’s like a loyalty program for your own security. “Enter the code sent to your phone.” I get a text that says, “Your code is 834291.” I stare at it, and I think, “Is this a code or the combination to a safe?” Then I realize the only thing I’m really protecting is my own ego. “I’m so important that I need two steps to get into my own email.”  

Now, let’s talk about the gym. I joined a gym because I wanted to be healthier. The first week I was the only person who could actually figure out how to use the treadmill without stepping off it every two minutes. The trainer walked by, smiled, and said, “You’re doing great! Just keep going.” I wanted to say, “I’m not going anywhere; I’m just trying not to fall off this moving belt.”  

And the classes—spin, yoga, HIIT. I tried a HIIT class once. The instructor yelled, “Give me 30 seconds of all‑out effort!” I looked at my watch, realized I’d already spent 30 seconds trying to figure out which button to press to start the timer, and then I spent the next 30 seconds feeling like I’d just run a marathon in a hallway.  

But the best part of the gym is the locker room. Nothing like a room full of half‑naked strangers to remind you that everyone’s body is a work in progress. I saw a guy with a tattoo that said “Live Love Lift.” I thought, “That’s a nice motto. I’m still waiting for my tattoo that says ‘Live, Love, and Figure Out How to Use the Wi‑Fi.’”

Speaking of Wi‑Fi, have you noticed how the signal strength indicator is basically a mood ring for your internet? It goes from full bars—“I’m connected, I’m happy”—to one bar—“I’m barely hanging on, why is my life like this?” I once had a video call where the signal dropped to one bar right as I was about to announce my promotion. The other person’s face turned into a pixelated ghost. I said, “Sorry, my internet just got a little… emotional.”  

And finally, the whole “smart home” thing. My thermostat learns my schedule and adjusts itself. I come home after a long day, and it’s set to 78 °F because it “learned” I like it warm when I’m exhausted. I’m like, “Thermostat, you don’t know me. You don’t know that I’ve been walking around in socks because the floor is colder than my ex’s heart.”  

So that’s my three minutes of adult life—cereal choices, password nightmares, gym anxiety, Wi‑Fi drama, and a thermostat that thinks it’s a therapist. If any of this sounds familiar, feel free to laugh. If not, well… you’re probably a robot, and I’m glad you’re here to watch the show.  

**[Mic drop, walk off]**

question: standup-routine

content:
*(Adjusts mic, steps back slightly)*

You ever notice how making plans as an adult has become less like hanging out and more like coordinating a small international aid mission?

I don’t miss the old days dramatically. I just miss the simplicity. Remember when someone would just say, “Hey, want to grab a beer Friday?” And Friday would come, and you’d be there. Now? It’s a logistical operation. You need a whiteboard. You need to check three different time zones. At some point, you’re just asking yourself: did I invite friends, or am I booking a conference call?

It starts in the group chat. You know the type. Three people haven’t exchanged messages in six weeks, then suddenly: “We really need to all get together soon!” 

Which is lovely! Truly! It’s like emotional window shopping. No checkout, no receipt, just the warm feeling of potentially knowing each other again. But then… nothing. Because apparently, “soon” isn’t a day on the calendar. “Soon” is what you type when you’re actively avoiding looking at your own schedule.

So if you actually want to lock something in, you become a project manager. I’m talking confirmation texts, backup locations, at least one passive-aggressive reply-all just to verify nobody’s soul has left their body. You’re not meeting friends. You’re managing stakeholders. And statistically, you’re the only one invested in the Q3 deliverable.

Then you finally pick a day. Everyone’s genuinely thrilled. “Can’t wait!” “So excited!” “It’s been way too long!” And then… absolute silence. Radio dead. You start spiraling. Did I pick a bad restaurant? Is my energy weird? Did I accidentally join a cult?

Then, twelve minutes before meet-up time, the text arrives: “Running five minutes behind!”

We both know what that means. That’s not a delay. That’s the audio cue of someone currently arguing with themselves about whether sweatpants count as formal attire. They’re not stuck in traffic. They’re currently using their thumb to pry open a bag of chips they forgot they bought.

And yet… we keep doing it. Because when it actually works—when all four of you walk in on time, the drinks arrive, and someone inevitably tells the exact same story they’ve told since sophomore year—you remember why you tolerate the negotiation phase. It’s fragile. It’s temporary. But it lands.

So I’ll keep dropping the “let’s get together soon!” messages. I’ll keep treating “soon” like a flexible contract. And if anyone actually replies with a day, a time, and a physical address? I’ll probably show up. Assuming I haven’t already convinced myself otherwise by noon.

Thank you, you’ve been amazing!

content:
**A 3-Minute Stand-Up Routine**

Thank you. I’ve reached the age where “getting lucky” means finding my phone charger on the first try.

I’m too old to be surprised by technology. When I was younger, if my laptop made a weird noise, I thought, “Oh no, it’s dying.” Now I hear a weird noise from my laptop and I think, “There you are. I knew you had one in you.”

I also have a new relationship with my phone. It’s less “useful device” and more “anxious roommate who never sleeps.” I put my phone down to charge it, and it immediately starts acting like I’ve abandoned it. I’ll be across the room, and I hear: “Bing. Bing. Bing. You there? You there? You there?” I’m like, “I’m right here! I’m not leaving you! I’m just making a sandwich!”

But the worst part is that I’ve started talking to my phone like it’s a person who owes me money. I’ll say, “Open the map app,” and it takes so long I’m like, “What are you doing? Are you getting dressed? Should I call your mother?”

I also don’t trust “self-checkout” anymore. The machine acts like it’s doing me a favor. I scan one item, and it says, “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Unexpected item? That’s a bag of spinach. I put it there. I didn’t sneak it in. I have receipts.

And then a teenager appears with the confidence of a hostage negotiator and the patience of a traffic cone. He scans my bag, walks away, and I’m left standing there wondering what crime I’ve committed.

That’s why I don’t like grocery stores anymore. It used to be a place where you got food. Now it’s a place where you prove to a robot that you are not a threat to society.

I’ve also become very bad at small talk. I used to be able to stand in an elevator with someone and say, “Nice day, huh?” Now I just calculate how much eye contact is legally required before I look at the floor.

There’s a moment in conversation when someone says, “How are you?” and you have two options: the socially acceptable answer or the honest answer. The socially acceptable answer is “Good, you?” The honest answer is, “I have nine tabs open, four of them are related to a problem I don’t want to solve, and one is me researching whether it’s normal to be this tired after doing absolutely nothing.”

But I don’t say that. I say, “Good, you?” And they say, “Busy,” which is adult for “I have not experienced joy since 2017, but I have a calendar invite.”

The older I get, the more I realize my body is no longer a machine. It’s more like a group chat. My knees say one thing, my back says another, and my stomach is just sending memes at 2 a.m.

I’ll lie down and my back goes, “We should discuss your posture.” My knee goes, “Remember that stair you took in 2013?” And my brain goes, “Should we be worried?” Yes. Yes, we should be worried.

Thank you, you’ve been great.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
# "I'm Doing My Best"

*(walks up, adjusts mic)*

So I've been trying to become a person who makes phone calls. Like, actually calls people. Because I read somewhere that it's good for your mental health.

And I did it. I called my dentist to reschedule an appointment. And the receptionist said, "Can I get your date of birth?" And I said it. And she said, "And your name?" And I said it. And then there was this pause. And she said, "I'm sorry, I'm not finding that." And I just... *accepted death.*

I didn't say "try a different spelling." I didn't say "maybe it's under my mom's name." I just said, "Yeah, that's fair," and hung up. And now I have a cavity the size of a parking garage.

*(beat)*

The thing is, I'm not shy. I'm not anxious. I just have this deeply held belief that if a system doesn't immediately recognize me, I must not exist. And I'm not going to argue with the universe about it.

*(pause)*

I do this at self-checkout too. You know self-checkout? It's a machine that was designed to make you feel like you're shoplifting your own groceries.

"Unexpected item in bagging area."

It's *my* bananas. I bought them. They're in the bag because I *put* them there. We are in agreement, you and I. And yet you look at me like I'm running a smuggling operation.

And the worst part is—there's always an attendant. And they walk over with that little key card, and they swipe it, and they look at you. Not at the screen. At *you.* Like you've been caught. Like you were trying to get away with a cantaloupe.

I once had an attendant sigh at me. Not a frustrated sigh. A *disappointed* sigh. Like a parent watching their kid strike out in T-ball.

*(beat)*

But here's the thing—I keep going back. Every week. Because I keep thinking, "This time, I will be the person who scans the items correctly on the first try." And every week, the machine says "unexpected item," and I say "I'm sorry" to it. Out loud. To a machine.

And the attendant hears me. And they don't help. They just stand there, arms crossed, like a zookeeper watching an animal fail to solve a puzzle.

*(pause)*

And I think that's just adulthood. Just a series of machines and receptionists and systems that don't recognize you, and you just keep saying "I'm sorry" and trying again next week.

*(beat)*

I'm gonna go reschedule that dentist appointment.

*(waves, walks off)*

content:
# "I'm Doing My Best"

*(walks up, adjusts mic)*

So I turned 34 last month, and I've reached the age where my body sends me error messages like a printer. I woke up last Tuesday and my neck just said, "We're not doing that anymore." No injury. No accident. I slept *wrong*. I slept wrong and my body filed a grievance.

I'm at the point where I have to warm up before I do things that used to be the warm-up. I have to stretch before I stretch. I'm basically a grandmother loading into a minivan.

*(pause)*

And nobody warns you about the grocery store thing. When you're young, grocery shopping is a punishment your mom gives you. "Go get the milk." Now I'm in there at 9 PM on a Wednesday, holding a cantaloupe up to my ear like I'm trying to hear a heartbeat. I'm *listening* to the melon. I don't even know what I'm listening for. What does a good cantaloupe sound like? What does a bad one confess?

*(sets imaginary melon down)*

I bought it. It was bad. I knew it was bad in the store. I just didn't want to admit it.

*(pause)*

And I've started doing this thing where I make plans and then I pray they get cancelled. Not by the other person — I pray for a *natural disaster*. A small one. Like a localized flood. Just enough water to make it socially acceptable to stay home. I'll check the weather app like I'm checking stock prices. "Come on, come on, give me a 40 percent chance of thunderstorms." And if it's sunny? I'm *furious*. At the sun. At God. "Really? This is what you're giving me?"

*(pause)*

The worst part is I'm the one who made the plans. I'm the one who said, "Hey, let's get dinner Thursday." And then Thursday comes and I'm like, "Who *said* that? Who was that person? They're not me. They were a different guy. He's gone now."

*(pause)*

I've also started having opinions about *sponges*. I'm in the kitchen holding a sponge thinking, "This is a bad sponge." And I mean it. I feel it in my chest. This sponge is letting me down. And I can't explain why. It's just a sponge. But I've decided it's a *bad* one, and I will not be using it. I'll use the other one. The good one. I don't know what makes it good. It just *is*.

*(pause)*

And the thing nobody tells you about getting older is that you don't get wiser. You just get more confident in your bad decisions. At 20, you make a dumb choice and you think, "Wow, that was dumb." At 34, you make the same dumb choice and you go, "Yeah. This is who I am now."

*(pause)*

Thank you, you've been a beautiful audience. I'm gonna go home and listen to a cantaloupe.

*(waves, exits)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Thanks, everybody.

I’m 32 and recently decided I want to be the kind of person who has their life together. That lasted four days. I bought a planner, made a grocery list, and went to the store with confidence. Then I got to the self-checkout machine, which is the only place in society where you are simultaneously trusted and treated like a criminal.

“Please wait for assistance.”

I’m standing there holding one banana like it’s evidence. The machine says, “Unexpected item in bagging area.” Ma’am, the unexpected item is my will to live.

Then I tried streaming services. I canceled three subscriptions last month because I wanted to save money. The app made me watch a 47-second video about how much it will miss me. It showed me my own viewing history.

“You haven’t watched this show since March.”

Yeah, because in March I still had hope. Now every time I open an app, it asks if I’d like to resume something I abandoned during a darker time in my life.

I also joined a gym. Not because I’m athletic, but because I saw a commercial with people running through fog and thought, “That looks efficient.” First day, I walk in, and every machine has a screen now. I didn’t ask for a television while I suffer. I want to stare at the wall and question my choices without distractions.

The treadmill offered me a workout plan, a heart-rate zone, and a podcast about entrepreneurship. I just wanted to walk at an incline and feel superior to the people stretching. I left after twelve minutes because the machine started congratulating me like I’d completed a marathon.

The worst part is the class schedule.

“Spin.”  
“Boxing.”  
“Yoga.”  
“Hot yoga.”

Why is it hot? Because lying on a mat pretending your hips are flexible wasn’t uncomfortable enough? I walked into a hot yoga class once and a woman in the corner was folded like a lawn chair. She looked peaceful. I looked like a golden retriever that had wandered into a sauna. I asked the instructor for modifications and she said, “Just breathe,” which is not a physical instruction.

But I keep going back, because adulthood is mostly just showing up to things you’re bad at and hoping nobody mentions it. I tried meal prepping last Sunday. Cut up chicken, rice, broccoli, put it in containers, felt like a CEO. By Wednesday I was eating shredded cheese over the sink like a raccoon with a credit score.

Still, small victories. I remembered my reusable bags. I canceled a subscription. I walked on the treadmill for nine minutes. And when the self-checkout yelled at me, I did not apologize. I stood there, silent, making eye contact with the little camera, until a teenager came over and rescued us both.

Thank you, you’ve been great.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Have you ever bought one of those robot vacuums? You know the ones. They look like a small, metallic moonlander that landed in your kitchen. You bring it home, you plug it in, and you feel a surge of productivity. You think, "I am going to be so organized." Then the machine starts making that sound. The beep. The warning. It's not cleaning. It's begging for help.

The first hour is just a horror movie. It's bumping into your couch legs. It's sensing the edge of the rug and deciding that's the end of the world. You sit there, watching it panic, and you feel bad. You actually apologize. "Oops, buddy, there's a leg." The machine doesn't care. It just keeps beeping. It's a robot with anxiety.

And then comes the charging. You have to put it on the dock. You have to make sure the cables are plugged in. If it doesn't charge, it won't move. It's not a tool, it's a dependent. I feel like I'm raising a child who just wants to nap and eat electricity. I bought this thing to save time, but now I'm spending time managing the battery life. I'm the parent, it's the toddler.

And don't get me started on the "Smart" features. You can set schedules. You can tell it to clean specific rooms. You can voice command it. "Hey, vacuum, go clean the living room." And it just sits there. Like it didn't understand the language. It's not smart. It's just a very expensive hamster wheel.

We live in a time where we buy machines to do things for us, and then we spend more time fixing the machines than doing the things. I bought a vacuum to clean my house. Now I'm cleaning the vacuum's battery port. I'm the one doing the work.

We're all just trying to keep up with the appliances. The toaster, the microwave, the robot. We think we're the masters, but really, we're just the keepers of the batteries. You know the app. You open it. It says "Cleaning in progress." But the little circle on the map is just spinning in place. It's not moving. It's just vibrating. It's a GPS that goes nowhere. You wait for the notification that says "Done." Then you look at the clock. It's been twenty minutes. You check again. "Cleaning in progress." You're not cleaning. You're just waiting for a notification that you're not actually doing anything.

So if you see my robot vacuum crying on the floor, don't worry. I'm there. I'm charging it. And I'm still waiting for the day I can just... sit down.

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’ve come to a realization about adulthood: none of us actually know what we’re doing. We’re just all really good at pretending we have a system.

Take the group dinner text. You know the one. Someone drops, “Hey, what do you want to eat?” And suddenly, five adults turn into a parliamentary session. You get the classic, “I’m easy, whatever you want!” Which is a lie. Nobody is easy. “Easy” is just a placeholder for “I will quietly reject your first suggestion and then pretend I’m flexible.”

So you throw out a place. Immediately, someone says, “Oh, I had that last week.” Another person says, “Is it too loud?” A third person asks if they have vegetarian options, even though nobody’s vegetarian, they just want to keep the menu open. You’re not picking dinner anymore. You’re trying to pass a bill through a fractious senate. And the whole time, the original person who asked is just sitting there, watching the thread like it’s a live wire.

Finally, someone suggests a place that’s literally across the street from half the group. And everyone’s like, “Yeah, that works!” Not because it’s great. Because it’s the first option that didn’t require a spreadsheet. We don’t actually care about the food. We care about reaching a consensus so we can stop performing decision-making.

And it’s not just dinner. It’s everything. I bought a coffee maker last month. Not a complicated one. Just a drip machine with a water tank and a button. I spent forty minutes reading the manual like it was a lease agreement. There was a troubleshooting section that said, “If the brew is weak, check the grind size.” I don’t have a grind size. I have pre-ground coffee from a bag that says “medium roast” like it’s a personality trait. I followed the instructions, and the machine made a sound like it was reconsidering its life choices. I just stood there, holding a paper filter, wondering when “making coffee” became a skill that requires a warranty.

We’ve built a world that promises convenience, but delivers complexity with a customer service number. And the worst part is how we talk about it. We say things like, “It should be simple,” like simplicity is a moral obligation. It’s not. Sometimes a door has a handle on both sides because the architect wanted you to feel options. Sometimes a remote has sixty buttons because someone thought you might want to switch inputs while also adjusting the bass and checking the weather.

Even texting has turned into a tactical exercise. You type something. You delete it. You type it again. You stare at the three dots appear, disappear, appear again. You’re not having a conversation. You’re negotiating terms. “Hey, how’s it going?” “Good, you?” That’s not a message. That’s a ceasefire.

But here’s the thing that actually keeps me going: we’re all faking the same level of confidence. The person who looks like they have their life together is probably standing in their kitchen at 11 p.m., holding a measuring cup, Googling “how much rice is too much rice.” We’re not falling behind. We’re just all improvising in the same room, hoping nobody asks us to run the projector.

question: standup-routine

content:
**"The Optimization"**

*(walks to mic, adjusts it, takes a breath)*

I used to think being an adult was hard. Now I'm not sure it's even a thing anymore. I think we just got... *optimized.*

I was at the grocery store last week. I walked up to the cereal aisle, and I'm standing there, just *vibing.* I'm not picking a brand. I'm just... existing. And then some guy next to me pulls out a little app and scans every box on the shelf. And he's like, "Oh, this one's got a lower glycemic index, but this one has a better protein-to-fiber ratio, so if I'm optimizing for my Tuesday, I'll take this one."

And I'm just *staring.* It's 11 a.m. on a Saturday. He's optimizing his *Tuesday.*

And it's not even just food. It's *everything.* I went to a restaurant last month and I ordered the soup. Just soup. And the server, she's got this little tablet, and she's like, "Would you like to *build* your soup experience?" And I'm like, "No, I'd like the soup." And she's like, "Okay! Great. And are you *pairing* that with a palate-cleansing crouton?" And I said, "I am eating the soup." And she wrote that down. I don't know what that means. I don't know what "I am eating the soup" means as a *data point.*

And the worst part is — and I say this with love — we *let* them do this to us. I have a fitness app that told me yesterday that I "missed my step goal." I *missed* it. I was in a meeting. I was *sitting.* I wasn't trying to walk a mile. I was trying to not get fired. And the app said, "You're 847 steps from your goal. You can earn a badge." I'm forty-three years old. I want a *badge* for sitting in a conference room. I want a little digital confetti for *not dying.*

And we've even optimized *our feelings.* I was on the train last night, and some guy was on his phone, and he's got this app that's like, "How are you feeling right now? Rate your anxiety from one to ten." And he's sitting there, on the 8:15 train to work, and he's *rating his anxiety.* And then he gets a little chart. A *line graph.* Of his sadness. And he's like, "Oh, my anxiety peaked at 7:42. Interesting."

And I just thought: the human being who invented the *concept* of being sad would not be sitting on a train, *graphing* it.

*(pause)*

And I think that's the thing. We used to just *be* sad. You'd be sad, and you'd be sad, and then you'd be less sad. No app. No badge. No "you've achieved 60% of your sadness quota." Just... the feeling. And then it wasn't.

*(beat)*

I'm not saying we should throw out our phones. I'm saying... I just want to eat the soup. And I want to be sad on a Tuesday, with no *optimization.* And if I walk less than eight thousand steps, I want to be *annoyed,* not *gamified.*

I just want to be a person who is *slightly* behind on his goals.

*(to the mic, softer)*

...Can I get a soup?

*(drops the mic, walks off)*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
I’m at the age where “a big weekend” means I went to two stores.

Not two stores in the same shopping center. Two separate stores. Moved the car and everything.

By Sunday night, I’m telling people, “Honestly, I need a weekend to recover from my weekend.”

I’ve started making to-do lists, which is a great way to move anxiety out of your head and onto a piece of paper.

Now it’s official. Now the anxiety has bullet points.

I put easy stuff on there so I can build momentum. “Wake up.” Done. “Have coffee.” Absolutely.

Then I get ambitious: “Resolve insurance issue.”

That stays on the list until the paper becomes a historical document.

---

Every company says, “You can do everything through our app.”

No, I can do everything *except the thing I need to do*.

I can change my profile photo. I can choose a theme. I can see a cheerful animation of a wallet.

But to cancel something, I have to call a man who works Tuesdays during an eclipse.

And before he helps me, he needs to know why I’m leaving.

Why is canceling a subscription the only breakup where the other person gets to assign homework?

“Have you considered our premium plan?”

I haven’t considered your regular plan since February. That’s the problem.

---

I bought a smartwatch to improve my health.

Mostly, it criticizes me with the confidence of something that doesn’t have knees.

“Time to stand!”

I’m on a bus.

“Time to stand!”

We’re going around a corner. Are you trying to improve my circulation or get my wallet?

Then it tells me I slept badly. I know. I was there.

I don’t need a graph of my suffering.

It gives me a sleep score of 43. Great. Now I’m tired *and* I failed.

---

The hardest part of adulthood is deciding what to eat every single day.

As a kid, I thought adults had a system. Turns out the system is opening the fridge, staring into it, and hoping your personality changes.

I’ll look at some spinach and think, “That belongs to the person I was when I bought it.”

That person had plans.

That person was going to make bowls.

Current me is eating crackers over the sink because getting a plate involved feels like making a commitment.

---

And somehow, despite all this, people still ask, “Where do you see yourself in five years?”

Five years?

I bought bananas this morning and I can’t confidently tell you how that’s going to end.

Ask me something realistic.

“Do you think you’ll move the laundry from the washer to the dryer?”

Yes.

Not immediately. Let’s not turn this into pressure.

But it’s on the list.

content:
**"Slightly Sentient" — A 3-Minute Stand-Up Routine**

---

Hey everybody! How's it going? Good to be here.

So I went grocery shopping the other day. I go in with a plan. I have a list. I have a system. I'm basically a military operation. *Get in. Get the avocados. Get out.*

But then I hit the cereal aisle, and suddenly I'm having an existential crisis. Do I want something healthy? Do I want something that turns my milk purple? Why is there a cereal that's just clusters of what appears to be gravel? Who's buying this? Who's eating gravel cereal going, *"Mmm, reminds me of my morning jog through a quarry."*

I stood there for ten minutes. That's longer than some of my relationships.

And then — the self-checkout. Oh, the self-checkout. That machine is basically a boss that just yells at you. *"Unexpected item in the bagging area."* Yeah, that's my dignity. I put it there by accident. I didn't plan on losing it at 2 PM on a Tuesday, but here we are.

*(beat)*

So I get home and decide I'm going to cook. I'm going to *be* an adult. I buy vegetables — actual vegetables — and I stare at a bell pepper on the counter like it personally insulted me. What am I supposed to do with you? You're not an apple. You're not a potato. You're just a pepper with no sense of purpose.

I Googled a recipe. The recipe said *"julienne the vegetables."* Julienne? That sounds like a French woman's name. That's not a cooking instruction, that's a guest list.

*(beat)*

Anyway, I chopped the vegetables badly. A raccoon with a grudge could've done better. But I cooked the whole thing. It was... edible. Barely. My smoke detector went off — and that was the first time anything in my kitchen has been that *enthusiastic* about my cooking.

Then I crashed on the couch. Because that's the reward. I'm an adult now. I bought groceries. I cooked a meal. And now I get to lie horizontally and stare at the ceiling until I forget why I got up.

That's my bedtime routine, by the way. I don't even go to bed. I just... fade into the furniture.

You know what — I'm not a functioning adult. I'm a slightly sentient pile of receipts and avocado anxiety.

Thank you, you've been a great audience!

---

*Approximate delivery time: ~3 minutes with natural pauses and laughter beats.*

question: standup-routine

content:
**"The Upgrade Treadmill"**

*[Walks on stage, adjusts mic]*

So I got a smartwatch. You know, one of those fitness trackers? And the first thing it tells me is my heart rate is too high. I'm like, "It's a WATCH. You're not supposed to judge me, you're supposed to tell me the TIME."

It's like having a very fit friend who follows you everywhere. "Hey, you sat down. That's... not great. Your heart rate dropped. Are you DYING? Should I call someone?"

I went for a walk. The watch said, "Good job! You took 47 steps!" I said, "I walked to my mailbox. That's not exercise, that's... checking if the mailman has finally given up on me."

*[Mimes checking watch]*

And the sleep tracking. Oh my God. It's like, "You were in bed for eight hours but only got six hours of sleep." I was IN BED. What else do you want from me? I was unconscious! You think I was up doing crimes? I was ASLEEP. That's the whole point of a bed!

But here's the thing that really gets me. My watch knows when I'm stressed. It buzzes: "Breathe. Your heart rate is elevated." I'm like, "I KNOW. THAT'S WHY I'M STRESSED. You're not helping. You're a circle. You're literally a circle on my wrist telling me to breathe. I've been breathing since 1987. I think I've got it."

*[Beat]*

I tried to return it. The guy at the store said, "But sir, it tracks your steps!" I said, "I have legs. I can feel them. They've been attached to me my whole life. If they fall off, I'll know. That's not a feature, that's just... being a person."

And the worst part? Now I'm competitive with myself. Yesterday I walked to the fridge. The watch said, "New record! Most steps in a 24-hour period!" I said, "That's sad. That's SO sad. I used to run marathons. Now my personal best is... dairy."

*[Looks at watch]*

My resting heart rate is now 58. Used to be 72. I'm getting fitter by doing absolutely nothing. I'm basically a professional athlete. I should be on a Wheaties box. "The Man Who Sat Still."

*[Checks watch again, annoyed]*

It just told me to stand up. I'm literally standing. ON A STAGE. IN FRONT OF PEOPLE. This is the most standing I've ever done.

*[Exhales, smiles]*

Thanks, you've been great. Try the veal.

*[Walks off, watch buzzes]*

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
**"My Smart Fridge Judges Me"**

So I got a smart fridge. Everybody told me I needed one. "It'll tell you when you're out of milk!" Great. I didn't know I needed a fridge with a *notification system.* I just wanted cold food.

Now my refrigerator has a screen on the door, and it's basically a tiny, cold, silent roommate who keeps score.

I opened it at two in the morning last week, and it displayed a message: "Looks like you're having a snack." Excuse me? I didn't ask for your opinion. I'm a grown man. I'm allowed to eat a sleeve of Oreos standing up in the dark like a raccoon.

And it's not just the fridge. My whole house is smart now. I have a smart speaker. I asked it to play some relaxing music, and it said, "Playing relaxing playlist, based on your recent activity." What recent activity? I cried to a Phil Collins song for forty minutes on Tuesday. That's not a playlist, that's a cry for help, and you just lean into it?

My thermostat learned my schedule. Which would be great, except it learned that I leave the house at 8:15 and come back at 6:30, and now it's decided I'm an absentee landlord of my own life. It keeps the house at sixty-two degrees, and when I get home, I'm standing in the kitchen in a parka, going, "Hello? Is anybody paying attention to me?"

The worst part is my doorbell camera. It sends me an alert every time something moves. Leaves. Shadows. A pigeon once. So I'm getting notifications on my phone all day: "Motion detected at front door." And I'm at work, sweating, thinking, is it a burglar? Is it a stray cat? And it turns out it's the wind again. The wind is a menace, and the camera doesn't seem to think it's a threat, but it wants me to know about it every eleven minutes.

I wanted technology to make my life easier. Instead I have five devices in my house that all have opinions, and none of them agree with each other. My speaker plays jazz, my lights turn purple at random, and my fridge is texting my phone to say, "You're low on eggs," in the exact tone my mother used.

So if you're thinking about upgrading, my advice is simple. Just buy a regular fridge. Keep your secrets. Let the wind move the leaves in peace.

Also, I'm out of milk again, and I didn't hear about it from the fridge, which means it's disappointed in me. Thank you, you're a wonderful audience. Goodnight.

question: standup-routine

content:
I realized recently that I’m in my thirties and I have no idea how money works. I just... pay it. That’s my entire financial strategy. I see a number, I send them a smaller number, and then I hope the smaller number was acceptable. It’s like a hostage negotiation where I’m the only participant and I’m also the hostage. I don’t know what my interest rate is. I don’t want to know. I think if I learned it, I’d have to move to the woods and start a podcast about foraging. I signed a mortgage once. The lawyer said “fixed rate” and I said “I love that, please, give me that” and then I gave him my social security number and a drawing of a bird I did with my non-dominant hand.

At work, I’ve become an expert in the thumbs up emoji. That’s my entire professional contribution. Someone sends me a spreadsheet, I hit thumbs up. I don’t open it. I don’t know what’s in it. Could be quarterly projections, could be a recipe for lasagna. I’m saying yes to both. Because in the modern workplace, confidence is way more important than literacy. I’ve watched guys get promoted because they said “let’s circle back on that” with enough conviction. Meanwhile, I’m over here actually circling back, like an idiot, doing the work. I’ll be in a meeting and someone will say “can you take point on that?” and I’ll say “absolutely” and then spend the next hour in the supply closet trying to figure out what “that” was. It’s not even a supply closet. It’s a closet with a printer in it. But mostly I’m in there whispering “what did I promise them.”

And nobody teaches you the important stuff. I can analyze symbolism in 19th century novels, but I don’t know if I’m supposed to wash the inside of my jeans. Is that a thing? Do you turn them inside out? I’ve been washing them right-side out this whole time. Maybe that’s why my life is falling apart. Maybe the denim is holding onto trauma. I keep a fire extinguisher in my kitchen that I’ve never opened. It’s just there for moral support. It’s like “I believe in you, kitchen.” Same with the first aid kit. Band-aids from 2019. If I get a cut now, I’m using a napkin and prayer.

My favorite is when people say “you have to read the terms and conditions.” No, I don’t. That’s why it’s called terms and conditions. I didn’t write them. I don’t know what a cookie is. I thought that was a snack until I was twenty-six. Now there are little banners on every website asking about my “data privacy preferences.” I don’t have preferences. I have hope. And maybe a small amount of fear. Click accept. Just let me look up the weather. Every app wants to know my location. Why? I’m going to the grocery store. I’m not doing anything interesting. I’m buying lettuce and hiding it behind the chips so my roommates think I’m healthy. That’s my location. That’s my data. Follow me. I dare you.

The truth is, we’re all just guessing. I read that astronauts still use duct tape on the space station. If the smartest people in the world, with billions of dollars and physics degrees, are up there going “eh, tape it,” then I think I’m doing okay. I don’t know what I’m doing, but neither do they. And they’re in space. So... I’m basically an astronaut. Just with more debt and less zero gravity. Thank you, you’ve been great.

content:
Sure, here’s a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that steers clear of puns:

---

**[Walks on stage, adjusts mic, surveys the crowd]**

Hey, how’s everyone doing tonight? Yeah? Good. I’m glad you’re here. I just want to start by saying... I’m not a “cool” person. I’ve tried, but I’m not. Like, I’m the kind of person who says “you too” at the wrong time. You ever do that? The waiter’s like, “Enjoy your meal,” and I’m like, “You too!”—as if he’s gonna sit down with a plate of spaghetti in the kitchen. Now I can never go back to Olive Garden. It’s done.

And speaking of eating out—why do restaurants give you such a big show about the water options? “Would you like still, sparkling, or tap?” Like, calm down, I just want it cold and wet. I’m not pairing it with a ’97 Bordeaux. And then there’s always that one friend who’s like, “Actually, could I get room temperature water?” Room temperature water! What are you, a medieval king? Should I serve it to you in a goblet? 

I’ve been trying to work on myself lately. You know, self-care. I downloaded one of those meditation apps, right? But it’s so passive-aggressive. I missed a session once, and the notification popped up like, “We noticed you haven’t meditated today. Everything okay?” Like, no, everything’s not okay, Calm. I’m stressed, that’s why I downloaded you! Now I’m just stressed *and* ashamed—good job.

Oh, and the worst is when the app tries to “motivate” you. It’s like, “Consistency is key. Successful people meditate every day.” Okay, well, successful people also own yachts, and I’m out here debating if I can afford guac at Chipotle. Let’s set the bar a little lower, shall we?

And let’s talk about grocery stores for a second. Why do they always put the most embarrassing items on sale? Like, I’ll go in for some milk, and the cashier’s like, “Did you know hemorrhoid cream is buy one, get one free?” And now I have to be like, “Uh, yeah, I’m good on that...for now.” But then you *do* buy it because who’s passing up a deal like that? Now you’re walking out of the store with two tubes of shame and no milk.

Oh, and self-checkout? A nightmare. Every time, without fail, the machine screams, “Unexpected item in the bagging area!” Unexpected? It’s a loaf of bread. What were you expecting, a flamingo? And then the attendant has to come over, swipe a card, and press a bunch of buttons like they’re defusing a bomb. I’m just standing there like, “I just wanted to buy Pop-Tarts, I didn’t sign up for this level of tension.”

But you know what? I’ve realized life is just a series of awkward moments strung together—and that’s fine. Because if you can’t laugh at yourself...don’t worry, I will.

**[Pauses, smiles, raises hand for a wave]**

You guys have been great! Thanks so much—I’m off to argue with a meditation app. Have a good night!

**[Walks off stage]**

--- 

Hope that gave you a chuckle!

question: standup-routine
prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Hey everyone! Great to be here! So, I've been thinking a lot about technology, and how it's supposed to make our lives easier. But sometimes, I feel like it just gives us a whole new set of problems. Like, remember when a phone was just a phone? Now it's my camera, my GPS, my fitness tracker... I swear, one day I'll just ask it to make me a coffee and it won't be surprised.

And the passwords! We’re supposed to remember like 100 different passwords. I changed all my passwords to 'incorrect' because if I forget, my computer will say, "Your password is incorrect." Problem-solving at its best, right?

And the updates, oh the updates! My phone just asked me to update it again. The update description says, "Bug fixes and improvements." I feel like that's just tech code for "We messed something up last time, and we're trying to fix it without admitting it."

Speaking of technology, have you seen these new smart homes? Everything's connected. I can control my lights, my thermostat, even my fridge, from my phone. It sounds convenient until you're halfway around the world and you get a notification: "Your fridge door is open." Great, now I can panic about my electricity bill in two different time zones!

And fitness trackers. They’re like that one friend who’s always a little too honest. "Hey, you've only walked 500 steps today." Thanks, Fitbit. Now I feel like a lazy slob in high definition.

I tried talking back to my fitness tracker. I said, "Oh yeah? Well, you haven't moved at all!" It didn’t respond. I guess some battles you just can't win.

And online dating! That's another tech marvel. My friend told me he's "dating someone from another country." Turns out he's just in a very committed relationship with his laptop. Really, if you're swiping on your phone more than you're actually going out, you're not dating online, you're just collecting matches like they're Pokémon.

Have you tried watching TV with your parents recently? Every show has to be paused every five minutes to explain what's going on. "Who's that?" "Mom, that's the same guy as before, he just put on a hat."

And what's with smart TVs that are smarter than you? I push one wrong button, and suddenly I'm in the settings menu trying to figure out how to get back to Netflix. I'm like, "I just wanted to change the volume, and now I’m programming the satellite coordinates!"

Anyway, I'm still figuring out all this tech. But hey, if all else fails, just turn it off and then on again, right? That’s the ultimate tech advice. Thank you, everyone! You've been a fantastic crowd!

prompt: Write a 3-minute stand-up comedy routine that isn't based on puns.
content:
Good evening! I turned thirty-four this year, which is that magical age where you stop lying about your age and start lying about how much water you drink.

My doctor asked, "How much water do you drink a day?" And I said, "Probably eight glasses." I drink *maybe* one glass, and that's only if I accidentally swallow while brushing my teeth. The rest of the day I'm just running on coffee and hope.

I tried to become a responsible adult this year. I bought a plant. Not a fake one, a real one. The lady at the store said, "This one is impossible to kill." Two weeks later it looked like it had given up on purpose. I was watering it, talking to it, moving it toward the sunlight like I was presenting it to the gods. Meanwhile, there's a weed growing out of a crack in the sidewalk outside my apartment with zero help from anyone, just thriving out of spite.

So I decided to get healthier in other ways. I went to the grocery store and used the self-checkout, which is a lie, because there's always an employee standing right there watching you do their job badly.

That machine does not trust me at all. I scan one banana and it goes, "Please place the item in the bagging area." I DID. It's right there. Then it stops everything: "Attendant has been notified." Now the whole store is looking at me like I tried to steal a banana. The attendant walks over, doesn't even look at my bags, just types in a secret code like she's defusing a bomb, and walks away. I didn't get arrested, but I did get humbled by a piece of fruit.

After that I thought, okay, maybe I need the gym. I signed up in January like everyone else. For the first week, I had to wait twenty minutes for a treadmill because the whole city suddenly decided to become athletes. By February, it was empty. By March, I was part of the problem.

The worst part of the gym isn't even working out. It's that one guy who treats the mirror like it's a photo shoot. He's not exercising, he's just standing there flexing and nodding at himself, like, "Yep. Still me." I caught myself doing the same thing after doing *four* push-ups. Four. I was in the mirror like I had just won a championship.

At home, I tried to be handy. I ordered a bookshelf and thought, "How hard can this be? It's just rectangles." Six hours later I had built something that leaned. Not a little lean — it leaned like it was tired. I put one book on it and the whole thing sighed. I had three screws left over. Three. The instructions never mentioned extra screws. So either I invented a more efficient bookshelf, or that thing is a trap waiting for a victim.

And now I understand why adults are always tired. It's not work. It's going to bed. When I was a kid, I fell asleep instantly. Now I lie down and my brain goes, "Hey, remember that awkward thing you said in 2014? Let's go over that again in detail. Also, did you lock the door? You did, but what if you only *think* you did?"

So I get up, check the door, get back in bed, and now I'm wide awake thinking about the plant. Is it thirsty? Am I thirsty? Maybe me and the plant have the same problem. We're both just sitting near a window, not drinking enough water, hoping someone else figures it out.

So tomorrow, we're both getting eight glasses. Well — he'll get one. I'll get coffee. But it's the thought that counts.

Thank you, you've been great!

content:
**Title:** The Convenience Trap
**Target Time:** Approx. 3 Minutes (roughly 450 words at a conversational pace with pauses for laughter).

**(Walks out, adjusts the mic, smiles at the crowd)**

Thank you, guys. It’s great to be here. Looking around, we all look like functioning adults. We put on pants, we left the house. That’s a massive victory in 2024. 

Because I feel like the hardest part of being an adult right now is that everything is designed to be "convenient," which somehow just makes me angrier. Like the self-checkout machine at the grocery store. Whose idea was it to turn the customer into an unpaid trainee? 

*(Pause)*

I walk in just wanting to buy toothpaste and a single banana. Suddenly I’m on the clock for Kroger. And the machine is the worst boss I’ve ever had. It is so aggressive. You scan one item, and before the beep even finishes, the robot voice is yelling at you: *"PLACE THE ITEM IN THE BAGGING AREA."* 

I’m moving as fast as I can, Sharon! Give me a second! 

And God forbid you bring your own bag. You put a reusable tote down and the machine has a full-blown panic attack. *"UNEXPECTED ITEM IN BAGGING AREA. HELP IS ON THE WAY."* The light starts flashing red. Now I’m standing there looking like I’m trying to hot-wire a Honda Civic, waiting for a seventeen-year-old named Kyle to walk over, sigh at me, and swipe his little badge of forgiveness. 

*(Laughs, shakes head)*

So, to avoid Kyle, I just stay home and order food. Which is the darkest financial trap we have all agreed to ignore. Have you looked at the math on food delivery apps lately? It makes no sense. You want a twelve-dollar burrito. Great. By the time you hit "checkout," that burrito is forty-seven dollars. 

How? There’s the delivery fee, the service fee, the local regulatory fee, the "small order" fee—which is just the app bullying you for not being a glutton—and the tip. I am essentially financing a Honda Accord for a burrito. 

And the worst part is the map. Why do they give us a live GPS tracker of the driver? We don't need that level of power! Ten years ago, you ordered a pizza, and it showed up when it showed up. Now, I’m sitting in my underwear in the dark, staring at my phone like I’m a CIA director tracking a drone strike in the Middle East. 

*(Holds hand up like looking at a phone, squinting intensely)*

"Wait a minute. Why is Brendon turning left on 4th Street? The restaurant is on 5th. Brendon has gone rogue! Abort mission, he's in a cul-de-sac, MY FRIES ARE GETTING COLD!"

It’s turning us into monsters. And you can't even make direct eye contact with Brendon when he gets there. The app literally has a default setting that says, "Leave at door." We’ve turned the basic human transaction of receiving sustenance into a hostage exchange. 

*(Mimes peeking through blinds)*

I stand behind my front door, breathing heavily, looking through the little peephole. Just waiting for Brendon to put the bag down and drive away, because God forbid he sees the creature that paid forty-seven dollars for lukewarm Taco Bell. As soon as his taillights disappear, I crack the door open, snatch the bag like a raccoon with a credit score, and drag it into my cave. 

That’s peak civilization, guys. We used to hunt mammoths, and now I’m terrified to make eye contact with a guy in a Prius. 

You guys have been awesome, thank you so much, have a great night! 

**(Waves, puts mic back in the stand, walks off)**
